abstract: Second order properties of cost functions for recurrent networks are investigated. We analyze a layered fully recurrent architecture, the virtue of this architecture is that it features the conventional feedforward architecture as a special case. A detailed description of recursive computation of the full Hessian of the network cost function is provided. We discuss the possibility of invoking simplifying approximations of the Hessian and show how weight decays iron the cost function and thereby greatly assist training . We present tentative pruning results, using Hassibi et al.'s Optimal Brain Surgeon, demonstrating that recurrent networks can construct an efficient internal memory.

paragraphs: This paper studies the curvature of cost functions used to train recurrent neural networks. It analyzes a layered, fully recurrent architecture that includes conventional feedforward networks as a special case. This provides a framework for examining how recurrent connections affect the optimization problem while retaining a connection to feedforward architectures.

The authors describe a recursive computation of the full Hessian, the matrix that records second-order changes in the cost function with respect to weights. They also discuss simplifying approximations. Their analysis shows how weight decay can smooth the cost function and substantially assist training, linking a regularization mechanism to the geometry of optimization.

The paper then presents tentative pruning results using Optimal Brain Surgeon. These results demonstrate that recurrent networks can construct an efficient internal memory. The contribution combines mathematical machinery for studying recurrent-network curvature with an initial application to removing weights, connecting the organization of a network's parameters to the compactness of the memory it develops.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes recurrent-network cost curvature, explains how weight decay assists training, and presents tentative pruning results for efficient internal memory.

title: Recurrent Networks: Second Order Properties and Pruning

paragraphs: SEEMORE is a neurally inspired system for recognizing familiar objects despite changes in viewing angle, distance, and nonrigid shape. Its database contains 100 objects spanning rigid, flexible, articulated, statistical, and complex examples. This range makes recognition involve more than matching a single unchanging shape from a fixed viewpoint.

The system uses 102 color and shape feature channels within a simple feedforward architecture. With a nearest-neighbor classifier, it correctly identifies 97% of 600 previously unseen test views, comprising six views of each object. Chance performance is 1%. The images are color video views presenting objects individually.

Comparable performance is reported for the subset of 15 nonrigid objects, supporting recognition across changes that go beyond rigid viewpoint transformations. The system's generalization also reveals natural category structure that was not explicitly encoded in the input feature dimensions. The findings show how combining multiple visual cues can support recognition of known objects and produce meaningful similarities among them.
summary.tldr: SEEMORE combines color and shape cues to recognize 100 known objects with 97% accuracy across 600 novel views.

title: SEEMORE: A View-Based Approach to 3-D Object Recognition Using Multiple Visual Cues

The constructive algorithm pro(cid:173) posed here enables large hierarchies consisting of several hundred experts to be trained effectively. We show that HME's trained by our automatic growing procedure yield better generalization per(cid:173) formance than traditional static and balanced hierarchies. Eval(cid:173) uation of the algorithm is performed (1) on vowel classification and (2) within a hybrid version of the JANUS r9] speech recog(cid:173) nition system using a subset of the Switchboard large-vocabulary speaker-independent continuous speech recognition database.

paragraphs: A hierarchical mixture of experts organizes multiple predictors into a hierarchy. Its structure determines how many experts are available and how they are arranged. This paper treats that structure as something to adapt during learning, proposing an automatic procedure that both grows the hierarchy and prunes it.

The constructive approach makes it possible to train large hierarchies containing several hundred experts effectively. Growth and pruning provide a way to change the model’s organization instead of committing in advance to a fixed, balanced structure. This makes the choice of architecture part of the learning procedure and provides a practical route to larger expert systems.

The authors evaluate the method on vowel classification and within a hybrid JANUS speech recognizer using a subset of the Switchboard database. They report better generalization than traditional static, balanced hierarchies. The finding supports the idea that how experts are organized matters alongside their individual training: an automatically developed hierarchy can predict new examples better than the fixed structures used in these comparisons.
summary.tldr: Automatically growing and pruning expert hierarchies enables large models and improves generalization over fixed, balanced structures.

title: Adaptively Growing Hierarchical Mixtures of Experts

abstract: We present an algorithm which compensates for the mismatches between characteristics of real-world problems and assumptions of independent component analysis algorithm. To provide additional information to the ICA network, we incorporate top-down selec(cid:173) tive attention. An MLP classifier is added to the separated signal channel and the error of the classifier is backpropagated to the ICA network. This backpropagation process results in estimation of expected ICA output signal for the top-down attention. Then, the unmixing matrix is retrained according to a new cost function representing the backpropagated error as well as independence. It modifies the density of recovered signals to the density appropriate for classification. For noisy speech signal recorded in real environ(cid:173) ments, the algorithm improved the recognition performance and showed robustness against parametric changes.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis separates signals using assumptions that may not match real-world recordings. This paper introduces an algorithm that supplements those assumptions with information from the recognition task. Its form of top-down selective attention lets a classifier influence the signals recovered by the ICA network.

The method adds a multilayer perceptron classifier to a separated signal channel and sends the classifier's error backward through the ICA network. This feedback estimates an expected ICA output for attention. The unmixing matrix is then retrained with a cost function that accounts for both the classification error and independence, connecting signal separation directly to what the recognizer needs.

The resulting adjustment changes the distribution of recovered signals toward one suitable for classification. On noisy speech recorded in real environments, the authors report improved recognition and robustness to parameter changes. The stated finding supports using task feedback to compensate for mismatches in ICA assumptions, with the separation stage and recognition stage influencing one another through the learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Feeding speech-classifier errors back into ICA improved recognition of real noisy recordings and robustness to parameter changes.

title: Combining ICA and Top-Down Attention for Robust Speech Recognition

abstract: This article presents a Support Vector Machine (SVM) like learning sys- tem to handle multi-label problems. Such problems are usually decom- posed into many two-class problems but the expressive power of such a system can be weak [5, 7]. We explore a new direct approach. It is based on a large margin ranking system that shares a lot of common proper- ties with SVMs. We tested it on a Yeast gene functional classiﬁcation problem with positive results.
originalAbstract: This article presents a Support Vector Machine (SVM) like learning sys- tem to handle multi-label problems. Such problems are usually decom- posed into many two-class problems but the expressive power of such a system can be weak [5, 7]. We explore a new direct approach. It is based on a large margin ranking system that shares a lot of common proper- ties with SVMs. We tested it on a Yeast gene functional classiﬁcation problem with positive results.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification tasks in which one example can belong to several categories. Its motivating application is assigning functions to yeast genes. The authors argue that the usual strategy of breaking a multilabel problem into many separate binary decisions can have limited expressive power, motivating a method that handles the labeling problem more directly.

Their proposed learning system uses large-margin ranking and shares several properties with support vector machines. The central change is to organize learning around ranking labels, rather than treating every category decision as a separate two-class problem. This gives the method a way to address the relative ordering of labels within a common learning formulation.

The authors report positive results on yeast gene functional classification. That finding supports the usefulness of their direct ranking approach in the stated application. The contribution is a different formulation of multilabel learning: it brings the large-margin perspective associated with SVMs to a setting where a single exclusive class assignment is insufficient.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes an SVM-like large-margin ranking method for multilabel classification and reports positive results on yeast gene functions.

title: A kernel method for multi-labelled classification

abstract: Motivated by our recent work on rooted tree matching, in this paper we provide a solution to the problem of matching two free (i.e., unrooted) trees by constructing an association graph whose maximal cliques are in one-to-one correspondence with maximal common subtrees. We then solve the problem using simple replicator dynamics from evolutionary game theory. Experiments on hundreds of uniformly random trees are presented. The results are impressive: despite the inherent inability of these simple dynamics to escape from local optima, they always returned a globally optimal solution.
originalAbstract: Motivated by our recent work on rooted tree matching, in this paper we provide a solution to the problem of matching two free (i.e., unrooted) trees by constructing an association graph whose maximal cliques are in one-to-one correspondence with maximal common subtrees. We then solve the problem using simple replicator dynamics from evolutionary game theory. Experiments on hundreds of uniformly random trees are presented. The results are impressive: despite the inherent inability of these simple dynamics to escape from local optima, they always returned a globally optimal solution.

paragraphs: The paper studies matching two trees that have no designated root. It approaches the task by constructing an association graph that expresses possible correspondences between the trees. This changes the representation of the matching problem so that graph structure can be used to identify subtrees shared by the two inputs.

The key construction gives a one-to-one correspondence between maximal cliques in the association graph and maximal common subtrees. A maximal solution cannot simply be extended, although that does not by itself make it globally largest. The authors then use simple replicator dynamics from evolutionary game theory to search for solutions in this graph-based formulation.

Experiments cover hundreds of uniformly random trees. In those experiments, the dynamics always returned a globally optimal solution. This is a strong empirical result because the dynamics cannot escape local optima. The paper therefore combines a precise structural correspondence with encouraging optimization behavior, while its reported success on the tested trees does not establish a universal global-optimality guarantee.
summary.tldr: An association-graph formulation and replicator dynamics found globally optimal unrooted-tree matches in every reported random-tree experiment.

title: Matching Free Trees with Replicator Equations

abstract: We investigate the generalization performance of some learning prob- lems in Hilbert function Spaces. We introduce a concept of scale- sensitive effective data dimension, and show that it characterizes the con- vergence rate of the underlying learning problem. Using this concept, we can naturally extend results for parametric estimation problems in ﬁnite dimensional spaces to non-parametric kernel learning methods. We de- rive upper bounds on the generalization performance and show that the resulting convergent rates are optimal under various circumstances.
originalAbstract: We investigate the generalization performance of some learning prob- lems in Hilbert function Spaces. We introduce a concept of scale- sensitive effective data dimension, and show that it characterizes the con- vergence rate of the underlying learning problem. Using this concept, we can naturally extend results for parametric estimation problems in ﬁnite dimensional spaces to non-parametric kernel learning methods. We de- rive upper bounds on the generalization performance and show that the resulting convergent rates are optimal under various circumstances.

paragraphs: The paper studies how well certain learning methods in Hilbert function spaces generalize beyond their training data. These spaces provide the setting for the kernel learning problems considered. The authors introduce a scale-sensitive effective data dimension to describe the complexity relevant to learning, rather than relying only on the formal dimension of the surrounding space.

They show that this effective dimension characterizes the convergence rate of the underlying learning problem. In practical terms, the concept connects the relevant complexity of the data with how quickly learning improves as information accumulates. Its scale sensitivity means that complexity is considered at the level relevant to the analysis, rather than treated as one fixed dimension.

This framework extends results from finite-dimensional parametric estimation to nonparametric kernel methods. The authors derive upper bounds on generalization performance and show that the resulting convergence rates are optimal under various circumstances. The optimality claim is conditional on those circumstances, while the broader contribution is a shared language for analyzing these different learning settings.
summary.tldr: Scale-sensitive effective dimension characterizes convergence in kernel learning and yields generalization bounds with optimal rates under various conditions.

title: Effective Dimension and Generalization of Kernel Learning

abstract: Certain simple images are known to trigger a percept of trans- parency: the input image I is perceived as the sum of two images I(x; y) = I1(x; y) + I2(x; y). This percept is puzzling. First, why do we choose the \more complicated" description with two images rather than the \simpler" explanation I(x; y) = I1(x; y) + 0 ? Sec- ond, given the inﬂnite number of ways to express I as a sum of two images, how do we compute the \best" decomposition ? Here we suggest that transparency is the rational percept of a sys- tem that is adapted to the statistics of natural scenes. We present a probabilistic model of images based on the qualitative statistics of derivative ﬂlters and \corner detectors" in natural scenes and use this model to ﬂnd the most probable decomposition of a novel image. The optimization is performed using loopy belief propa- gation. We show that our model computes perceptually \correct" decompositions on synthetic images and discuss its application to real images.

This percept is puzzling. First, why do we choose the \more complicated" description with two images rather than the \simpler" explanation I(x; y) = I1(x; y) + 0 ? Sec- ond, given the inﬂnite number of ways to express I as a sum of two images, how do we compute the \best" decomposition ? Here we suggest that transparency is the rational percept of a sys- tem that is adapted to the statistics of natural scenes. We present a probabilistic model of images based on the qualitative statistics of derivative ﬂlters and \corner detectors" in natural scenes and use this model to ﬂnd the most probable decomposition of a novel image. The optimization is performed using loopy belief propa- gation. We show that our model computes perceptually \correct" decompositions on synthetic images and discuss its application to real images.

paragraphs: The paper asks why some images are perceived as two transparent layers and how a visual system might choose a particular decomposition. An image can be written as the sum of two component images in infinitely many ways, including the trivial choice of the original image plus nothing. The percept therefore requires a principle for preferring some explanations over others.

The authors suggest that transparency can be understood as a rational percept for a system adapted to natural-scene statistics. They construct a probabilistic image model using qualitative statistics of derivative-filter and corner-detector responses. The model seeks the most probable decomposition of a new image, with optimization carried out using loopy belief propagation.

On synthetic images, the model produces decompositions that the authors describe as perceptually correct. They also discuss application to real images. The demonstrated result supports the proposed statistical explanation in the synthetic setting: natural-image regularities can help select a perceptually appropriate layered interpretation from the many decompositions mathematically available.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model based on natural-scene statistics produces perceptually appropriate transparency decompositions on synthetic images.

title: Learning to Perceive Transparency from the Statistics of Natural Scenes

abstract: Regularization plays a central role in the analysis of modern data, where non-regularized fitting is likely to lead to over-fitted models, useless for both prediction and interpretation. We consider the design of incremental algorithms which follow paths of regularized solutions, as the regularization varies. These approaches often result in methods which are both efficient and highly flexible. We suggest a general path-following algorithm based on second-order approximations, prove that under mild conditions it remains “very close” to the path of optimal solutions and illustrate it with examples.
originalAbstract: Regularization plays a central role in the analysis of modern data, where non-regularized fitting is likely to lead to over-fitted models, useless for both prediction and interpretation. We consider the design of incremental algorithms which follow paths of regularized solutions, as the regularization varies. These approaches often result in methods which are both efficient and highly flexible. We suggest a general path-following algorithm based on second-order approximations, prove that under mild conditions it remains “very close” to the path of optimal solutions and illustrate it with examples.

paragraphs: Regularization controls how strongly a fitted model is constrained, helping address overfitting that can damage prediction and interpretation. Changing its strength produces a sequence of different optimal models. This paper studies how to follow that sequence incrementally as the regularization setting changes.

The proposed general algorithm uses second-order approximations to track the path of regularized solutions. Such approximations represent local curvature, allowing the procedure to account for a solution path that bends as the regularization varies. The computational aim is to move through related solutions in an organized way, taking advantage of their connection along the path.

The authors prove that, under mild conditions, the algorithm stays very close to the path of optimal solutions, and they illustrate the approach with examples. This is a conditional approximation guarantee, rather than a claim that every computed point is exactly optimal. Its significance is that incremental path following receives theoretical support as a flexible way to explore regularized fits.
summary.tldr: A general algorithm uses second-order approximations to follow curved regularization paths and, under mild conditions, stays close to the optimal solutions.

title: Following Curved Regularized Optimization Solution Paths

abstract: We prove generalization error bounds for predicting entries in a partially observed matrix by fitting the observed entries with a low-rank matrix. In justifying the analysis approach we take to obtain the bounds, we present an example of a class of functions of finite pseudodimension such that the sums of functions from this class have unbounded pseudodimension.
originalAbstract: We prove generalization error bounds for predicting entries in a partially observed matrix by fitting the observed entries with a low-rank matrix. In justifying the analysis approach we take to obtain the bounds, we present an example of a class of functions of finite pseudodimension such that the sums of functions from this class have unbounded pseudodimension.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction in a matrix for which only some entries have been observed. Its approach fits those observations with a low-rank matrix and uses that fit to predict other entries. The central question is whether agreement with the available entries provides a reliable basis for predictions beyond them.

The authors prove generalization-error bounds for this procedure. Such bounds address the gap between fitting the observed data and performing well on entries to be predicted. The contribution therefore supplies theoretical support for using a low-rank restriction in collaborative prediction, connecting the chosen model structure to control of prediction error.

The analysis also includes a caution about measuring the complexity of function classes. The authors construct a class with finite pseudodimension whose sums have unbounded pseudodimension. This shows that a finite complexity measure for the component class does not, by itself, guarantee the same property for sums. The example helps justify the analytical approach used to obtain the matrix-prediction bounds.
summary.tldr: The paper proves generalization bounds for low-rank matrix prediction and shows why finite component pseudodimension alone cannot control sums.

title: Generalization Error Bounds for Collaborative Prediction with Low-Rank Matrices

abstract: We consider the problem of network anomaly detection in large distributed systems. In this setting, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) has been proposed as a method for discover- ing anomalies by continuously tracking the projection of the data onto a residual subspace. This method was shown to work well empirically in highly aggregated networks, that is, those with a limited number of large nodes and at coarse time scales. This approach, how- ever, has scalability limitations. To overcome these limitations, we develop a PCA-based anomaly detector in which adaptive local data (cid:2)lters send to a coordinator just enough data to enable accurate global detection. Our method is based on a stochastic matrix perturba- tion analysis that characterizes the tradeoff between the accuracy of anomaly detection and the amount of data communicated over the network.

In this setting, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) has been proposed as a method for discover- ing anomalies by continuously tracking the projection of the data onto a residual subspace. This method was shown to work well empirically in highly aggregated networks, that is, those with a limited number of large nodes and at coarse time scales. This approach, how- ever, has scalability limitations. To overcome these limitations, we develop a PCA-based anomaly detector in which adaptive local data (cid:2)lters send to a coordinator just enough data to enable accurate global detection. Our method is based on a stochastic matrix perturba- tion analysis that characterizes the tradeoff between the accuracy of anomaly detection and the amount of data communicated over the network.

paragraphs: The paper addresses anomaly detection in large distributed systems using principal component analysis. The starting approach monitors data projected into a residual subspace for signs of unusual behavior. Although this approach had worked well empirically for highly aggregated networks with relatively few large nodes and coarse time scales, it faced scalability problems.

The proposed detector distributes part of the work across the network. Adaptive filters at local sites control which data reach a coordinator, sending enough information to support accurate global detection. This makes communication itself part of the detector's design: local decisions about reporting data affect what the coordinator can infer about the system.

The method is grounded in a stochastic matrix perturbation analysis that characterizes the relationship between detection accuracy and communication volume. That relationship provides a principled way to understand the consequences of reducing transmitted data. The contribution is a PCA-based distributed architecture whose communication demands and detection accuracy are explicitly connected, addressing a central obstacle to scaling global anomaly monitoring.
summary.tldr: Adaptive local filters reduce network communication while supporting global PCA anomaly detection through an analyzed accuracy–communication tradeoff.

title: In-Network PCA and Anomaly Detection

abstract: We introduces a new probability distribution over a potentially infinite number of binary Markov chains which we call the Markov Indian buffet process. This process extends the IBP to allow temporal dependencies in the hidden variables. We use this stochastic process to build a nonparametric extension of the factorial hidden Markov model. After working out an inference scheme which combines slice sampling and dynamic programming we demonstrate how the infinite factorial hidden Markov model can be used for blind source separation.
originalAbstract: We introduces a new probability distribution over a potentially infinite number of binary Markov chains which we call the Markov Indian buffet process. This process extends the IBP to allow temporal dependencies in the hidden variables. We use this stochastic process to build a nonparametric extension of the factorial hidden Markov model. After working out an inference scheme which combines slice sampling and dynamic programming we demonstrate how the infinite factorial hidden Markov model can be used for blind source separation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the Markov Indian buffet process, a probability distribution over a potentially infinite collection of binary Markov chains. Each chain represents a hidden quantity that can change between two states over time. The process extends the Indian buffet process so that hidden variables can have temporal dependencies.

The authors use this construction to form a nonparametric version of the factorial hidden Markov model. The potentially infinite collection provides a way to represent an unfixed number of hidden chains, while their Markov structure retains dependence across time. These two aspects belong together: flexibility in the collection of hidden variables is combined with a model of how those variables evolve.

To perform inference, the paper develops a scheme combining slice sampling and dynamic programming. This supplies a computational procedure for working with the proposed model, alongside its probabilistic definition. The authors demonstrate its use for blind source separation, illustrating how temporally evolving hidden components can be used in a task that seeks to separate underlying sources from observations.
summary.tldr: A Markov extension of the Indian buffet process creates a factorial hidden Markov model with a potentially infinite collection of binary chains.

title: The Infinite Factorial Hidden Markov Model

abstract: Alignment of time series is an important problem to solve in many scientific disciplines. In particular, temporal alignment of two or more subjects performing similar activities is a challenging problem due to the large temporal scale difference between human actions as well as the inter/intra subject variability. In this paper we present canonical time warping (CTW), an extension of canonical correlation analysis (CCA) for spatio-temporal alignment of the behavior between two subjects. CTW extends previous work on CCA in two ways: (i) it combines CCA with dynamic time warping for temporal alignment; and (ii) it extends CCA to allow local spatial deformations. We show CTWs effectiveness in three experiments: alignment of synthetic data, alignment of motion capture data of two subjects performing similar actions, and alignment of two people with similar facial expressions. Our results demonstrate that CTW provides both visually and qualitatively better alignment than state-of-the-art techniques based on dynamic time warping.

In this paper we present canonical time warping (CTW), an extension of canonical correlation analysis (CCA) for spatio-temporal alignment of the behavior between two subjects. CTW extends previous work on CCA in two ways: (i) it combines CCA with dynamic time warping for temporal alignment; and (ii) it extends CCA to allow local spatial deformations. We show CTWs effectiveness in three experiments: alignment of synthetic data, alignment of motion capture data of two subjects performing similar actions, and alignment of two people with similar facial expressions. Our results demonstrate that CTW provides both visually and qualitatively better alignment than state-of-the-art techniques based on dynamic time warping.

paragraphs: Two people performing similar actions may differ in both timing and the spatial details of their movements. Aligning their recordings therefore requires more than matching corresponding timestamps. This paper introduces canonical time warping, or CTW, to align behavior between two subjects while accounting for temporal differences and variation within and between subjects.

CTW combines canonical correlation analysis with dynamic time warping. The combination brings together a way to relate the subjects' representations and a way to adjust their temporal correspondence. The method also extends canonical correlation analysis to allow local spatial deformations. These additions address differences in when an action occurs and how its observed form varies.

The authors evaluate CTW on synthetic data, motion-capture recordings of similar actions, and recordings of similar facial expressions. They report visually and qualitatively better alignment than leading techniques based on dynamic time warping. These findings support the value of handling spatial variation alongside timing differences in the tested behavior-alignment problems.
summary.tldr: Canonical time warping combines temporal alignment and local spatial deformation to improve alignment of similar human behaviors.

title: Canonical Time Warping for Alignment of Human Behavior

abstract: Kernel learning is a powerful framework for nonlinear data modeling. Using the kernel trick, a number of problems have been formulated as semidefinite programs (SDPs). These include Maximum Variance Unfolding (MVU) (Weinberger et al., 2004) in nonlinear dimensionality reduction, and Pairwise Constraint Propagation (PCP) (Li et al., 2008) in constrained clustering. Although in theory SDPs can be efficiently solved, the high computational complexity incurred in numerically processing the huge linear matrix inequality constraints has rendered the SDP approach unscalable. In this paper, we show that a large class of kernel learning problems can be reformulated as semidefinite-quadratic-linear programs (SQLPs), which only contain a simple positive semidefinite constraint, a second-order cone constraint and a number of linear constraints. These constraints are much easier to process numerically, and the gain in speedup over previous approaches is at least of the order $m^{2.5}$, where m is the matrix dimension. Experimental results are also presented to show the superb computational efficiency of our approach.
originalAbstract: Kernel learning is a powerful framework for nonlinear data modeling. Using the kernel trick, a number of problems have been formulated as semidefinite programs (SDPs). These include Maximum Variance Unfolding (MVU) (Weinberger et al., 2004) in nonlinear dimensionality reduction, and Pairwise Constraint Propagation (PCP) (Li et al., 2008) in constrained clustering. Although in theory SDPs can be efficiently solved, the high computational complexity incurred in numerically processing the huge linear matrix inequality constraints has rendered the SDP approach unscalable. In this paper, we show that a large class of kernel learning problems can be reformulated as semidefinite-quadratic-linear programs (SQLPs), which only contain a simple positive semidefinite constraint, a second-order cone constraint and a number of linear constraints. These constraints are much easier to process numerically, and the gain in speedup over previous approaches is at least of the order $m^{2.5}$, where m is the matrix dimension. paragraphs: The paper addresses a computational bottleneck in kernel learning for nonlinear data modeling. Problems such as Maximum Variance Unfolding and Pairwise Constraint Propagation can be expressed as semidefinite programs. Although this formulation has favorable theoretical solvability properties, processing its large matrix inequality constraints can make numerical computation impractical at scale.

The authors show that a large class of kernel-learning problems can instead be expressed as semidefinite-quadratic-linear programs. The reformulation contains a simple positive semidefinite constraint, a second-order cone constraint, and linear constraints. The key contribution is a change in the form of the optimization problem that makes its constraints easier to handle numerically.

The stated speedup over earlier approaches is at least on the order of m to the power 2.5, where m denotes the matrix dimension. Experiments also demonstrate strong computational efficiency. The result shows why the specific mathematical representation of a learning problem matters: two formulations aimed at the same task can impose very different numerical workloads, especially as their matrices grow.
summary.tldr: Reformulating a large class of kernel-learning problems with simpler constraints yields substantial computational speedups over previous semidefinite approaches.

title: Fast Graph Laplacian Regularized Kernel Learning via Semidefinite–Quadratic–Linear Programming

abstract: Predicting the execution time of computer programs is an important but challenging problem in the community of computer systems. Existing methods require experts to perform detailed analysis of program code in order to construct predictors or select important features. We recently developed a new system to automatically extract a large number of features from program execution on sample inputs, on which prediction models can be constructed without expert knowledge. In this paper we study the construction of predictive models for this problem. Our two SPORE algorithms are able to build relationships between responses (e.g., the execution time of a computer program) and features, and select a few from hundreds of the retrieved features to construct an explicitly sparse and non-linear model to predict the response variable. The compact and explicitly polynomial form of the estimated model could reveal important insights into the computer program (e.g., features and their non-linear combinations that dominate the execution time), enabling a better understanding of the program’s behavior. title: Predicting Execution Time of Computer Programs Using Sparse Polynomial Regression

abstract: In many machine learning domains (such as scene understanding), several related sub-tasks (such as scene categorization, depth estimation, object detection) operate on the same raw data and provide correlated outputs. Each of these tasks is often notoriously hard, and state-of-the-art classifiers already exist for many sub-tasks. It is desirable to have an algorithm that can capture such correlation without requiring to make any changes to the inner workings of any classifier. We propose Feedback Enabled Cascaded Classification Models (FE-CCM), that maximizes the joint likelihood of the sub-tasks, while requiring only a ‘black-box’ interface to the original classifier for each sub-task. We use a two-layer cascade of classifiers, which are repeated instantiations of the original ones, with the output of the first layer fed into the second layer as input. Our training method involves a feedback step that allows later classifiers to provide earlier classifiers information about what error modes to focus on. We show that our method significantly improves performance in all the sub-tasks in two different domains: (i) scene understanding, where we consider depth estimation, scene categorization, event categorization, object detection, geometric labeling and saliency detection, and (ii) robotic grasping, where we consider grasp point detection and object classification.

This paper develops a way to use those relationships while retaining existing classifiers as black boxes. Scene understanding includes depth, scene and event categorization, object detection, geometric labeling, and saliency; robotic grasping includes grasp point detection and object classification. These results support combining correlated predictions with training feedback as a way to improve a collection of existing task-specific systems.
summary.tldr: A two-layer classifier cascade uses training feedback to exploit related tasks and improves every evaluated subtask in scene understanding and robotic grasping.

title: Towards Holistic Scene Understanding: Feedback Enabled Cascaded Classification Models

abstract: Topic modeling is a generalization of clustering that posits that observations (words in a document) are generated by \emph{multiple} latent factors (topics), as opposed to just one. This increased representational power comes at the cost of a more challenging unsupervised learning problem of estimating the topic-word distributions when only words are observed, and the topics are hidden. This work provides a simple and efficient learning procedure that is guaranteed to recover the parameters for a wide class of topic models, including Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). For LDA, the procedure correctly recovers both the topic-word distributions and the parameters of the Dirichlet prior over the topic mixtures, using only trigram statistics (\emph{i.e.}, third order moments, which may be estimated with documents containing just three words). The method, called Excess Correlation Analysis, is based on a spectral decomposition of low-order moments via two singular value decompositions (SVDs). Moreover, the algorithm is scalable, since the SVDs are carried out only on $k \times k$ matrices, where $k$ is the number of latent factors (topics) and is typically much smaller than the dimension of the observation (word) space.

paragraphs: Topic models describe documents using multiple hidden topics, with each topic associated with a distribution over words. This is more expressive than assigning each document to a single cluster, but it makes learning harder: the words are visible while the topics and their contributions remain hidden. The paper develops a simple, efficient procedure for recovering these hidden model parameters.

The method, Excess Correlation Analysis, uses low-order statistical moments and two singular value decompositions. For Latent Dirichlet Allocation, third-order word statistics suffice to recover both the topic-word distributions and the parameters governing topic mixtures. Such statistics can be estimated from documents containing only three words, so the method does not inherently require long documents.

The recovery guarantee applies to a wide class of topic models that includes LDA. A key computational feature is that the decompositions operate on matrices sized by the number of topics, rather than the vocabulary size. Since the number of topics is typically much smaller, this makes the central spectral operations comparatively compact and supports scalability.
summary.tldr: Excess Correlation Analysis recovers parameters of a broad class of topic models using third-order statistics and two small spectral decompositions.

title: A Spectral Algorithm for Latent Dirichlet Allocation

abstract: Mirror descent with an entropic regularizer is known to achieve shifting regret bounds that are logarithmic in the dimension. This is done using either a carefully designed projection or by a weight sharing technique. Via a novel unified analysis, we show that these two approaches deliver essentially equivalent bounds on a notion of regret generalizing shifting, adaptive, discounted, and other related regrets. Our analysis also captures and extends the generalized weight sharing technique of Bousquet and Warmuth, and can be refined in several ways, including improvements for small losses and adaptive tuning of parameters.
originalAbstract: Mirror descent with an entropic regularizer is known to achieve shifting regret bounds that are logarithmic in the dimension. This is done using either a carefully designed projection or by a weight sharing technique. Via a novel unified analysis, we show that these two approaches deliver essentially equivalent bounds on a notion of regret generalizing shifting, adaptive, discounted, and other related regrets. Our analysis also captures and extends the generalized weight sharing technique of Bousquet and Warmuth, and can be refined in several ways, including improvements for small losses and adaptive tuning of parameters.

paragraphs: Online learning methods can be evaluated against comparison strategies that change over time. Shifting regret measures performance in such a setting, making it useful when one fixed comparison is insufficient. Entropic mirror descent already achieves shifting-regret bounds that depend logarithmically on dimension through either carefully designed projections or weight sharing.

The paper develops a unified analysis showing that these two mechanisms yield essentially equivalent bounds. Its regret formulation includes shifting, adaptive, discounted, and related notions within a common treatment. This connects guarantees that would otherwise appear to require separate analyses and clarifies the relationship between two established ways of managing changing comparisons.

The analysis also captures and extends generalized weight sharing. Further refinements improve bounds when losses are small and allow adaptive parameter tuning. These are theoretical contributions about the guarantees available from the methods. Their significance is that a common mathematical framework can explain multiple regret criteria and algorithmic mechanisms while also revealing where stronger, more responsive guarantees can be obtained.
summary.tldr: A unified regret analysis connects entropic mirror-descent projections and weight sharing, with refinements for small losses and adaptive tuning.

title: Mirror Descent Meets Fixed Share (and feels no regret)

abstract: We establish minimax risk lower bounds for distributed statistical estimation given a budget $B$ of the total number of bits that may be communicated. Such lower bounds in turn reveal the minimum amount of communication required by any procedure to achieve the classical optimal rate for statistical estimation. We study two classes of protocols in which machines send messages either independently or interactively. The lower bounds are established for a variety of problems, from estimating the mean of a population to estimating parameters in linear regression or binary classification.
originalAbstract: We establish minimax risk lower bounds for distributed statistical estimation given a budget $B$ of the total number of bits that may be communicated. The lower bounds are established for a variety of problems, from estimating the mean of a population to estimating parameters in linear regression or binary classification.

paragraphs: When statistical data are spread across machines, estimation depends on what those machines can communicate. This paper studies the fundamental accuracy limits imposed by a budget of B communicated bits. Its focus is the best performance any allowed procedure could achieve, rather than the performance of a particular proposed algorithm.

The authors establish lower bounds on minimax risk: limits on how small the worst-case estimation error can be. Such bounds connect a communication budget to unavoidable statistical uncertainty. They also reveal how much communication is necessary to attain the classical optimal estimation rate. A necessary amount of communication establishes a barrier; it does not by itself supply a procedure that reaches that rate.

The analysis covers both independent messaging protocols and interactive ones, allowing communication structure to enter the theoretical question. It treats several estimation problems, including population means and parameters for linear regression and binary classification. Together, these results provide a way to assess when communication restrictions fundamentally prevent distributed estimation from matching classical statistical performance.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes unavoidable estimation error under communication budgets and derives necessary communication for classical optimal statistical rates.

title: Information-theoretic lower bounds for distributed statistical estimation with communication constraints

abstract: We show that the usual score function for conditional Markov networks can be written as the expectation over the scores of their spanning trees. We also show that a small random sample of these output trees can attain a significant fraction of the margin obtained by the complete graph and we provide conditions under which we can perform tractable inference. The experimental results confirm that practical learning is scalable to realistic datasets using this approach.
originalAbstract: We show that the usual score function for conditional Markov networks can be written as the expectation over the scores of their spanning trees. We also show that a small random sample of these output trees can attain a significant fraction of the margin obtained by the complete graph and we provide conditions under which we can perform tractable inference. The experimental results confirm that practical learning is scalable to realistic datasets using this approach.

paragraphs: Multilabel prediction involves choosing several labels whose relationships can matter to the result. Conditional Markov networks represent such structured outputs with a score function. This paper investigates how a collection of spanning trees can represent that score and provide a more manageable basis for learning.

The authors show that the usual network score can be written as an expectation over scores associated with its spanning trees. They further show that a small random sample of output trees can retain a significant fraction of the margin achieved by the complete graph. The margin result explains why sampling relatively few trees can still preserve a meaningful part of the full model's separation.

The paper also gives conditions under which inference is tractable. That qualification matters: computational tractability is established under those conditions, rather than for every possible structured prediction problem. Experiments confirm that the approach supports practical learning on realistic datasets. Together, the score decomposition, margin result, and inference conditions provide a basis for scalable learning through sampled tree structures.
summary.tldr: Randomly sampled spanning trees can retain a significant fraction of a full structured model's margin and support tractable inference under stated conditions.

title: Multilabel Structured Output Learning with Random Spanning Trees of Max-Margin Markov Networks

abstract: We consider the problem of learning sparse additive models, i.e., functions of the form: $f(\vecx) = \sum_{l \in S} \phi_{l}(x_l)$, $\vecx \in \matR^d$ from point queries of $f$. Here $S$ is an unknown subset of coordinate variables with $\abs{S} = k \ll d$. Assuming $\phi_l$'s to be smooth, we propose a set of points at which to sample $f$ and an efficient randomized algorithm that recovers a \textit{uniform approximation} to each unknown $\phi_l$. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of our scheme along with sample complexity bounds. Our algorithm utilizes recent results from compressive sensing theory along with a novel convex quadratic program for recovering robust uniform approximations to univariate functions, from point queries corrupted with arbitrary bounded noise. Lastly we theoretically analyze the impact of noise -- either arbitrary but bounded, or stochastic -- on the performance of our algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies a function of many input coordinates whose value is actually the sum of smooth functions of only a few coordinates. Both the relevant coordinates and their individual contributions are unknown. The objective is to reconstruct each contribution uniformly, using queries that return function values at chosen inputs.

The authors specify sampling points and a randomized recovery algorithm. Their method combines compressive sensing with a new convex quadratic program for approximating one-dimensional functions. This recovery step can tolerate query errors that are arbitrary but bounded, rather than requiring every observation to be exact.

The results are theoretical: the paper establishes sample-complexity bounds and analyzes both bounded and stochastic noise. Its guarantees depend on the sparse additive structure and smoothness assumptions. This makes the work a study of when high-dimensional function learning can exploit a small number of active coordinates, rather than a claim about unrestricted functions.
summary.tldr: Sparse additive functions can be recovered efficiently from carefully chosen noisy queries.

title: Efficient Sampling for Learning Sparse Additive Models in High Dimensions

abstract: We present max-margin Bayesian clustering (BMC), a general and robust framework that incorporates the max-margin criterion into Bayesian clustering models, as well as two concrete models of BMC to demonstrate its flexibility and effectiveness in dealing with different clustering tasks. The Dirichlet process max-margin Gaussian mixture is a nonparametric Bayesian clustering model that relaxes the underlying Gaussian assumption of Dirichlet process Gaussian mixtures by incorporating max-margin posterior constraints, and is able to infer the number of clusters from data. We further extend the ideas to present max-margin clustering topic model, which can learn the latent topic representation of each document while at the same time cluster documents in the max-margin fashion. Extensive experiments are performed on a number of real datasets, and the results indicate superior clustering performance of our methods compared to related baselines.

We further extend the ideas to present max-margin clustering topic model, which can learn the latent topic representation of each document while at the same time cluster documents in the max-margin fashion. Extensive experiments are performed on a number of real datasets, and the results indicate superior clustering performance of our methods compared to related baselines.

paragraphs: The paper combines Bayesian clustering with a maximum-margin criterion. Bayesian models describe uncertainty and latent group structure, while the added margin criterion shapes how clusters are separated. The authors present a general framework and two concrete models to show how the combination can serve different clustering tasks.

The first model extends a Dirichlet process Gaussian mixture with maximum-margin constraints on the posterior. These constraints relax the underlying Gaussian assumption of the original mixture model, while the nonparametric construction allows the number of clusters to be inferred from data. This provides a way to incorporate separation requirements into a model that also determines its cluster count.

The second model applies the idea to documents, jointly learning each document's latent topic representation and clustering documents in a maximum-margin fashion. Experiments across several real datasets indicate better clustering performance than related baselines. The two examples demonstrate the framework's flexibility: the margin criterion can influence both a mixture-based clustering model and a model that learns document representations alongside cluster assignments.
summary.tldr: Maximum-margin Bayesian clustering combines probabilistic models with separation constraints, with successful mixture-model and document-clustering applications.

title: Robust Bayesian Max-Margin Clustering

abstract: We propose a simple method to learn linear causal cyclic models in the presence of latent variables. The method relies on equilibrium data of the model recorded under a specific kind of interventions (``shift interventions''). The location and strength of these interventions do not have to be known and can be estimated from the data. Our method, called BACKSHIFT, only uses second moments of the data and performs simple joint matrix diagonalization, applied to differences between covariance matrices. We give a sufficient and necessary condition for identifiability of the system, which is fulfilled almost surely under some quite general assumptions if and only if there are at least three distinct experimental settings, one of which can be pure observational data. We demonstrate the performance on some simulated data and applications in flow cytometry and financial time series.

paragraphs: BACKSHIFT learns linear causal models that can contain feedback cycles and latent variables. It uses equilibrium observations collected under shift interventions. A central feature is that the intervention locations and strengths need not be supplied beforehand; the method can estimate them from the data alongside the causal system.

The computation uses only second moments, specifically differences between covariance matrices from different experimental settings. BACKSHIFT applies joint matrix diagonalization to those differences. This makes variation between settings the basis for identifying the causal relationships, while keeping the method centered on comparatively simple matrix operations.

The authors establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability, meaning that the system can be uniquely distinguished from the available information. Under the stated general assumptions, this condition holds almost surely if and only if at least three distinct experimental settings are available; one may be purely observational. They demonstrate the method on simulations, flow cytometry, and financial time series. Its scope therefore combines feedback and hidden variables with a specific intervention and equilibrium-data setting.
summary.tldr: BACKSHIFT uses covariance differences across intervention settings to identify linear cyclic causal systems without knowing intervention locations or strengths.

title: BACKSHIFT: Learning causal cyclic graphs from unknown shift interventions

abstract: We study the problem of black-box optimization of a function $f$ of any dimension, given function evaluations perturbed by noise. The function is assumed to be locally smooth around one of its global optima, but this smoothness is unknown. Our contribution is an adaptive optimization algorithm, POO or parallel optimistic optimization, that is able to deal with this setting. POO performs almost as well as the best known algorithms requiring the knowledge of the smoothness. Furthermore, POO works for a larger class of functions than what was previously considered, especially for functions that are difficult to optimize, in a very precise sense. We provide a finite-time analysis of POO's performance, which shows that its error after $n$ evaluations is at most a factor of $\sqrt{\ln n}$ away from the error of the best known optimization algorithms using the knowledge of the smoothness.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization searches for a function's optimum using evaluations rather than an explicit formula. Here, those evaluations contain noise, and the function can have any dimension. The paper assumes local smoothness around at least one global optimum, but the optimizer does not know that smoothness in advance.

The proposed algorithm, parallel optimistic optimization, or POO, adapts to this missing information. Its purpose is to approach the performance of algorithms that receive the smoothness information beforehand. This matters because the theoretical properties needed to configure an optimization method may themselves be unavailable when the only access to a function is through noisy evaluations.

A finite-time analysis bounds POO's error after n evaluations within a factor of sqrt(ln n) of the best known methods that know the smoothness. The authors also establish applicability to a broader function class, including functions they characterize as difficult to optimize. The result quantifies the cost of adaptation while retaining the stated local-smoothness assumption.
summary.tldr: POO optimizes noisy functions with unknown local smoothness, with a finite-time error guarantee close to methods that know the smoothness.

title: Black-box optimization of noisy functions with unknown smoothness

abstract: In simple perceptual decisions the brain has to identify a stimulus based on noisy sensory samples from the stimulus. Basic statistical considerations state that the reliability of the stimulus information, i.e., the amount of noise in the samples, should be taken into account when the decision is made. However, for perceptual decision making experiments it has been questioned whether the brain indeed uses the reliability for making decisions when confronted with unpredictable changes in stimulus reliability. We here show that even the basic drift diffusion model, which has frequently been used to explain experimental findings in perceptual decision making, implicitly relies on estimates of stimulus reliability. We then show that only those variants of the drift diffusion model which allow stimulus-specific reliabilities are consistent with neurophysiological findings. Our analysis suggests that the brain estimates the reliability of the stimulus on a short time scale of at most a few hundred milliseconds.

paragraphs: Perceptual decisions depend on noisy sensory samples, so the reliability of those samples affects how informative they are. The paper examines whether the brain takes that reliability into account when it changes unpredictably. Its approach analyzes drift diffusion models, which are frequently used to explain perceptual decision-making findings.

The authors first show that even the basic drift diffusion model implicitly depends on estimates of stimulus reliability. This makes reliability part of the model's operation even when it is not treated as an explicit additional mechanism. They then compare model variants with neurophysiological findings and conclude that only variants allowing stimulus-specific reliabilities are consistent with those findings.

The analysis suggests that the brain estimates reliability within at most a few hundred milliseconds. This timing is an inference from the analysis, rather than an unqualified assertion that every perceptual setting has the same timescale. The contribution clarifies what familiar decision models already assume and connects their treatment of noise to evidence about neural processing.
summary.tldr: Drift diffusion model analysis suggests that perceptual decisions use stimulus-specific reliability estimates formed within a few hundred milliseconds.

title: The Brain Uses Reliability of Stimulus Information when Making Perceptual Decisions

abstract: This paper proposes an efficient algorithm (HOLRR) to handle regression tasks where the outputs have a tensor structure. We formulate the regression problem as the minimization of a least square criterion under a multilinear rank constraint, a difficult non convex problem. HOLRR computes efficiently an approximate solution of this problem, with solid theoretical guarantees. A kernel extension is also presented. Experiments on synthetic and real data show that HOLRR computes accurate solutions while being computationally very competitive.
originalAbstract: This paper proposes an efficient algorithm (HOLRR) to handle regression tasks where the outputs have a tensor structure. We formulate the regression problem as the minimization of a least square criterion under a multilinear rank constraint, a difficult non convex problem. HOLRR computes efficiently an approximate solution of this problem, with solid theoretical guarantees. A kernel extension is also presented. Experiments on synthetic and real data show that HOLRR computes accurate solutions while being computationally very competitive.

paragraphs: This paper considers regression in which the output has tensor structure: predictions form a multidimensional array. The proposed method, HOLRR, formulates the task using a least-squares objective with a multilinear rank constraint. That constraint restricts the complexity of the tensor-valued regression while keeping its multidimensional structure part of the problem.

The resulting optimization is nonconvex and difficult to solve directly. HOLRR efficiently computes an approximate solution, and the authors provide theoretical guarantees for that approximation. This distinction is central to the contribution: the algorithm supplies a supported, efficient approximation to the constrained problem rather than claiming an exact solution to every instance.

The paper also presents a kernel extension and evaluates HOLRR on synthetic and real data. The experiments show accurate solutions with very competitive computational performance. Taken together, the formulation, approximation guarantees, and empirical results support low-rank tensor regression as a practical approach when responses have multiple dimensions. The work connects the structure of the output to both the optimization objective and an efficient solution method.
summary.tldr: HOLRR efficiently approximates low-rank regression with tensor-valued outputs, backed by theoretical guarantees and competitive empirical results.

title: Low-Rank Regression with Tensor Responses

abstract: Segmentation of 3D images is a fundamental problem in biomedical image analysis. Deep learning (DL) approaches have achieved the state-of-the-art segmentation performance. To exploit the 3D contexts using neural networks, known DL segmentation methods, including 3D convolution, 2D convolution on the planes orthogonal to 2D slices, and LSTM in multiple directions, all suffer incompatibility with the highly anisotropic dimensions in common 3D biomedical images. In this paper, we propose a new DL framework for 3D image segmentation, based on a combination of a fully convolutional network (FCN) and a recurrent neural network (RNN), which are responsible for exploiting the intra-slice and inter-slice contexts, respectively. To our best knowledge, this is the first DL framework for 3D image segmentation that explicitly leverages 3D image anisotropism. Evaluating using a dataset from the ISBI Neuronal Structure Segmentation Challenge and in-house image stacks for 3D fungus segmentation, our approach achieves promising results, comparing to the known DL-based 3D segmentation approaches.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional biomedical images often have strongly unequal dimensions or sampling characteristics across directions. This anisotropy makes it difficult to apply methods that handle spatial context in a uniform way. The paper addresses segmentation, the task of assigning image regions to the structures of interest, with an architecture designed around this directional difference.

The model divides the work between two neural networks. A fully convolutional network extracts context within individual image slices, while a recurrent neural network captures context between slices. This division explicitly separates information inside a slice from information across the image stack. The authors present it as, to their knowledge, the first deep segmentation framework to explicitly exploit this anisotropy.

Evaluation uses neuronal images from the ISBI Neuronal Structure Segmentation Challenge and in-house stacks for three-dimensional fungus segmentation. The reported results are promising relative to known deep learning approaches for three-dimensional segmentation. The finding supports tailoring the architecture to the structure of biomedical image acquisition, while the abstract’s wording stops short of claiming universal superiority across datasets or imaging conditions.
summary.tldr: A convolutional network handles within-slice context while a recurrent network handles between-slice context for anisotropic biomedical image segmentation.

title: Combining Fully Convolutional and Recurrent Neural Networks for 3D Biomedical Image Segmentation

abstract: The Stochastic Block Model (SBM) is a widely used random graph model for networks with communities. Despite the recent burst of interest in community detection under the SBM from statistical and computational points of view, there are still gaps in understanding the fundamental limits of recovery. In this paper, we consider the SBM in its full generality, where there is no restriction on the number and sizes of communities or how they grow with the number of nodes, as well as on the connectivity probabilities inside or across communities. For such stochastic block models, we provide guarantees for exact recovery via a semidefinite program as well as upper and lower bounds on SBM parameters for exact recoverability. Our results exploit the tradeoffs among the various parameters of heterogenous SBM and provide recovery guarantees for many new interesting SBM configurations.

paragraphs: The stochastic block model describes networks whose nodes belong to communities, with connection probabilities determined by community membership. This paper studies when those communities can be recovered exactly. Its focus is a general setting in which community sizes, community counts, and connection patterns can differ substantially across the same network.

The model allows unrestricted numbers and sizes of communities, including different ways these quantities can grow with the number of nodes. It also permits general connection probabilities within and between communities. Within this setting, the authors establish exact-recovery guarantees for a semidefinite program and derive upper and lower bounds on model parameters governing recoverability.

The results account for tradeoffs among the parameters rather than considering each source of heterogeneity in isolation. This yields recovery guarantees for many additional model configurations. Allowing a broad model family does not mean every configuration is recoverable; the bounds characterize conditions relevant to that question. The contribution expands understanding of recovery in networks with uneven community structure.
summary.tldr: Recovery bounds exploit tradeoffs among community sizes and connection probabilities in general heterogeneous stochastic block models.

title: Exploiting Tradeoffs for Exact Recovery in Heterogeneous Stochastic Block Models

abstract: The blind application of machine learning runs the risk of amplifying biases present in data. Such a danger is facing us with word embedding, a popular framework to represent text data as vectors which has been used in many machine learning and natural language processing tasks. We show that even word embeddings trained on Google News articles exhibit female/male gender stereotypes to a disturbing extent. This raises concerns because their widespread use, as we describe, often tends to amplify these biases. Geometrically, gender bias is first shown to be captured by a direction in the word embedding. Second, gender neutral words are shown to be linearly separable from gender definition words in the word embedding. Using these properties, we provide a methodology for modifying an embedding to remove gender stereotypes, such as the association between the words receptionist and female, while maintaining desired associations such as between the words queen and female. Using crowd-worker evaluation as well as standard benchmarks, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithms significantly reduce gender bias in embeddings while preserving the its useful properties such as the ability to cluster related concepts and to solve analogy tasks. The resulting embeddings can be used in applications without amplifying gender bias.

paragraphs: Word embeddings represent words as vectors that other language-processing systems can reuse. This paper shows that embeddings trained on Google News contain substantial female/male gender stereotypes. Because downstream applications use those representations, the authors argue that applying them without examining their associations can amplify biases already present in the training material.

The method uses two geometric observations: gender bias is captured by a direction in the embedding, and gender-neutral words are linearly separable from words whose definitions involve gender. These properties guide changes intended to remove stereotypical associations while retaining meaningful ones. The aim is to change associations such as receptionist with female while preserving associations such as queen with female.

Crowd-worker evaluations and standard benchmarks show significant empirical reductions in gender bias while maintaining useful capabilities, including grouping related concepts and solving analogies. The result demonstrates that modifying embedding geometry can address the targeted stereotypes without discarding those measured semantic abilities. The authors present the modified embeddings as a way for applications to use these representations without amplifying the gender bias they address.
summary.tldr: Geometric modifications reduce measured gender stereotypes in word embeddings while preserving meaningful gender associations and tested semantic capabilities.

title: Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings

abstract: We present a practical way of introducing convolutional structure into Gaussian processes, making them more suited to high-dimensional inputs like images. The main contribution of our work is the construction of an inter-domain inducing point approximation that is well-tailored to the convolutional kernel. This allows us to gain the generalisation benefit of a convolutional kernel, together with fast but accurate posterior inference. We investigate several variations of the convolutional kernel, and apply it to MNIST and CIFAR-10, where we obtain significant improvements over existing Gaussian process models. We also show how the marginal likelihood can be used to find an optimal weighting between convolutional and RBF kernels to further improve performance. This illustration of the usefulness of the marginal likelihood may help automate discovering architectures in larger models.

paragraphs: This paper introduces convolutional structure into Gaussian processes to make them better suited to inputs such as images. Its goal is to combine the generalization benefits of a convolutional kernel with practical probabilistic inference. The central challenge is making that structured model computationally usable while retaining accurate estimates of its posterior.

The main contribution is an inter-domain inducing point approximation designed specifically for the convolutional kernel. This supplies an efficient approximation tailored to the model’s structure. The authors investigate several convolutional kernel variants and evaluate them on MNIST and CIFAR-10, reporting significant improvements over existing Gaussian process models.

The paper also uses marginal likelihood to select a weighting between convolutional and RBF kernels, which further improves performance. This gives a concrete example of using the model’s probabilistic objective to choose how different structural assumptions are combined. The authors suggest that this capability may help automate architecture discovery in larger models; that broader possibility is distinct from the demonstrated kernel-weighting result.
summary.tldr: A tailored inference approximation makes convolutional Gaussian processes practical and improves image-task performance over existing Gaussian process models.

title: Convolutional Gaussian Processes

abstract: We propose a method for feature selection that employs kernel-based measures of independence to find a subset of covariates that is maximally predictive of the response. Building on past work in kernel dimension reduction, we show how to perform feature selection via a constrained optimization problem involving the trace of the conditional covariance operator. We prove various consistency results for this procedure, and also demonstrate that our method compares favorably with other state-of-the-art algorithms on a variety of synthetic and real data sets.
originalAbstract: We propose a method for feature selection that employs kernel-based measures of independence to find a subset of covariates that is maximally predictive of the response. Building on past work in kernel dimension reduction, we show how to perform feature selection via a constrained optimization problem involving the trace of the conditional covariance operator. We prove various consistency results for this procedure, and also demonstrate that our method compares favorably with other state-of-the-art algorithms on a variety of synthetic and real data sets.

paragraphs: The paper studies feature selection: choosing a subset of input variables that carries as much predictive information about an outcome as possible. Its approach uses kernel-based measures of independence to assess that information. This connects the selection problem to statistical relationships between the response and the candidate covariates.

Building on kernel dimension reduction, the authors formulate selection as a constrained optimization problem involving the trace of a conditional covariance operator. The conditional aspect makes the criterion concern what remains uncertain about the response after accounting for selected inputs. Minimizing this quantity provides a mathematical target for finding a predictive subset of variables.

The authors prove several consistency results and compare the procedure with other leading feature-selection algorithms on synthetic and real datasets. The reported comparisons are favorable. These contributions address both the statistical justification of the selection criterion and its practical behavior: the theory supports the procedure through consistency results, while the experiments show how it performs on the datasets examined.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based feature-selection method minimizes conditional covariance to identify predictive subsets, with consistency results and favorable empirical comparisons.

title: Kernel Feature Selection via Conditional Covariance Minimization

abstract: A low rank matrix X has been contaminated by uniformly distributed noise, missing values, outliers and corrupt entries. Reconstruction of X from the singular values and singular vectors of the contaminated matrix Y is a key problem in machine learning, computer vision and data science. In this paper we show that common contamination models (including arbitrary combinations of uniform noise, missing values, outliers and corrupt entries) can be described efficiently using a single framework. We develop an asymptotically optimal algorithm that estimates X by manipulation of the singular values of Y, which applies to any of the contamination models considered. Finally, we find an explicit signal-to-noise cutoff, below which estimation of X from the singular value decomposition of Y must fail, in a well-defined sense.

paragraphs: A low-rank matrix can encode useful structure even when its observed entries are noisy, missing, or corrupted. This paper studies reconstructing that underlying matrix from the singular values and singular vectors of the contaminated observation. The challenge is separating recoverable structure from the effects of contamination.

The authors place several common contamination models into one framework, including arbitrary combinations of the considered noise, missing-value, outlier, and corrupt-entry models. They then derive an algorithm that estimates the original matrix by changing the observed singular values. The algorithm is asymptotically optimal and applies across the contamination models covered by the analysis.

The paper also identifies an explicit signal-to-noise threshold below which estimation from the observed matrix's singular value decomposition must fail in a specified sense. This pairs an estimation procedure with a boundary on what that information can support. The result concerns the stated decomposition-based recovery setting, and its optimality is asymptotic rather than an unrestricted guarantee for every finite matrix.
summary.tldr: A unified contamination framework yields asymptotically optimal singular-value shrinkage and a signal-to-noise cutoff for decomposition-based recovery.

title: Optimal Shrinkage of Singular Values Under Random Data Contamination

abstract: We consider distributed statistical optimization in one-shot setting, where there are $m$ machines each observing $n$ i.i.d samples. Based on its observed samples, each machine then sends an $O(\log(mn))$-length message to a server, at which a parameter minimizing an expected loss is to be estimated. We propose an algorithm called Multi-Resolution Estimator (MRE) whose expected error is no larger than $\tilde{O}( m^{-1/\max(d,2)} n^{-1/2})$, where $d$ is the dimension of the parameter space. This error bound meets existing lower bounds up to poly-logarithmic factors, and is thereby order optimal. The expected error of MRE, unlike existing algorithms, tends to zero as the number of machines ($m$) goes to infinity, even when the number of samples per machine ($n$) remains upper bounded by a constant. This property of the MRE algorithm makes it applicable in new machine learning paradigms where $m$ is much larger than $n$.
