paragraphs: This paper studies distributed estimation with an especially tight communication budget. Each of m machines observes n independent, identically distributed samples and sends one message to a server. The message length grows only logarithmically with mn, and the server must estimate a parameter minimizing expected loss from these messages.

The proposed Multi-Resolution Estimator has expected error bounded, up to polylogarithmic factors, by m to the power minus one over max(d, 2), multiplied by n to the power minus one-half. Here d is the parameter dimension. This dependence shows how the machine count, local sample count, and dimensionality enter the guarantee. The bound matches existing lower bounds up to those logarithmic factors.

A distinctive consequence is that expected error approaches zero as the number of machines increases even when each machine’s sample count stays bounded by a constant. The paper contrasts this property with existing algorithms. It makes the method relevant to settings with many machines holding very little data, while retaining the one-message-per-machine restriction.
summary.tldr: A one-shot distributed estimator achieves near-optimal error rates and remains consistent as machines increase despite bounded local sample counts.

title: Order Optimal One-Shot Distributed Learning

abstract: Aimed at explaining the surprisingly good generalization behavior of overparameterized deep networks, recent works have developed a variety of generalization bounds for deep learning, all based on the fundamental learning-theoretic technique of uniform convergence. While it is well-known that many of these existing bounds are numerically large, through numerous experiments, we bring to light a more concerning aspect of these bounds: in practice, these bounds can {\em increase} with the training dataset size. Guided by our observations, we then present examples of overparameterized linear classifiers and neural networks trained by gradient descent (GD) where uniform convergence provably cannot ``explain generalization'' -- even if we take into account the implicit bias of GD {\em to the fullest extent possible}. More precisely, even if we consider only the set of classifiers output by GD, which have test errors less than some small $\epsilon$ in our settings, we show that applying (two-sided) uniform convergence on this set of classifiers will yield only a vacuous generalization guarantee larger than $1-\epsilon$. Through these findings, we cast doubt on the power of uniform convergence-based generalization bounds to provide a complete picture of why overparameterized deep networks generalize well.

paragraphs: Uniform convergence bounds try to explain generalization by controlling the gap between training and population performance across a collection of predictors. This paper investigates whether that approach can fully explain why overparameterized networks generalize well. Experiments reveal a troubling pattern: some such bounds can grow as the training dataset becomes larger.

Motivated by those observations, the authors construct examples involving overparameterized linear classifiers and neural networks trained with gradient descent. Even after restricting attention to the classifiers gradient descent actually outputs, two-sided uniform convergence produces a vacuous guarantee. In their settings, those classifiers have test errors below a small epsilon, while the resulting guarantee exceeds one minus epsilon.

The restriction to gradient-descent outputs matters because it already accounts for the optimizer's implicit bias as fully as possible within the stated analysis. The failure therefore persists beyond simply considering an unnecessarily broad class of networks. These examples cast doubt on uniform convergence as a complete explanation of deep-network generalization, rather than establishing that it is uninformative in every learning problem.
summary.tldr: Constructed examples show that two-sided uniform convergence can give vacuous guarantees even for gradient-descent predictors that generalize well.

title: Uniform convergence may be unable to explain generalization in deep learning

abstract: The plateau phenomenon, wherein the loss value stops decreasing during the process of learning, has been reported by various researchers. The phenomenon is actively inspected in the 1990s and found to be due to the fundamental hierarchical structure of neural network models. Then the phenomenon has been thought as inevitable. However, the phenomenon seldom occurs in the context of recent deep learning. There is a gap between theory and reality. In this paper, using statistical mechanical formulation, we clarified the relationship between the plateau phenomenon and the statistical property of the data learned. It is shown that the data whose covariance has small and dispersed eigenvalues tend to make the plateau phenomenon inconspicuous.

paragraphs: A training plateau is a period when a neural network's loss stops decreasing. Earlier analyses connected this behavior to the hierarchical structure of neural networks, encouraging the view that plateaus were inevitable. The paper addresses the tension between that expectation and the observation that the phenomenon is less conspicuous in recent deep learning.

The authors use a statistical mechanical formulation to connect plateau behavior with statistical properties of the training data. Their result concerns the eigenvalues of the data covariance, which describe how variation is distributed across directions in the data. They find that small, dispersed covariance eigenvalues tend to make plateaus less noticeable.

This shifts the explanation from network structure alone toward the interaction between the model and its data. The finding helps account for why an effect emphasized in earlier theory might be less apparent in other learning settings. Its strength is a tendency tied to the covariance spectrum: it does not claim that such data eliminate every plateau or that hierarchical structure ceases to matter.
summary.tldr: A statistical mechanical analysis finds that small, dispersed data-covariance eigenvalues tend to make neural-network training plateaus less conspicuous.

title: Data-Dependence of Plateau Phenomenon in Learning with Neural Network --- Statistical Mechanical Analysis

abstract: We consider Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) where the rewards are unknown and may change in an adversarial manner. We provide an algorithm that achieves a regret bound of $O( \sqrt{\tau (\ln|S|+\ln|A|)T}\ln(T))$, where $S$ is the state space, $A$ is the action space, $\tau$ is the mixing time of the MDP, and $T$ is the number of periods. The algorithm's computational complexity is polynomial in $|S|$ and $|A|$. We then consider a setting often encountered in practice, where the state space of the MDP is too large to allow for exact solutions. By approximating the state-action occupancy measures with a linear architecture of dimension $d\ll|S|$, we propose a modified algorithm with a computational complexity polynomial in $d$ and independent of $|S|$. We also prove a regret bound for this modified algorithm, which to the best of our knowledge, is the first $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound in the large-scale MDP setting with adversarially changing rewards.

paragraphs: This paper studies Markov decision processes whose rewards are unknown and can change adversarially. The aim is to control accumulated regret despite those changes. The authors first give an algorithm with regret bounded by O(sqrt(tau (ln|S| + ln|A|) T) ln T), where tau measures mixing time and T is the number of periods.

The initial algorithm has computation polynomial in the numbers of states and actions. That can still be impractical when the state space is very large. To address this, the paper approximates state-action occupancy measures, which describe how time is distributed across states and actions, using a linear representation of dimension d much smaller than the state space.

The modified algorithm has computational complexity polynomial in d and independent of the number of states. The authors also establish a regret bound with square-root dependence on T up to logarithmic factors, reporting it as the first such result they know of for large-scale MDPs with adversarially changing rewards. The contribution joins scalable representation with a theoretical performance guarantee.
summary.tldr: A low-dimensional occupancy-measure approximation enables scalable learning with a square-root-time regret bound under adversarially changing rewards.

title: Large Scale Markov Decision Processes with Changing Rewards

abstract: We ask whether the neural network interpretation methods can be fooled via adversarial model manipulation, which is defined as a model fine-tuning step that aims to radically alter the explanations without hurting the accuracy of the original models, e.g., VGG19, ResNet50, and DenseNet121. By incorporating the interpretation results directly in the penalty term of the objective function for fine-tuning, we show that the state-of-the-art saliency map based interpreters, e.g., LRP, Grad-CAM, and SimpleGrad, can be easily fooled with our model manipulation. We propose two types of fooling, Passive and Active, and demonstrate such foolings generalize well to the entire validation set as well as transfer to other interpretation methods. Our results are validated by both visually showing the fooled explanations and reporting quantitative metrics that measure the deviations from the original explanations. We claim that the stability of neural network interpretation method with respect to our adversarial model manipulation is an important criterion to check for developing robust and reliable neural network interpretation method.

paragraphs: Saliency-based interpretation methods aim to show which parts of an input matter to a neural network's prediction. This paper asks whether those explanations can be deliberately changed by modifying the model while preserving its accuracy. The intervention is a fine-tuning step aimed at the explanation itself, so the object being manipulated is the trained network.

The authors place interpretation results directly into a penalty term in the fine-tuning objective. They demonstrate attacks on methods including LRP, Grad-CAM, and SimpleGrad, using models such as VGG19, ResNet50, and DenseNet121. Two forms of manipulation, called Passive and Active, produce altered explanations that generalize across the validation set and transfer to other interpretation methods.

The evaluation combines visual examples with quantitative measurements of how far explanations move from their originals. These results show that maintained predictive accuracy can coexist with substantially altered saliency explanations. The authors therefore argue that resistance to adversarial model manipulation should be a criterion when developing reliable interpretation methods, alongside the usefulness of their displayed explanations.
summary.tldr: Targeted model fine-tuning can substantially alter saliency explanations while preserving accuracy, exposing a stability problem for interpretation methods.

title: Fooling Neural Network Interpretations via Adversarial Model Manipulation

abstract: We perform volume analysis of Multiplicative Weights Updates (MWU) and its optimistic variant (OMWU) in zero-sum as well as coordination games. Our analysis provides new insights into these game/dynamical systems, which seem hard to achieve via the classical techniques within Computer Science and Machine Learning. First, we examine these dynamics not in their original space (simplex of actions) but in a dual space (aggregate payoffs of actions). Second, we explore how the volume of a set of initial conditions evolves over time when it is pushed forward according to the algorithm. This is reminiscent of approaches in evolutionary game theory where replicator dynamics, the continuous-time analogue of MWU, is known to preserve volume in all games. Interestingly, when we examine discrete-time dynamics, the choices of the game and the algorithm both play a critical role. So whereas MWU expands volume in zero-sum games and is thus Lyapunov chaotic, we show that OMWU contracts volume, providing an alternative understanding for its known convergent behavior. Yet, we also prove a no-free-lunch type of theorem, in the sense that when examining coordination games the roles are reversed. Using these tools, we prove two novel, rather negative properties of MWU in zero-sum games. (1) Extremism: even in games with a unique fully-mixed Nash equilibrium, the system recurrently gets stuck near pure-strategy profiles, despite them being clearly unstable from game-theoretic perspective. (2) Unavoidability: given any set of good states (with a rather relaxed interpretation of “good” states), the system cannot avoid bad states indefinitely.

paragraphs: The paper studies how multiplicative weights updates and its optimistic variant evolve when used to learn in games. Instead of tracking action probabilities directly, the authors analyze accumulated action payoffs. They follow the volume occupied by a collection of initial conditions as the learning rule moves those conditions forward, revealing properties of whole groups of trajectories.

For zero-sum games, ordinary multiplicative weights expands volume and exhibits Lyapunov chaos, while its optimistic variant contracts volume. The contraction gives another perspective on the optimistic method's known convergence. However, the relationship reverses in coordination games. The effect of optimism therefore depends on the interaction between the learning algorithm and the type of game.

The volume analysis also establishes two negative properties of ordinary multiplicative weights in zero-sum games. Even with a unique equilibrium assigning positive probability to every action, trajectories repeatedly linger near pure-strategy profiles that are unstable from a game-theoretic perspective. In addition, under the paper's broad interpretation of good states, the dynamics cannot avoid bad states forever. These results expose behavior that equilibrium existence alone does not describe.
summary.tldr: Tracking evolving volumes reveals chaos and recurring extreme behavior in multiplicative weights, while showing that optimism's effects depend on the game.

title: Chaos, Extremism and Optimism: Volume Analysis of Learning in Games

abstract: Vanilla autoencoders often produce manifolds that overfit to noisy training data, or have the wrong local connectivity and geometry. Autoencoder regularization techniques, e.g., the denoising autoencoder, have had some success in reducing overfitting, whereas recent graph-based methods that exploit local connectivity information provided by neighborhood graphs have had some success in mitigating local connectivity errors. Neither of these two approaches satisfactorily reduce both overfitting and connectivity errors; moreover, graph-based methods typically involve considerable preprocessing and tuning. To simultaneously address the two issues of overfitting and local connectivity, we propose a new graph-based autoencoder, the Neighborhood Reconstructing Autoencoder (NRAE). Unlike existing graph-based methods that attempt to encode the training data to some prescribed latent space distribution -- one consequence being that only the encoder is the object of the regularization -- NRAE merges local connectivity information contained in the neighborhood graphs with local quadratic approximations of the decoder function to formulate a new neighborhood reconstruction loss. Compared to existing graph-based methods, our new loss function is simple and easy to implement, and the resulting algorithm is scalable and computationally efficient; the only required preprocessing step is the construction of the neighborhood graph. Extensive experiments with standard datasets demonstrate that, compared to existing methods, NRAE improves both overfitting and local connectivity in the learned manifold, in some cases by significant margins. Code for NRAE is available at https://github.com/Gabe-YHLee/NRAE-public.
originalAbstract: Vanilla autoencoders often produce manifolds that overfit to noisy training data, or have the wrong local connectivity and geometry. Autoencoder regularization techniques, e.g., the denoising autoencoder, have had some success in reducing overfitting, whereas recent graph-based methods that exploit local connectivity information provided by neighborhood graphs have had some success in mitigating local connectivity errors. Neither of these two approaches satisfactorily reduce both overfitting and connectivity errors; moreover, graph-based methods typically involve considerable preprocessing and tuning. To simultaneously address the two issues of overfitting and local connectivity, we propose a new graph-based autoencoder, the Neighborhood Reconstructing Autoencoder (NRAE). Unlike existing graph-based methods that attempt to encode the training data to some prescribed latent space distribution -- one consequence being that only the encoder is the object of the regularization -- NRAE merges local connectivity information contained in the neighborhood graphs with local quadratic approximations of the decoder function to formulate a new neighborhood reconstruction loss. Compared to existing graph-based methods, our new loss function is simple and easy to implement, and the resulting algorithm is scalable and computationally efficient; the only required preprocessing step is the construction of the neighborhood graph. Extensive experiments with standard datasets demonstrate that, compared to existing methods, NRAE improves both overfitting and local connectivity in the learned manifold, in some cases by significant margins. Code for NRAE is available at https://github.com/Gabe-YHLee/NRAE-public.

paragraphs: An autoencoder can reconstruct individual training examples while learning an underlying manifold that fits noise or connects nearby points incorrectly. Existing regularization and graph-based approaches have addressed parts of this problem, but the paper argues that neither satisfactorily handles both issues. Neighborhood Reconstructing Autoencoders, or NRAE, target them together.

NRAE combines neighborhood-graph information with local quadratic approximations of the decoder to construct a neighborhood reconstruction loss. This makes the decoder's local behavior part of the objective. In contrast, the graph-based methods discussed in the abstract impose a prescribed latent distribution, with regularization consequently focused only on the encoder. NRAE ties the reconstruction process directly to local connectivity information.

The authors describe the loss as simple to implement and the algorithm as scalable and computationally efficient. Constructing a neighborhood graph is its only required preprocessing step. Experiments on standard datasets report improvements in both overfitting and local connectivity, sometimes by substantial margins. These findings support training for the quality of reconstructed neighborhoods alongside the quality of individual reconstructions.
summary.tldr: NRAE uses neighborhood information and local decoder approximations to reduce both overfitting and connectivity errors in learned manifolds.

title: Neighborhood Reconstructing Autoencoders

abstract: In second-order optimization, a potential bottleneck can be computing the Hessian matrix of the optimized function at every iteration. Randomized sketching has emerged as a powerful technique for constructing estimates of the Hessian which can be used to perform approximate Newton steps. This involves multiplication by a random sketching matrix, which introduces a trade-off between the computational cost of sketching and the convergence rate of the optimization. A theoretically desirable but practically much too expensive choice is to use a dense Gaussian sketching matrix, which produces unbiased estimates of the exact Newton step and offers strong problem-independent convergence guarantees. We show that the Gaussian matrix can be drastically sparsified, substantially reducing the computational cost, without affecting its convergence properties in any way. This approach, called Newton-LESS, is based on a recently introduced sketching technique: LEverage Score Sparsified (LESS) embeddings. We prove that Newton-LESS enjoys nearly the same problem-independent local convergence rate as Gaussian embeddings for a large class of functions. In particular, this leads to a new state-of-the-art convergence result for an iterative least squares solver. Finally, we substantially extend LESS embeddings to include uniformly sparsified random sign matrices which can be implemented efficiently and perform well in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Newton-style optimization uses curvature information, but constructing the Hessian at every iteration can be expensive. Randomized sketching approximates that information using a smaller computation. Dense Gaussian sketches offer attractive theoretical behavior, yet their computational cost creates tension between inexpensive sketching and fast optimization convergence.

Newton-LESS uses leverage-score-sparsified embeddings to make the sketch much sparser. The aim is to reduce the cost of constructing the approximation while retaining the convergence behavior associated with Gaussian sketches. For a large class of functions, the authors prove nearly the same problem-independent local convergence rate as with Gaussian embeddings.

This analysis yields a new state-of-the-art convergence result for an iterative least-squares solver. The paper also extends LESS embeddings to uniformly sparsified random-sign matrices, which admit efficient implementations and perform well in numerical experiments. The significance lies in the combination of cheaper sketching and strong convergence guarantees. The theorem described in the abstract is local and applies to a specified function class, so its scope concerns convergence in that analyzed regime.
summary.tldr: Newton-LESS makes Hessian sketching cheaper while retaining nearly Gaussian-sketch local convergence rates for a large class of functions.

title: Newton-LESS: Sparsification without Trade-offs for the Sketched Newton Update

abstract: While effective, deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. In particular, recent work has shown that such attacks could be generated by another deep network, leading to significant speedups over optimization-based perturbations. However, the ability of such generative methods to generalize to different test-time situations has not been systematically studied. In this paper, we, therefore, investigate the transferability of generated perturbations when the conditions at inference time differ from the training ones in terms of the target architecture, target data, and target task. Specifically, we identify the mid-level features extracted by the intermediate layers of DNNs as common ground across different architectures, datasets, and tasks. This lets us introduce a loss function based on such mid-level features to learn an effective, transferable perturbation generator. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art universal and transferable attack strategies.

paragraphs: A neural network can learn to generate adversarial perturbations, providing a faster alternative to optimizing a new perturbation through a more expensive procedure. This paper examines whether such generators remain effective when their deployment conditions differ from training. It studies transfer across target network architectures, target datasets, and target tasks, making generalization of the attack itself the central question.

The proposed approach focuses on intermediate network representations. The authors identify these mid-level features as shared ground across the different architectures, data, and tasks they consider. They then build a loss function around those features to train a perturbation generator. The motivation is to target representations that carry relevance across settings, helping the learned perturbations transfer beyond their original training conditions.

Experiments show the approach outperforming the compared state-of-the-art universal and transferable attack strategies. The finding supports mid-level features as a useful basis for learning transferable perturbations in the evaluated settings. More broadly, the work separates the speed advantage of generative attacks from the distinct question of whether their effectiveness survives changes in what they attack.
summary.tldr: Training perturbation generators with a mid-level feature loss improves adversarial transfer across the evaluated architectures, datasets, and tasks.

title: Learning Transferable Adversarial Perturbations

abstract: While probabilistic models are an important tool for studying causality, doing so suffers from the intractability of inference. As a step towards tractable causal models, we consider the problem of learning interventional distributions using sum-product networks (SPNs) that are over-parameterized by gate functions, e.g., neural networks. Providing an arbitrarily intervened causal graph as input, effectively subsuming Pearl's do-operator, the gate function predicts the parameters of the SPN. The resulting interventional SPNs are motivated and illustrated by a structural causal model themed around personal health. Our empirical evaluation against competing methods from both generative and causal modelling demonstrates that interventional SPNs indeed are both expressive and causally adequate.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational difficulty of causal inference in probabilistic models. It studies how to learn distributions under interventions using sum-product networks, or SPNs, as a step toward tractable causal modeling. The target is a model that can represent how a distribution changes when an intervention modifies the underlying causal system.

The proposed interventional SPN uses gate functions, such as neural networks, to predict its parameters. A causal graph with an intervention applied is supplied to the gate function, which then configures the SPN for that intervention. In this way, intervention information enters the probabilistic model through a graph-conditioned parameter prediction mechanism, effectively incorporating the role of Pearl's do-operator.

The authors motivate and illustrate the construction with a structural causal model concerning personal health. Empirical comparisons with both generative and causal modeling methods support the resulting models' expressiveness and causal adequacy. The contribution links flexible parameter prediction to tractable probabilistic modeling, providing a concrete architecture for learning interventional distributions.
summary.tldr: Interventional SPNs use a gate network to translate intervened causal graphs into parameters for tractable probabilistic models.

title: Interventional Sum-Product Networks: Causal Inference with Tractable Probabilistic Models

abstract: Can we use machine learning to compress graph data? The absence of ordering in graphs poses a significant challenge to conventional compression algorithms, limiting their attainable gains as well as their ability to discover relevant patterns. On the other hand, most graph compression approaches rely on domain-dependent handcrafted representations and cannot adapt to different underlying graph distributions. This work aims to establish the necessary principles a lossless graph compression method should follow to approach the entropy storage lower bound. Instead of making rigid assumptions about the graph distribution, we formulate the compressor as a probabilistic model that can be learned from data and generalise to unseen instances. Our “Partition and Code” framework entails three steps: first, a partitioning algorithm decomposes the graph into subgraphs, then these are mapped to the elements of a small dictionary on which we learn a probability distribution, and finally, an entropy encoder translates the representation into bits. All the components (partitioning, dictionary and distribution) are parametric and can be trained with gradient descent. We theoretically compare the compression quality of several graph encodings and prove, under mild conditions, that PnC achieves compression gains that grow either linearly or quadratically with the number of vertices. Empirically, PnC yields significant compression improvements on diverse real-world networks.

paragraphs: Graph compression is difficult because graphs lack an inherent ordering, while many specialized compressors rely on handcrafted representations for particular domains. Partition and Code treats lossless compression as a learnable probabilistic modeling problem. Its goal is to adapt to graph distributions and generalize to unseen graphs while pursuing efficient storage.

The framework first partitions a graph into subgraphs. It then maps these pieces to a small dictionary whose probability distribution is learned, and an entropy encoder converts the representation into bits. The partitioner, dictionary, and distribution are all parametric and trainable with gradient descent, allowing the representation and coding model to adapt together.

The paper analyzes principles for approaching the entropy storage lower bound and compares several graph encodings theoretically. Under mild conditions, it proves compression gains that grow linearly or quadratically with the number of vertices. Experiments also report significant compression improvements on diverse real-world networks. These results support learning recurring graph structure as a route to better lossless compression, with the growth guarantees remaining conditional on the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Partition and Code learns graph partitions, a subgraph dictionary, and coding probabilities to improve lossless graph compression.

title: Partition and Code: learning how to compress graphs

abstract: In this paper, we address two learning problems. Suppose a family of $\ell$ unknown sparse vectors is fixed, where each vector has at most $k$ non-zero elements. In the first problem, we concentrate on robust learning the supports of all vectors from the family using a sequence of noisy responses. Each response to a query vector shows the sign of the inner product between a randomly chosen vector from the family and the query vector. In the second problem, we aim at designing queries such that all sparse vectors from the family can be approximately reconstructed based on the error-free responses. This learning model was introduced in the work of Gandikota et al., 2020, and these problems can be seen as generalizations of support recovery and approximate recovery problems, well-studied under the framework of 1-bit compressed sensing. As the main contribution of the paper, we prove the existence of learning algorithms for the first problem which work without any assumptions. Under a mild structural assumption on the unknown vectors, we also show the existence of learning algorithms for the second problem and rigorously analyze their query complexity.

paragraphs: The paper considers a fixed family of unknown sparse vectors, each with at most k nonzero entries. A query returns the sign of its inner product with a randomly chosen member of the family, so responses mix information from different unknown vectors.

The first task is support recovery: identifying which coordinates are nonzero in every vector, using noisy responses. The authors prove the existence of learning algorithms without additional assumptions on the vectors beyond the stated problem setup. This addresses structural identification despite both mixing and noise.

The second task seeks approximate recovery of the vectors themselves from error-free responses. For this stronger objective, the authors establish algorithms under a mild structural assumption on the unknown vectors. They also rigorously analyze the number of queries required.

These tasks extend support and approximate recovery from one-bit compressed sensing to mixtures of responses. The results distinguish what can be learned about nonzero locations under noise from what can be reconstructed numerically with noiseless feedback and an extra structural condition.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes algorithms for sparse-vector support recovery from noisy mixed sign responses and conditional approximate recovery from noiseless responses.

title: On learning sparse vectors from mixture of responses

abstract: Recently, there is a growing interest in studying pairwise learning since it includes many important machine learning tasks as specific examples, e.g., metric learning, AUC maximization and ranking. While stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is an efficient method, there is a lacking study on its generalization behavior for pairwise learning. In this paper, we present a systematic study on the generalization analysis of SGD for pairwise learning to understand the balance between generalization and optimization. We develop a novel high-probability generalization bound for uniformly-stable algorithms to incorporate the variance information for better generalization, based on which we establish the first nonsmooth learning algorithm to achieve almost optimal high-probability and dimension-independent generalization bounds in linear time. We consider both convex and nonconvex pairwise learning problems. Our stability analysis for convex problems shows how the interpolation can help generalization. We establish a uniform convergence of gradients, and apply it to derive the first generalization bounds on population gradients for nonconvex problems. Finally, we develop better generalization bounds for gradient-dominated problems.

paragraphs: Pairwise learning includes tasks such as ranking, metric learning, and AUC maximization, where the learning objective involves pairs of examples. This paper studies how stochastic gradient descent generalizes in that setting. Its goal is to understand the relationship between making progress on the training objective and obtaining reliable behavior beyond the training data.

The authors develop a high-probability generalization bound for uniformly stable algorithms that incorporates variance information. Using it, they establish a nonsmooth learning algorithm with nearly optimal, dimension-independent generalization bounds and linear running time. For convex problems, their stability analysis also explains how interpolation can help generalization.

For nonconvex problems, the paper proves uniform convergence of gradients and derives generalization bounds for population gradients. These results concern how gradient behavior on observed data relates to the underlying learning problem. Stronger bounds are also obtained for gradient-dominated problems. Together, the analyses cover several distinct optimization settings while preserving the differences between guarantees about prediction objectives and guarantees about their gradients.
summary.tldr: New stability and gradient analyses establish generalization guarantees for SGD in convex and nonconvex pairwise learning.

title: Generalization Guarantee of SGD for Pairwise Learning

abstract: In recent years there has been a considerable amount of research on local post hoc explanations for neural networks. However, work on building interpretable neural architectures has been relatively sparse. In this paper, we present a novel neural architecture, CoFrNet, inspired by the form of continued fractions which are known to have many attractive properties in number theory, such as fast convergence of approximations to real numbers. We show that CoFrNets can be efficiently trained as well as interpreted leveraging their particular functional form. Moreover, we prove that such architectures are universal approximators based on a proof strategy that is different than the typical strategy used to prove universal approximation results for neural networks based on infinite width (or depth), which is likely to be of independent interest. We experiment on nonlinear synthetic functions and are able to accurately model as well as estimate feature attributions and even higher order terms in some cases, which is a testament to the representational power as well as interpretability of such architectures. To further showcase the power of CoFrNets, we experiment on seven real datasets spanning tabular, text and image modalities, and show that they are either comparable or significantly better than other interpretable models and multilayer perceptrons, sometimes approaching the accuracies of state-of-the-art models.

paragraphs: Explaining a trained neural network after the fact is different from designing an architecture whose mathematical form supports interpretation. CoFrNets pursue the latter approach. Their structure is inspired by continued fractions, which have useful approximation properties in number theory. The paper investigates whether that structure can support both expressive prediction and understandable models.

The authors show how CoFrNets can be trained efficiently and interpreted through their functional form. They also prove universal approximation, using a proof strategy different from the usual arguments based on unlimited network width or depth. This result establishes representational capability; the experiments separately examine how the architecture performs and what can be extracted from it.

On nonlinear synthetic functions, CoFrNets accurately model the functions and estimate feature contributions, including higher-order terms in some cases. Across seven real datasets covering tabular, text, and image inputs, their performance is comparable to or significantly better than other interpretable models and multilayer perceptrons. Some results approach the accuracy of state-of-the-art models.
summary.tldr: CoFrNets use a continued-fraction-inspired architecture to combine expressive prediction with interpretation through the model’s functional form.

title: CoFrNets: Interpretable Neural Architecture Inspired by Continued Fractions

abstract: In this paper, we bridge the gap between the state-of-the-art theoretical results for matrix completion with the nuclear norm and their equivalent in \textit{inductive matrix completion}: (1) In the distribution-free setting, we prove bounds improving the previously best scaling of $O(rd^2)$ to $\widetilde{O}(d^{3/2}\sqrt{r})$, where $d$ is the dimension of the side information and $r$ is the rank. (2) We introduce the (smoothed) \textit{adjusted trace-norm minimization} strategy, an inductive analogue of the weighted trace norm, for which we show guarantees of the order $\widetilde{O}(dr)$ under arbitrary sampling. In the inductive case, a similar rate was previously achieved only under uniform sampling and for exact recovery. Both our results align with the state of the art in the particular case of standard (non-inductive) matrix completion, where they are known to be tight up to log terms. Experiments further confirm that our strategy outperforms standard inductive matrix completion on various synthetic datasets and real problems, justifying its place as an important tool in the arsenal of methods for matrix completion using side information.

paragraphs: Inductive matrix completion uses side information to help infer missing matrix entries. This paper strengthens the theoretical understanding of how such methods generalize, aiming to bring their guarantees into line with those available for ordinary matrix completion. Its bounds track the dimension d of the side information and the matrix rank r.

For nuclear-norm methods in a distribution-free setting, the authors improve the previously best scaling from O(rd²) to approximately d to the three-halves power times the square root of r, ignoring logarithmic factors. They also introduce a smoothed adjusted trace-norm strategy with guarantees scaling approximately as dr under arbitrary sampling. Previously, a similar inductive rate required uniform sampling and concerned exact recovery.

Both results agree with established bounds when specialized to ordinary matrix completion, where those bounds are tight up to logarithmic terms. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real problems further show that the proposed strategy outperforms standard inductive matrix completion. The contribution thus combines sharper guarantees with evidence that adjusting the regularization strategy can improve completion using side information.
summary.tldr: Sharper generalization bounds and an adjusted trace-norm method improve the theory and reported performance of matrix completion with side information.

title: Fine-grained Generalization Analysis of Inductive Matrix Completion

abstract: Stabilizing an unknown control system is one of the most fundamental problems in control systems engineering. In this paper, we provide a simple, model-free algorithm for stabilizing fully observed dynamical systems. While model-free methods have become increasingly popular in practice due to their simplicity and flexibility, stabilization via direct policy search has received surprisingly little attention. Our algorithm proceeds by solving a series of discounted LQR problems, where the discount factor is gradually increased. We prove that this method efficiently recovers a stabilizing controller for linear systems, and for smooth, nonlinear systems within a neighborhood of their equilibria. Our approach overcomes a significant limitation of prior work, namely the need for a pre-given stabilizing control policy. We empirically evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on common control benchmarks.

paragraphs: Before a controller can optimize useful behavior, it may need to keep an unknown dynamical system stable. The paper addresses this foundational problem through direct policy search. It considers fully observed systems and develops a model-free algorithm, meaning the approach does not require first supplying an explicit model of the system’s dynamics.

The algorithm solves a sequence of discounted linear quadratic regulator problems while gradually increasing the discount factor. This staged procedure provides a route to a stabilizing controller without requiring an already stabilizing control policy as its starting point. Removing that prerequisite addresses a significant limitation of earlier work described in the paper.

The authors prove efficient recovery of a stabilizing controller for linear systems. For smooth nonlinear systems, the guarantee applies within a neighborhood of an equilibrium, giving a local stabilization result. Evaluations on common control benchmarks examine the method empirically. The contribution is both an algorithmic construction and a guarantee that policy-gradient methods can establish stability under the stated system conditions.
summary.tldr: A model-free policy-gradient method learns stabilizing controllers without an initial stabilizing policy, with guarantees for linear and locally smooth nonlinear systems.

title: Stabilizing Dynamical Systems via Policy Gradient Methods

abstract: Many businesses nowadays rely on large quantities of time series data making time series forecasting an important research area. Global forecasting models and multivariate models that are trained across sets of time series have shown huge potential in providing accurate forecasts compared with the traditional univariate forecasting models that work on isolated series. However, there are currently no comprehensive time series forecasting archives that contain datasets of time series from similar sources available for researchers to evaluate the performance of new global or multivariate forecasting algorithms over varied datasets. In this paper, we present such a comprehensive forecasting archive containing 25 publicly available time series datasets from varied domains, with different characteristics in terms of frequency, series lengths, and inclusion of missing values. We also characterise the datasets, and identify similarities and differences among them, by conducting a feature analysis. Furthermore, we present the performance of a set of standard baseline forecasting methods over all datasets across ten error metrics, for the benefit of researchers using the archive to benchmark their forecasting algorithms.

paragraphs: Forecasting methods increasingly learn across collections of time series instead of treating every series independently. Evaluating these global and multivariate approaches requires datasets containing suitable groups of series, with enough variety to test performance across different conditions. This paper addresses the lack of a comprehensive archive designed to support those comparisons.

The archive brings together 25 publicly available datasets from different domains. They vary in observation frequency, sequence length, and whether values are missing. These differences give researchers multiple forecasting conditions to work with. The authors also analyze dataset features to characterize which collections resemble one another and which capture different kinds of forecasting problems.

Alongside the data, the paper reports results for standard forecasting baselines using ten error metrics across the archive. Those results provide reference points for evaluating new methods. The contribution is therefore both a dataset collection and a benchmarking foundation: researchers can compare algorithms across varied data and scoring measures rather than relying on an isolated dataset.
summary.tldr: The Monash archive combines 25 diverse time-series datasets with feature analyses and baseline results to support broader forecasting comparisons.

title: Monash Time Series Forecasting Archive

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) methods can generally be categorized into two types: RL-based and Imitation-based. RL-based methods could in principle enjoy out-of-distribution generalization but suffer from erroneous off-policy evaluation. Imitation-based methods avoid off-policy evaluation but are too conservative to surpass the dataset. In this study, we propose an alternative approach, inheriting the training stability of imitation-style methods while still allowing logical out-of-distribution generalization. We decompose the conventional reward-maximizing policy in offline RL into a guide-policy and an execute-policy. During training, the guide-poicy and execute-policy are learned using only data from the dataset, in a supervised and decoupled manner. During evaluation, the guide-policy guides the execute-policy by telling where it should go so that the reward can be maximized, serving as the \textit{Prophet}. By doing so, our algorithm allows \textit{state-compositionality} from the dataset, rather than \textit{action-compositionality} conducted in prior imitation-style methods. We dumb this new approach Policy-guided Offline RL (\texttt{POR}). \texttt{POR} demonstrates the state-of-the-art performance on D4RL, a standard benchmark for offline RL. We also highlight the benefits of \texttt{POR} in terms of improving with supplementary suboptimal data and easily adapting to new tasks by only changing the guide-poicy.
originalAbstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) methods can generally be categorized into two types: RL-based and Imitation-based. RL-based methods could in principle enjoy out-of-distribution generalization but suffer from erroneous off-policy evaluation. Imitation-based methods avoid off-policy evaluation but are too conservative to surpass the dataset. In this study, we propose an alternative approach, inheriting the training stability of imitation-style methods while still allowing logical out-of-distribution generalization. We decompose the conventional reward-maximizing policy in offline RL into a guide-policy and an execute-policy. During training, the guide-poicy and execute-policy are learned using only data from the dataset, in a supervised and decoupled manner. During evaluation, the guide-policy guides the execute-policy by telling where it should go so that the reward can be maximized, serving as the \textit{Prophet}. By doing so, our algorithm allows \textit{state-compositionality} from the dataset, rather than \textit{action-compositionality} conducted in prior imitation-style methods. We dumb this new approach Policy-guided Offline RL (\texttt{POR}). \texttt{POR} demonstrates the state-of-the-art performance on D4RL, a standard benchmark for offline RL. We also highlight the benefits of \texttt{POR} in terms of improving with supplementary suboptimal data and easily adapting to new tasks by only changing the guide-poicy.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn useful behavior from an existing dataset. Methods that estimate the value of unfamiliar actions can make evaluation errors, while imitation methods can remain too close to the recorded behavior. Policy-guided Offline RL, or POR, aims to retain the stability of supervised imitation while allowing new combinations of behavior supported by the dataset.

POR separates decision-making into a guide policy and an execution policy. Both are trained separately through supervised learning using only the available data. At evaluation time, the guide tells the execution policy where to go to obtain higher rewards. This division enables composition at the level of states, rather than the action composition used by earlier imitation approaches.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on the D4RL benchmark. They also highlight improvements from adding suboptimal data and adaptation to new tasks by changing only the guide policy. These findings support the usefulness of separating reward-directed guidance from execution: the same execution component can support different guidance, while additional recorded behavior can expand what the system can compose.
summary.tldr: POR separates guidance from execution to combine stable offline imitation with state-based composition and strong benchmark performance.

title: A Policy-Guided Imitation Approach for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we present a new strategy to prove the convergence of Deep Learning architectures to a zero training (or even testing) loss by gradient flow. Our analysis is centered on the notion of Rayleigh quotients in order to prove Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequalities for a broader set of neural network architectures and loss functions. We show that Rayleigh quotients provide a unified view for several convergence analysis techniques in the literature. Our strategy produces a proof of convergence for various examples of parametric learning. In particular, our analysis does not require the number of parameters to tend to infinity, nor the number of samples to be finite, thus extending to test loss minimization and beyond the over-parameterized regime.

paragraphs: Proving that neural network training reaches zero loss often involves assumptions about network size or the amount of training data. This paper develops a proof strategy that reaches beyond analyses requiring infinitely many parameters or finitely many samples. It studies gradient flow, the continuous-time formulation of following the negative loss gradient.

The strategy centers on Rayleigh quotients and uses them to establish Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequalities. These inequalities connect the geometry of the loss to the progress made by gradient flow, providing a route to convergence proofs. The authors show that the Rayleigh quotient perspective also brings several existing convergence analysis techniques into a common framework.

The paper applies this strategy to various examples of parametric learning and a broader collection of architectures and loss functions. Because the analysis need not assume a finite sample set, it can extend to minimizing test loss as well as training loss. These are convergence results for the examples and settings covered by the analysis, rather than a guarantee for every network. The contribution expands the mathematical tools available for studying learning beyond the over-parameterized regime.
summary.tldr: Rayleigh quotients provide a unified route to gradient-flow convergence proofs without requiring infinite parameter counts or finite sample sets.

title: Convergence beyond the over-parameterized regime using Rayleigh quotients

abstract: We study the properties of various over-parameterized convolutional neural architectures through their respective Gaussian Process and Neural Tangent kernels. We prove that, with normalized multi-channel input and ReLU activation, the eigenfunctions of these kernels with the uniform measure are formed by products of spherical harmonics, defined over the channels of the different pixels. We next use hierarchical factorizable kernels to bound their respective eigenvalues. We show that the eigenvalues decay polynomially, quantify the rate of decay, and derive measures that reflect the composition of hierarchical features in these networks. Our theory provides a concrete quantitative characterization of the role of locality and hierarchy in the inductive bias of over-parameterized convolutional network architectures.

paragraphs: This paper investigates the inductive biases of over-parameterized convolutional architectures through their Gaussian Process and Neural Tangent kernels. Its focus is how locality and hierarchical structure shape the functions represented by these kernels. A spectral description makes those architectural preferences mathematically explicit rather than leaving them as broad intuitions about convolutional networks.

Under normalized multichannel inputs, ReLU activation, and the uniform measure, the authors identify the kernels' eigenfunctions. They are products of spherical harmonics defined across the channels at different pixels. This supplies a structured family of functions in which to analyze the kernels, with the input normalization and measure forming part of the stated mathematical setting.

The authors then use hierarchical factorizable kernels to bound the corresponding eigenvalues. They prove polynomial decay, quantify its rate, and derive measures reflecting how hierarchical features are composed. Together, these results give a quantitative account of the role of locality and hierarchy in the inductive bias of the convolutional architectures studied.
summary.tldr: Kernel eigenfunctions and eigenvalue bounds quantify how locality and hierarchy shape the inductive bias of over-parameterized convolutional networks.

title: On the Spectral Bias of Convolutional Neural Tangent and Gaussian Process Kernels

abstract: We address the problem of using observational data to estimate peer contagion effects, the influence of treatments applied to individuals in a network on the outcomes of their neighbors. A main challenge to such estimation is that homophily - the tendency of connected units to share similar latent traits - acts as an unobserved confounder for contagion effects. Informally, it's hard to tell whether your friends have similar outcomes because they were influenced by your treatment, or whether it's due to some common trait that caused you to be friends in the first place. Because these common causes are not usually directly observed, they cannot be simply adjusted for. We describe an approach to perform the required adjustment using node embeddings learned from the network itself. The main aim is to perform this adjustment nonparametrically, without functional form assumptions on either the process that generated the network or the treatment assignment and outcome processes. The key contributions are to nonparametrically formalize the causal effect in a way that accounts for homophily, and to show how embedding methods can be used to identify and estimate this effect.

paragraphs: When connected people have similar outcomes, the similarity may reflect influence between them or traits they already share. This paper studies the effect of a treatment applied to one person on their neighbors' outcomes using observational network data. The central obstacle is homophily: shared, unobserved traits can influence both social connections and the outcomes being analyzed.

Because those traits are not directly measured, researchers cannot simply include them as observed adjustment variables. The proposed approach instead uses node embeddings learned from the network itself to perform the required adjustment. Network structure thereby provides information for addressing the hidden common causes that complicate estimates of peer influence.

The authors formalize the causal effect nonparametrically and show how embedding methods can identify and estimate it while accounting for homophily. Their aim is to avoid specifying functional forms for network formation, treatment assignment, or outcomes. The contribution connects representation learning on networks to causal estimation, focusing on separating treatment spillovers from similarities associated with how connections arise.
summary.tldr: Network embeddings support nonparametric adjustment for homophily when identifying and estimating causal peer-influence effects.

title: Using Embeddings for Causal Estimation of Peer Influence in Social Networks

abstract: Machine learning systems perform well on pattern matching tasks, but their ability to perform algorithmic or logical reasoning is not well understood. One important reasoning capability is algorithmic extrapolation, in which models trained only on small/simple reasoning problems can synthesize complex strategies for large/complex problems at test time. Algorithmic extrapolation can be achieved through recurrent systems, which can be iterated many times to solve difficult reasoning problems. We observe that this approach fails to scale to highly complex problems because behavior degenerates when many iterations are applied -- an issue we refer to as "overthinking." We propose a recall architecture that keeps an explicit copy of the problem instance in memory so that it cannot be forgotten. We also employ a progressive training routine that prevents the model from learning behaviors that are specific to iteration number and instead pushes it to learn behaviors that can be repeated indefinitely. These innovations prevent the overthinking problem, and enable recurrent systems to solve extremely hard extrapolation tasks.

paragraphs: Algorithmic extrapolation asks whether a model trained on small, simple reasoning problems can handle larger, harder ones. Recurrent systems offer a way to attempt this: repeatedly apply the same computation, allowing more iterations for a difficult instance. The paper identifies a failure of this approach in which behavior deteriorates as the number of iterations grows, calling it overthinking.

The authors introduce two changes aimed at sustaining useful computation. A recall architecture preserves an explicit copy of the original problem in memory, keeping that information available throughout processing. A progressive training routine discourages behavior tied to a particular iteration number and instead encourages operations that can continue to be repeated.

Together, these changes address both retention of the problem and the repeatability of the learned computation. The authors report that they prevent overthinking and enable extremely difficult extrapolation tasks. The finding supports the importance of how recurrent computation is structured and trained when additional iterations are meant to extend reasoning beyond the complexity encountered during training.
summary.tldr: Preserving the problem in memory and progressively training repeatable computation prevents reported overthinking failures in recurrent reasoning systems.

title: End-to-end Algorithm Synthesis with Recurrent Networks: Extrapolation without Overthinking

abstract: Machine learning models based on temporal point processes are the state of the art in a wide variety of applications involving discrete events in continuous time. However, these models lack the ability to answer counterfactual questions, which are increasingly relevant as these models are being used to inform targeted interventions. In this work, our goal is to fill this gap. To this end, we first develop a causal model of thinning for temporal point processes that builds upon the Gumbel-Max structural causal model. This model satisfies a desirable counterfactual monotonicity condition, which is sufficient to identify counterfactual dynamics in the process of thinning. Then, given an observed realization of a temporal point process with a given intensity function, we develop a sampling algorithm that uses the above causal model of thinning and the superposition theorem to simulate counterfactual realizations of the temporal point process under a given alternative intensity function. Simulation experiments using synthetic and real epidemiological data show that the counterfactual realizations provided by our algorithm may give valuable insights to enhance targeted interventions.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes model discrete events occurring in continuous time. This paper asks how such models can answer a different kind of question: given the events that actually occurred, what might have happened under an alternative event intensity? This is relevant when event models help inform targeted interventions.

The authors construct a causal model of thinning, an event-selection process, using the Gumbel-Max structural causal model. Their construction satisfies counterfactual monotonicity, a condition sufficient to identify counterfactual dynamics within thinning. They combine that causal model with the superposition theorem to build a sampling algorithm. Starting from an observed event sequence and its intensity function, the algorithm simulates counterfactual sequences under a specified alternative intensity.

Experiments use synthetic data and real epidemiological data to explore the resulting counterfactual realizations. The results suggest that these simulations may provide useful insights for targeted interventions. The contribution links observed event histories to alternative scenarios through an explicit causal construction, with the identification claim grounded in the stated sufficient condition.
summary.tldr: A causal thinning model enables sampling counterfactual event sequences under alternative intensity functions.

title: Counterfactual Temporal Point Processes

abstract: We propose an optimistic model-based algorithm, dubbed SMRL, for finite-horizon episodic reinforcement learning (RL) when the transition model is specified by exponential family distributions with $d$ parameters and the reward is bounded and known. SMRL uses score matching, an unnormalized density estimation technique that enables efficient estimation of the model parameter by ridge regression. Under standard regularity assumptions, SMRL achieves $\tilde O(d\sqrt{H^3T})$ online regret, where $H$ is the length of each episode and $T$ is the total number of interactions (ignoring polynomial dependence on structural scale parameters).

SMRL uses score matching, an unnormalized density estimation technique that enables efficient estimation of the model parameter by ridge regression. Under standard regularity assumptions, SMRL achieves $\tilde O(d\sqrt{H^3T})$ online regret, where $H$ is the length of each episode and $T$ is the total number of interactions (ignoring polynomial dependence on structural scale parameters).

paragraphs: SMRL is a model-based reinforcement-learning algorithm for episodes of fixed finite length. It studies environments whose transition distributions belong to an exponential family described by d parameters. The reward is assumed to be bounded and known, so the learning problem centers on the unknown transition model.

The algorithm estimates that model with score matching, a density-estimation technique that can work with unnormalized distributions. In this setting, score matching makes parameter estimation possible through ridge regression. SMRL combines this estimation procedure with an optimistic approach to decision-making, providing a connection between a tractable statistical estimation method and an online learning guarantee.

Under standard regularity assumptions, the authors bound online regret at roughly d times the square root of H cubed times T, where H is episode length and T is total interactions. The stated rate suppresses logarithmic factors and polynomial dependence on structural scale parameters. Its significance is a quantitative bound on accumulated learning cost in the specified model class, with explicit dependence on parameter count, episode length, and experience.
summary.tldr: SMRL uses score matching to estimate exponential-family transition models efficiently and obtain a conditional online-regret guarantee.

title: Exponential Family Model-Based Reinforcement Learning via Score Matching

abstract: Domain adaptation framework of GANs has achieved great progress in recent years as a main successful approach of training contemporary GANs in the case of very limited training data. In this work, we significantly improve this framework by proposing an extremely compact parameter space for fine-tuning the generator. We introduce a novel domain-modulation technique that allows to optimize only 6 thousand-dimensional vector instead of 30 million weights of StyleGAN2 to adapt to a target domain. We apply this parameterization to the state-of-art domain adaptation methods and show that it has almost the same expressiveness as the full parameter space. Additionally, we propose a new regularization loss that considerably enhances the diversity of the fine-tuned generator. Inspired by the reduction in the size of the optimizing parameter space we consider the problem of multi-domain adaptation of GANs, i.e. setting when the same model can adapt to several domains depending on the input query. We propose the HyperDomainNet that is a hypernetwork that predicts our parameterization given the target domain. We empirically confirm that it can successfully learn a number of domains at once and may even generalize to unseen domains. Source code can be found at https://github.com/MACderRu/HyperDomainNet

paragraphs: Adapting a generative adversarial network to a target domain is useful when little training data is available. This paper reduces the number of parameters that must be optimized during that adaptation. Its domain-modulation technique represents the adjustment with a vector of six thousand values, instead of updating StyleGAN2's thirty million weights.

Applied to existing leading adaptation methods, the compact parameterization shows almost the same expressiveness as the full parameter space. The authors also introduce a regularization loss that substantially improves the diversity of the adapted generator. These contributions address both the size of the adaptation problem and the variety of outputs the resulting model produces.

The reduced parameter space also enables HyperDomainNet, a hypernetwork that predicts the modulation parameters for a requested target domain. This lets one model support multiple domains through its input query. Experiments show successful learning of several domains together and suggest possible generalization to unseen domains. That last result is presented as a possibility supported by empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: HyperDomainNet uses a compact generator-modulation vector to support GAN adaptation across multiple domains, with possible transfer to unseen ones.

title: HyperDomainNet: Universal Domain Adaptation for Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: In this paper, we consider a challenging but realistic continual learning problem, Few-Shot Continual Active Learning (FoCAL), where a CL agent is provided with unlabeled data for a new or a previously learned task in each increment and the agent only has limited labeling budget available. Towards this, we build on the continual learning and active learning literature and develop a framework that can allow a CL agent to continually learn new object classes from a few labeled training examples. Our framework represents each object class using a uniform Gaussian mixture model (GMM) and uses pseudo-rehearsal to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. The framework also uses uncertainty measures on the Gaussian representations of the previously learned classes to find the most informative samples to be labeled in an increment. We evaluate our approach on the CORe-50 dataset and on a real humanoid robot for the object classification task. The results show that our approach not only produces state-of-the-art results on the dataset but also allows a real robot to continually learn unseen objects in a real environment with limited labeling supervision provided by its user.

paragraphs: A robot learning over time must recognize new objects while retaining what it learned before. It may receive unlabeled data from either a new task or a previously encountered one, with only a small budget for asking a person to supply labels. The paper formalizes this combination as Few-Shot Continual Active Learning.

The framework represents each object category with a uniform Gaussian mixture model. It uses pseudo-rehearsal to reduce catastrophic forgetting, the loss of earlier knowledge during subsequent learning. It also measures uncertainty using the Gaussian representations of previously learned categories and uses that information to select samples for labeling. These components address retention and label selection within the same learning process.

Evaluation covers the CORe-50 object dataset and an actual humanoid robot. The authors report state-of-the-art dataset results and demonstrate that the robot can learn previously unseen objects in a real environment with limited user labeling. The results support combining continual learning with active sample selection when an agent must keep learning without receiving extensive annotations at every increment.
summary.tldr: A framework combining Gaussian class representations, pseudo-rehearsal, and uncertainty-based label selection enables continual object learning with limited supervision.

title: Few-Shot Continual Active Learning by a Robot

abstract: Communication efficiency has been widely recognized as the bottleneck for large-scale decentralized machine learning applications in multi-agent or federated environments. To tackle the communication bottleneck, there have been many efforts to design communication-compressed algorithms for decentralized nonconvex optimization, where the clients are only allowed to communicate a small amount of quantized information (aka bits) with their neighbors over a predefined graph topology. Despite significant efforts, the state-of-the-art algorithm in the nonconvex setting still suffers from a slower rate of convergence $O((G/T)^{2/3})$ compared with their uncompressed counterpart, where $G$ measures the data heterogeneity across different clients, and $T$ is the number of communication rounds. This paper proposes BEER, which adopts communication compression with gradient tracking, and shows it converges at a faster rate of $O(1/T)$. This significantly improves over the state-of-the-art rate, by matching the rate without compression even under arbitrary data heterogeneity. Numerical experiments are also provided to corroborate our theory and confirm the practical superiority of beer in the data heterogeneous regime.

paragraphs: In decentralized learning, clients communicate with neighboring clients over a fixed network. Sending fewer bits can reduce communication demands, but compression can also slow optimization. This paper addresses that tension for nonconvex problems, particularly when different clients hold substantially different data. Such heterogeneity appears explicitly in the earlier convergence rate discussed by the authors.

BEER combines compressed communication with gradient tracking. The tracking component accompanies the compressed exchanges so that the method can retain a faster convergence rate. The paper proves a rate of O(1/T), where T counts communication rounds, improving on the previously stated O((G/T)^(2/3)) rate, where G measures differences between clients' data.

The new rate matches the uncompressed counterpart even under arbitrary data heterogeneity. This means compression need not worsen the convergence-rate order in the analyzed setting. Numerical experiments support the theoretical result and report practical advantages when client data differ. The contribution links reduced communication to stronger optimization guarantees rather than treating those goals separately.
summary.tldr: BEER combines communication compression and gradient tracking to match an uncompressed O(1/T) convergence rate despite heterogeneous client data.

title: BEER: Fast $O(1/T)$ Rate for Decentralized Nonconvex Optimization with Communication Compression

abstract: Minimizing the inclusive Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is challenging since its gradient is defined as an integral over the posterior. Recently, multiple methods have been proposed to run SGD with biased gradient estimates obtained from a Markov chain. This paper provides the first non-asymptotic convergence analysis of these methods by establishing their mixing rate and gradient variance. To do this, we demonstrate that these methods—which we collectively refer to as Markov chain score ascent (MCSA) methods—can be cast as special cases of the Markov chain gradient descent framework. Furthermore, by leveraging this new understanding, we develop a novel MCSA scheme, parallel MCSA (pMCSA), that achieves a tighter bound on the gradient variance. We demonstrate that this improved theoretical result translates to superior empirical performance.

Recently, multiple methods have been proposed to run SGD with biased gradient estimates obtained from a Markov chain. This paper provides the first non-asymptotic convergence analysis of these methods by establishing their mixing rate and gradient variance. To do this, we demonstrate that these methods—which we collectively refer to as Markov chain score ascent (MCSA) methods—can be cast as special cases of the Markov chain gradient descent framework. Furthermore, by leveraging this new understanding, we develop a novel MCSA scheme, parallel MCSA (pMCSA), that achieves a tighter bound on the gradient variance. We demonstrate that this improved theoretical result translates to superior empirical performance.

paragraphs: Variational inference can fit an approximate posterior by minimizing inclusive Kullback-Leibler divergence. A difficulty is that the required gradient involves an expectation under the posterior itself. Several methods address this by drawing on a Markov chain, but the resulting gradient estimates are biased, complicating the analysis of stochastic gradient optimization.

The paper brings these methods together under the name Markov chain score ascent, or MCSA. It shows that they fit an existing framework for gradient descent with Markovian information. By establishing mixing rates and gradient variance, the authors provide non-asymptotic convergence analysis: guarantees that describe behavior before taking an unlimited-computation limit.

This shared analysis also guides a new method called parallel MCSA. The authors establish a tighter bound on its gradient variance and report that the theoretical improvement is accompanied by better empirical performance. The contribution therefore has two connected parts: explaining previously proposed methods through one mathematical framework and using that explanation to design an improved inference procedure.
summary.tldr: MCSA unifies variational inference methods using Markov-chain gradients and motivates a parallel variant with tighter variance bounds and better reported performance.

title: Markov Chain Score Ascent: A Unifying Framework of Variational Inference with Markovian Gradients

abstract: We study the learning problem of revealed preference in a stochastic setting: a learner observes the utility-maximizing actions of a set of agents whose utility follows some unknown distribution, and the learner aims to infer the distribution through the observations of actions. The problem can be viewed as a single-constraint special case of the inverse linear optimization problem. Existing works all assume that all the agents share one common utility which can easily be violated under practical contexts. In this paper, we consider two settings for the underlying utility distribution: a Gaussian setting where the customer utility follows the von Mises-Fisher distribution, and a $\delta$-corruption setting where the customer utility distribution concentrates on one fixed vector with high probability and is arbitrarily corrupted otherwise. We devise Bayesian approaches for parameter estimation and develop theoretical guarantees for the recovery of the true parameter. We illustrate the algorithm performance through numerical experiments.

Existing works all assume that all the agents share one common utility which can easily be violated under practical contexts. In this paper, we consider two settings for the underlying utility distribution: a Gaussian setting where the customer utility follows the von Mises-Fisher distribution, and a $\delta$-corruption setting where the customer utility distribution concentrates on one fixed vector with high probability and is arbitrarily corrupted otherwise.
