paragraphs: Revealed preference learning tries to infer what agents value by observing the actions they choose. This paper studies a stochastic version: agents maximize their own utilities, but those utilities come from an unknown distribution. The learner's goal is to recover that distribution from observed choices, allowing preferences to vary across agents.

The authors consider two forms of variation. One uses a von Mises-Fisher distribution for utility. The other is a corruption model in which utility is concentrated on a fixed vector with high probability but can be arbitrarily corrupted otherwise. These settings give structured alternatives to assuming that every agent shares exactly the same utility.

The proposed Bayesian approaches estimate the relevant parameters, and the paper develops theoretical guarantees for recovering the true parameter. Numerical experiments illustrate the algorithms' performance. The problem is also framed as a single-constraint special case of inverse linear optimization, connecting preference inference to learning an optimization model from its solutions. The central contribution is extending that inference problem to specified forms of heterogeneous or corrupted utility.
summary.tldr: Bayesian methods infer utility-distribution parameters from agents' choices under two stochastic preference models, with theoretical recovery guarantees.

title: Learning from Stochastically Revealed Preference

abstract: Temporal Difference (TD) learning is ubiquitous in reinforcement learning, where it is often combined with off-policy sampling and function approximation. Unfortunately learning with this combination (known as the deadly triad), exhibits instability and unbounded error. To account for this, modern Reinforcement Learning methods often implicitly (or sometimes explicitly) assume that regularization is sufficient to mitigate the problem in practice; indeed, the standard deadly triad examples from the literature can be ``fixed'' via proper regularization. In this paper, we introduce a series of new counterexamples to show that the instability and unbounded error of TD methods is not solved by regularization. We demonstrate that, in the off-policy setting with linear function approximation, TD methods can fail to learn a non-trivial value function under any amount of regularization; we further show that regularization can induce divergence under common conditions; and we show that one of the most promising methods to mitigate this divergence (Emphatic TD algorithms) may also diverge under regularization. We further demonstrate such divergence when using neural networks as function approximators. Thus, we argue that the role of regularization in TD methods needs to be reconsidered, given that it is insufficient to prevent divergence and may itself introduce instability. There needs to be much more care in the practical and theoretical application of regularization to Reinforcement Learning methods.

Regularization fixes several familiar examples, encouraging the belief that it can generally control the problem. This paper challenges that belief through new counterexamples that expose failures beyond those standard cases.

For off-policy learning with linear function approximation, the authors show settings in which no amount of regularization enables a TD method to learn a nontrivial value function. They also show that regularization can itself induce divergence under common conditions. Even Emphatic TD, a method intended to address divergence, can diverge when regularized.

The paper additionally demonstrates such divergence with neural-network function approximators. These results establish that regularization is insufficient as a general safeguard and can introduce instability of its own. They do not claim that every regularized TD method diverges. Their practical and theoretical significance is that successful regularization on familiar examples does not justify assuming stability in other off-policy learning settings.
summary.tldr: New counterexamples show that regularization can fail to stabilize off-policy TD learning and can sometimes cause divergence.

title: The Pitfalls of Regularization in Off-Policy TD Learning

abstract: Euclidean geometry is among the earliest forms of mathematical thinking. While the geometric primitives underlying its constructions, such as perfect lines and circles, do not often occur in the natural world, humans rarely struggle to perceive and reason with them. Will computer vision models trained on natural images show the same sensitivity to Euclidean geometry? Here we explore these questions by studying few-shot generalization in the universe of Euclidean geometry constructions. We introduce Geoclidean, a domain-specific language for Euclidean geometry, and use it to generate two datasets of geometric concept learning tasks for benchmarking generalization judgements of humans and machines. We find that humans are indeed sensitive to Euclidean geometry and generalize strongly from a few visual examples of a geometric concept. In contrast, low-level and high-level visual features from standard computer vision models pretrained on natural images do not support correct generalization. Thus Geoclidean represents a novel few-shot generalization benchmark for geometric concept learning, where the performance of humans and of AI models diverge. The Geoclidean framework and dataset are publicly available for download.

paragraphs: Geoclidean studies whether vision models can recognize geometric concepts after seeing only a few examples. Humans readily reason about ideal lines and circles even though perfect geometric primitives are uncommon in natural scenes. The paper asks whether models pretrained on natural images acquire a comparable sensitivity to Euclidean constructions.

The authors introduce a domain-specific language for describing Euclidean geometry and use it to generate two datasets of concept-learning tasks. These tasks provide a shared setting for comparing human and machine generalization judgments. The emphasis is on recognizing what new examples share with a geometric concept, rather than merely recognizing familiar objects from natural photographs.

The study finds that humans generalize strongly from a small number of visual examples. In contrast, both low-level and high-level features from the examined standard vision models fail to support correct generalization. Geoclidean therefore exposes a specific gap between human geometric reasoning and the representations learned by those models. Its language and datasets provide a public benchmark for investigating that gap.
summary.tldr: Geoclidean benchmarks geometric concept learning, revealing strong human few-shot generalization that the evaluated natural-image vision features do not support.

title: Geoclidean: Few-Shot Generalization in Euclidean Geometry

abstract: The predictive ability of supervised learning algorithms hinges on the quality of annotated examples, whose labels often come from multiple crowdsourced annotators with diverse expertise. To aggregate noisy crowdsourced annotations, many existing methods employ an annotator-specific instance-independent noise transition matrix to characterize the labeling skills of each annotator. Learning an instance-dependent noise transition model, however, is challenging and remains relatively less explored. To address this problem, in this paper, we formulate the noise transition model in a Bayesian framework and subsequently design a new label correction algorithm. Specifically, we approximate the instance-dependent noise transition matrices using a Bayesian network with a hierarchical spike and slab prior. To theoretically characterize the distance between the noise transition model and the true instance-dependent noise transition matrix, we provide a posterior-concentration theorem that ensures the posterior consistency in terms of the Hellinger distance. We further formulate the label correction process as a hypothesis testing problem and propose a novel algorithm to infer the true label from the noisy annotations based on the pairwise likelihood ratio test. Moreover, we establish an information-theoretic bound on the Bayes error for the proposed method. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced labels come from annotators with different expertise, and an annotator's mistakes may depend on the particular example being labeled. Many aggregation methods assign each annotator one fixed noise transition matrix, treating their error pattern as independent of the example. This paper develops a model that allows those error patterns to vary with the instance.

The authors place the noise model in a Bayesian framework and approximate instance-dependent transition matrices with a Bayesian network using a hierarchical spike-and-slab prior. They then treat label correction as hypothesis testing. Pairwise likelihood-ratio tests compare candidate labels using the observed annotations and the learned noise model to infer the underlying label.

The theoretical results include posterior concentration and consistency measured by Hellinger distance, which characterize how the inferred noise model approaches the true one. An additional information-theoretic bound describes Bayes error for the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets support its effectiveness. The contribution connects a more detailed account of annotator error with a principled procedure for correcting labels.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model of example-dependent annotator errors supports label correction through likelihood-ratio testing, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation.

title: Label Correction of Crowdsourced Noisy Annotations with an Instance-Dependent Noise Transition Model

abstract: Deep generative models can generate high-fidelity audio conditioned on varioustypes of representations (e.g., mel-spectrograms, Mel-frequency Cepstral Coefficients(MFCC)). Recently, such models have been used to synthesize audiowaveforms conditioned on highly compressed representations. Although suchmethods produce impressive results, they are prone to generate audible artifactswhen the conditioning is flawed or imperfect. An alternative modeling approach isto use diffusion models. However, these have mainly been used as speech vocoders(i.e., conditioned on mel-spectrograms) or generating relatively low samplingrate signals. In this work, we propose a high-fidelity multi-band diffusion-basedframework that generates any type of audio modality (e.g., speech, music, environmentalsounds) from low-bitrate discrete representations. At equal bit rate,the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art generative techniques in termsof perceptual quality. Training and evaluation code are available on the facebookresearch/audiocraft github project. Samples are available on the followinglink (https://ai.honu.io/papers/mbd/).

paragraphs: Generating audio from a highly compressed representation requires reconstructing a waveform from limited conditioning information. Existing generative approaches can produce impressive results, but imperfect conditioning can lead to audible artifacts. This paper investigates diffusion as an alternative way to generate high-fidelity audio from low-bitrate discrete representations, addressing the quality of reconstruction from compact tokens.

The authors propose a multi-band diffusion framework intended to handle different audio modalities, including speech, music, and environmental sounds. That scope extends beyond the speech-vocoder and relatively low-sampling-rate applications emphasized in earlier diffusion work described by the authors. The central contribution is a common generation framework whose input is a compressed discrete representation across these kinds of audio.

At equal bitrate, the proposed method achieves better perceptual quality than state-of-the-art generative techniques in the reported evaluation. Holding bitrate equal makes the result a comparison of audible quality under the same compression budget. The finding supports diffusion as a useful reconstruction approach when compact audio representations must still yield high-quality sound.
summary.tldr: Multi-band diffusion reconstructs diverse audio from low-bitrate discrete tokens with better reported perceptual quality than leading generative methods at equal bitrate.

title: From Discrete Tokens to High-Fidelity Audio Using Multi-Band Diffusion

abstract: Pandora’s Box is a central problem in decision making under uncertainty that can model various real life scenarios. In this problem we are given n boxes, each with a fixed opening cost, and an unknown value drawn from a known distribution, only revealed if we pay the opening cost. Our goal is to find a strategy for opening boxes to minimize the sum of the value selected and the opening cost paid.In this work we revisit Pandora’s Box when the value distributions are correlated, first studied in [CGT+20]. We show that the optimal algorithm for the independent case, given by Weitzman’s rule, directly works for the correlated case. In fact, our algorithm results in significantly improved approximation guarantees compared to the previous work, while also being substantially simpler. We also show how to implement the rule given only sample access to the correlated distribution of values. Specifically, we find that a number of samples that is polynomial in the number of boxes is sufficient for the algorithm to work.

paragraphs: In the Pandora’s Box problem studied here, each box has an opening cost and a hidden value. Paying the cost reveals that value. The decision-maker must choose which boxes to open and which revealed value to select, aiming to minimize the selected value plus the total cost of opening boxes.

The paper considers correlated values, where information revealed by one box can be related to values in others. Weitzman’s rule is optimal in the independent case. The authors show that the rule also applies directly to the correlated setting, obtaining substantially improved approximation guarantees over earlier work through a simpler algorithm.

This does not make the independent-case optimality claim an optimality claim for arbitrary correlations: the stated correlated-case result is an approximation guarantee. The paper also shows how to implement the rule using only samples from the joint distribution of values. A number of samples polynomial in the number of boxes is sufficient, connecting the theoretical rule to a setting where the distribution is accessed through observations.
summary.tldr: Weitzman’s rule extends to correlated Pandora’s Box values with improved approximation guarantees and an implementation requiring polynomially many samples.

title: Weitzman's Rule for Pandora's Box with Correlations

abstract: We study reinforcement learning (RL) in the setting of continuous time and space, for an infinite horizon with a discounted objective and the underlying dynamics driven by a stochastic differential equation. Built upon recent advances in the continuous approach to RL, we develop a notion of occupation time (specifically for a discounted objective), and show how it can be effectively used to derive performance difference and local approximation formulas. We further extend these results to illustrate their applications in the PG (policy gradient) and TRPO/PPO (trust region policy optimization/ proximal policy optimization) methods, which have been familiar and powerful tools in the discrete RL setting but under-developed in continuous RL. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness and advantages of our approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning in continuous time and space, with random system dynamics described by a stochastic differential equation. The objective extends over an infinite horizon while discounting future rewards. This setting requires mathematical tools suited to continuous evolution when analyzing how changing a policy changes its expected performance.

The authors develop a notion of occupation time tailored to the discounted objective. It describes time spent across the system’s states while accounting for the discounting of later behavior. They use this construction to derive performance-difference formulas and local approximations, creating a basis for comparing policies and reasoning about nearby policy changes.

These results are then extended to policy gradient, trust region policy optimization, and proximal policy optimization. Those methods are established in discrete reinforcement learning but less developed in the continuous setting considered here. Numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness and advantages of the proposed approach. The contribution links continuous-time analysis to practical policy-optimization methods under the specified stochastic dynamics and discounted objective.
summary.tldr: A discounted occupation-time formulation supports policy comparison and policy-optimization methods for reinforcement learning in continuous time and space.

title: Policy Optimization for Continuous Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various applications, but their performance can be sensitive to specific data properties of the graph datasets they operate on. Current literature on understanding the limitations of GNNs has primarily employed a \emph{model-driven} approach that leverage heuristics and domain knowledge from network science or graph theory to model the GNN behaviors, which is time-consuming and highly subjective. In this work, we propose a \emph{metadata-driven} approach to analyze the sensitivity of GNNs to graph data properties, motivated by the increasing availability of graph learning benchmarks. We perform a multivariate sparse regression analysis on the metadata derived from benchmarking GNN performance across diverse datasets, yielding a set of salient data properties. To validate the effectiveness of our data-driven approach, we focus on one identified data property, the degree distribution, and investigate how this property influences GNN performance through theoretical analysis and controlled experiments. Our theoretical findings reveal that datasets with more balanced degree distribution exhibit better linear separability of node representations, thus leading to better GNN performance. We also conduct controlled experiments using synthetic datasets with varying degree distributions, and the results align well with our theoretical findings. Collectively, both the theoretical analysis and controlled experiments verify that the proposed metadata-driven approach is effective in identifying critical data properties for GNNs.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can perform differently depending on the properties of the graphs they receive. This paper investigates those differences by analyzing information collected from existing benchmarks. Instead of beginning with a manually chosen explanation of model behavior, it looks for relationships between dataset properties and measured GNN performance across diverse datasets.

The authors use multivariate sparse regression to identify a small set of influential properties while considering several properties together. They then examine one identified factor in detail: the degree distribution, which describes how the number of connections varies across nodes. This turns a pattern found in benchmark metadata into a specific question that theoretical analysis and controlled experiments can investigate.

Their analysis links more balanced degree distributions to node representations that are easier to separate with a linear classifier, supporting better GNN performance. Experiments on synthetic graphs with varying degree distributions agree with the theoretical findings. Together, these results support metadata analysis as a useful way to identify consequential graph properties and direct deeper investigations of GNN behavior.
summary.tldr: Benchmark metadata helps identify graph properties that affect GNN performance, with degree distribution validated through theory and controlled experiments.

title: A Metadata-Driven Approach to Understand Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Text-to-SQL parsing, which aims at converting natural language instructions into executable SQLs, has gained increasing attention in recent years. In particular, GPT-4 and Claude-2 have shown impressive results in this task. However, most of the prevalent benchmarks, i.e., Spider, and WikiSQL, focus on database schema with few rows of database contents leaving the gap between academic study and real-world applications. To mitigate this gap, we present BIRD, a BIg benchmark for laRge-scale Database grounded in text-to-SQL tasks, containing 12,751 pairs of text-to-SQL data and 95 databases with a total size of 33.4 GB, spanning 37 professional domains. Our emphasis on database values highlights the new challenges of dirty database contents, external knowledge between NL questions and database contents, and SQL efficiency, particularly in the context of massive databases. To solve these problems, text-to-SQL models must feature database value comprehension in addition to semantic parsing. The experimental results demonstrate the significance of database values in generating accurate text-to-SQLs for big databases. Furthermore, even the most popular and effective text-to-SQL models, i.e. GPT-4, only achieve 54.89% in execution accuracy, which is still far from the human result of 92.96%, proving that challenges still stand. We also provide an efficiency analysis to offer insights into generating text-to-efficient-SQLs that are beneficial to industries. We believe that BIRD will contribute to advancing real-world applications of text-to-SQL research.The leaderboard and source code are available: https://bird-bench.github.io/.

paragraphs: Text-to-SQL systems turn natural-language requests into database queries. The paper argues that benchmarks emphasizing database structure with little actual content leave important practical challenges underexamined. A system working with large databases must understand stored values, handle messy content, connect questions to relevant external knowledge, and generate queries that run efficiently.

BIRD introduces 12,751 text-to-SQL pairs across 95 databases, totaling 33.4 GB and covering 37 professional domains. Its emphasis on database contents tests more than whether a model can translate a sentence into plausible SQL syntax. Successful queries must connect the user's meaning to what the database actually contains.

The reported evaluation places GPT-4 at 54.89% execution accuracy, compared with a human result of 92.96%. This gap demonstrates substantial remaining difficulty on the benchmark. The paper also analyzes query efficiency, highlighting that producing a correct answer and producing an efficient query are both relevant to database interfaces intended for practical use.
summary.tldr: BIRD tests text-to-SQL on large, content-rich databases and reveals a substantial execution-accuracy gap between GPT-4 and humans.

title: Can LLM Already Serve as A Database Interface? A BIg Bench for Large-Scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQLs

abstract: Prior research on policy adaptation in multi-agent games has often relied on online interaction with the target agent in training, which can be expensive and impractical in real-world scenarios. Inspired by recent progress in offline reinforcement learn- ing, this paper studies offline policy adaptation, which aims to utilize the target agent’s behavior data to exploit its weakness or enable effective cooperation. We investigate its distinct challenges of distributional shift and risk-free deviation, and propose a novel learning objective, conservative offline adaptation, that optimizes the worst-case performance against any dataset consistent proxy models. We pro- pose an efficient algorithm called Constrained Self-Play (CSP) that incorporates dataset information into regularized policy learning. We prove that CSP learns a near-optimal risk-free offline adaptation policy upon convergence. Empirical results demonstrate that CSP outperforms non-conservative baselines in various environments, including Maze, predator-prey, MuJoCo, and Google Football.

paragraphs: Adapting to another agent can help exploit its weaknesses in competition or cooperate with it more effectively. Many approaches require interacting with that agent during training, which can be expensive or impractical. This paper instead studies adaptation using an existing dataset of the target agent's behavior.

The difficulty is that recorded behavior may not determine how the target will behave under every policy the learner might adopt. The proposed conservative objective therefore optimizes worst-case performance across proxy models consistent with the dataset. This addresses distributional shift and the paper's risk-free deviation objective by making uncertainty about the target part of policy learning.

The authors introduce Constrained Self-Play, which incorporates dataset information into regularized policy learning. They prove that, upon convergence, it learns a near-optimal risk-free offline adaptation policy. Experiments report improvements over non-conservative baselines in Maze, predator-prey, MuJoCo, and Google Football. The theoretical claim explicitly depends on convergence, while the experiments show benefits across the evaluated environments.
summary.tldr: Constrained Self-Play adapts to other agents from offline behavior data by optimizing conservatively over dataset-consistent models.

title: Conservative Offline Policy Adaptation in Multi-Agent Games

abstract: Semantic segmentation datasets often exhibit two types of imbalance: \textit{class imbalance}, where some classes appear more frequently than others and \textit{size imbalance}, where some objects occupy more pixels than others. This causes traditional evaluation metrics to be biased towards \textit{majority classes} (e.g. overall pixel-wise accuracy) and \textit{large objects} (e.g. mean pixel-wise accuracy and per-dataset mean intersection over union). To address these shortcomings, we propose the use of fine-grained mIoUs along with corresponding worst-case metrics, thereby offering a more holistic evaluation of segmentation techniques. These fine-grained metrics offer less bias towards large objects, richer statistical information, and valuable insights into model and dataset auditing. Furthermore, we undertake an extensive benchmark study, where we train and evaluate 15 modern neural networks with the proposed metrics on 12 diverse natural and aerial segmentation datasets. Our benchmark study highlights the necessity of not basing evaluations on a single metric and confirms that fine-grained mIoUs reduce the bias towards large objects. Moreover, we identify the crucial role played by architecture designs and loss functions, which lead to best practices in optimizing fine-grained metrics. The code is available at \href{https://github.com/zifuwanggg/JDTLosses}{https://github.com/zifuwanggg/JDTLosses}.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories to image pixels, but a good aggregate score can obscure uneven performance. Frequent classes contribute more observations, and large objects occupy more pixels than small ones. This paper examines how those two imbalances affect common metrics, including measures that already average performance across classes.

The authors propose fine-grained mean intersection-over-union measures together with corresponding worst-case metrics. Their purpose is to reduce bias toward large objects and reveal more about the distribution of performance. This provides additional information for auditing datasets and models, beyond a single score that compresses different kinds of success and failure into one number.

The study trains and evaluates 15 modern networks on 12 natural and aerial segmentation datasets. Its findings confirm reduced large-object bias and support evaluating models with multiple metrics. The authors also identify architecture and loss-function choices as important for optimizing the fine-grained measures. Thus, the contribution addresses both how segmentation quality is assessed and how training choices relate to the more detailed assessment.
summary.tldr: Fine-grained segmentation metrics reduce large-object bias and reveal performance differences hidden by conventional aggregate scores.

title: Revisiting Evaluation Metrics for Semantic Segmentation: Optimization and Evaluation of Fine-grained Intersection over Union

abstract: Privacy and communication constraints are two major bottlenecks in federated learning (FL) and analytics (FA). We study the optimal accuracy of mean and frequency estimation (canonical models for FL and FA respectively) under joint communication and $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy (DP) constraints. We consider both the central and the multi-message shuffled DP models. We show that in order to achieve the optimal $\ell_2$ error under $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP, it is sufficient for each client to send $\Theta\left( n \min\left(\varepsilon, \varepsilon^2\right)\right)$ bits for FL %{\color{blue}(assuming the dimension $d \gg n \min\left(\varepsilon, \varepsilon^2\right)$)} and $\Theta\left(\log\left( n\min\left(\varepsilon, \varepsilon^2\right) \right)\right)$ bits for FA to the server, where $n$ is the number of participating clients. Without compression, each client needs $O(d)$ bits and $O\left(\log d\right)$ bits for the mean and frequency estimation problems respectively (where $d$ corresponds to the number of trainable parameters in FL or the domain size in FA), meaning that we can get significant savings in the regime $ n \min\left(\varepsilon, \varepsilon^2\right) = o(d)$, which is often the relevant regime in practice. In the first method, the random selection is revealed to the server, which results in a central DP guarantee with optimal privacy-communication-accuracy trade-offs. In the second method, the random data parts from the clients are shuffled by a secure shuffler resulting in a multi-message shuffling scheme with the same optimal trade-offs. abstract: Link prediction is a critical problem in graph learning with broad applications such as recommender systems and knowledge graph completion. Numerous research efforts have been directed at solving this problem, including approaches based on similarity metrics and Graph Neural Networks (GNN). However, most existing solutions are still rooted in conventional supervised learning, which makes it challenging to adapt over time to changing customer interests and to address the inherent dilemma of exploitation versus exploration in link prediction.To tackle these challenges, this paper reformulates link prediction as a sequential decision-making process, where each link prediction interaction occurs sequentially. We propose a novel fusion algorithm, PRB (PageRank Bandits), which is the first to combine contextual bandits with PageRank for collaborative exploitation and exploration. We also introduce a new reward formulation and provide a theoretical performance guarantee for PRB. Finally, we extensively evaluate PRB in both online and offline settings, comparing it with bandit-based and graph-based methods. The empirical success of PRB demonstrates the value of the proposed fusion approach. Our code is released at https://github.com/jiaruzouu/PRB.

paragraphs: Link prediction estimates which connections should exist in a graph, with applications such as recommendations and knowledge graph completion. Many existing approaches treat it as supervised learning. The paper argues that this framing makes it difficult to adapt to changing customer interests and to balance exploiting promising connections with exploring uncertain ones.

PageRank Bandits reframes the task as a sequence of decisions, with each link-prediction interaction occurring in turn. Its PRB algorithm combines contextual bandits with PageRank to coordinate exploitation and exploration. The bandit formulation explicitly places this trade-off inside the decision process, while PageRank brings graph-based information into the combined approach. The authors identify this combination as a first.

The paper also introduces a reward formulation and provides a theoretical performance guarantee for PRB. Evaluations cover both online and offline settings and compare the method with bandit-based and graph-based alternatives. The reported empirical success supports treating link prediction as an ongoing decision problem and combining the two approaches, especially when repeated interactions and changing interests are central to the task.
summary.tldr: PageRank Bandits combines contextual bandits and PageRank to handle link prediction as sequential decisions balancing exploitation and exploration.

title: PageRank Bandits for Link Prediction

abstract: Transformer models have gained significant attention due to their power in machine learning tasks. Their extensive deployment has raised concerns about the potential leakage of sensitive information during inference. However, when being applied to Transformers, existing approaches based on secure two-party computation (2PC) bring about efficiency limitations in two folds: (1) resource-intensive matrix multiplications in linear layers, and (2) complex non-linear activation functions like $\mathsf{GELU}$ and $\mathsf{Softmax}$. This work presents a new two-party inference framework $\mathsf{Nimbus}$ for Transformer models. Specifically, we propose a new 2PC paradigm to securely compute matrix multiplications based on an outer-product insight, which achieves $2.9\times \sim 12.5\times$ performance improvements compared to the state-of-the-art (SOTA) protocol. Furthermore, through a new observation of utilizing the input distribution, we propose an approach of low-degree polynomial approximation for $\mathsf{GELU}$ and $\mathsf{Softmax}$, which improves the performance of the SOTA polynomial approximation by $2.9\times \sim 4.0\times$, where the average accuracy loss of our approach is 0.08\% compared to the non-2PC inference without privacy. Compared with the SOTA two-party inference, $\mathsf{Nimbus}$ improves the end-to-end performance of $BERT_{base}$ inference by $2.7\times \sim 4.7\times$ across different network settings.

Existing approaches face two major efficiency bottlenecks: large matrix multiplications in linear layers and nonlinear operations such as GELU and Softmax. Nimbus introduces a framework that addresses both sources of cost.

For matrix multiplication, the authors develop a secure computation paradigm based on an outer-product formulation. They report performance improvements of 2.9 to 12.5 times over the state-of-the-art protocol. For GELU and Softmax, they use information about input distributions to construct low-degree polynomial approximations. Those approximations improve performance by 2.9 to 4.0 times over the compared state-of-the-art polynomial approach.

End-to-end BERT-base inference improves by 2.7 to 4.7 times over state-of-the-art two-party inference across different network settings. These results connect the gains in individual operations to overall execution, showing that optimizing both linear algebra and nonlinear approximations can substantially improve the practical efficiency of private Transformer inference.
summary.tldr: Nimbus speeds up secure two-party BERT-base inference by 2.7–4.7 times through improved matrix multiplication and efficient nonlinear approximations.

title: Nimbus: Secure and Efficient Two-Party Inference for Transformers

abstract: For classification and regression on tabular data, the dominance of gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) has recently been challenged by often much slower deep learning methods with extensive hyperparameter tuning. We address this discrepancy by introducing (a) RealMLP, an improved multilayer perceptron (MLP), and (b) strong meta-tuned default parameters for GBDTs and RealMLP. We tune RealMLP and the default parameters on a meta-train benchmark with 118 datasets and compare them to hyperparameter-optimized versions on a disjoint meta-test benchmark with 90 datasets, as well as the GBDT-friendly benchmark by Grinsztajn et al. (2022). Our benchmark results on medium-to-large tabular datasets (1K--500K samples) show that RealMLP offers a favorable time-accuracy tradeoff compared to other neural baselines and is competitive with GBDTs in terms of benchmark scores. Moreover, a combination of RealMLP and GBDTs with improved default parameters can achieve excellent results without hyperparameter tuning. Finally, we demonstrate that some of RealMLP's improvements can also considerably improve the performance of TabR with default parameters.

paragraphs: Strong results on tabular prediction can depend on extensive hyperparameter tuning, which adds computation and effort beyond fitting a model once. This paper addresses that practical cost by improving both a neural model and the default settings used for neural networks and gradient-boosted decision trees.

The authors introduce RealMLP, an improved multilayer perceptron, and select strong defaults using a collection of 118 datasets. They evaluate these choices on a separate collection of 90 datasets, alongside a benchmark favorable to boosted trees. Separating the collections tests whether defaults selected across earlier tasks remain useful on different datasets.

For datasets containing 1,000 to 500,000 samples, RealMLP achieves a favorable balance of training time and accuracy against other neural baselines and competitive benchmark scores against boosted trees. Combining RealMLP with boosted trees using improved defaults can produce excellent results without task-specific hyperparameter tuning. The authors also show that some RealMLP improvements benefit TabR with default settings, suggesting usefulness beyond a single model design.
summary.tldr: RealMLP and defaults selected across many datasets deliver strong tabular prediction results while reducing the need for task-specific tuning.

title: Better by default: Strong pre-tuned MLPs and boosted trees on tabular data

abstract: We consider the problem of model selection in a high-dimensional sparse linear regression model under privacy constraints. We propose a differentially private (DP) best subset selection method with strong statistical utility properties by adopting the well-known exponential mechanism for selecting the best model. To achieve computational expediency, we propose an efficient Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and under certain regularity conditions, we establish that it enjoys polynomial mixing time to its stationary distribution. As a result, we also establish both approximate differential privacy and statistical utility for the estimates of the mixed Metropolis-Hastings chain. Finally, we perform some illustrative experiments on simulated data showing that our algorithm can quickly identify active features under reasonable privacy budget constraints.

paragraphs: High-dimensional sparse regression seeks a small set of useful features among many candidates. Privacy requirements add another concern: selecting that set must protect information about the underlying data. The paper proposes a differentially private best-subset selection method that uses the exponential mechanism and has strong statistical utility properties.

To make selection computationally practical, the authors develop a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. This procedure uses a chain of random transitions to approach a target distribution. Under specified regularity conditions, they prove polynomial mixing time, meaning that the chain approaches its stationary distribution within a computational bound that grows polynomially with the relevant problem quantities.

The authors then establish approximate differential privacy and statistical utility for estimates obtained after the chain has mixed. Simulated-data experiments illustrate that the method can quickly identify active features under reasonable privacy budgets. The contribution links three requirements that must work together: protecting data, selecting statistically useful features, and computing the selection efficiently under the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: A private subset-selection method gains conditional polynomial-time sampling guarantees while retaining statistical utility.

title: On the Computational Complexity of Private High-dimensional Model Selection

abstract: The rapid development of large language and vision models (LLVMs) has been driven by advances in visual instruction tuning. Recently, open-source LLVMs have curated high-quality visual instruction tuning datasets and utilized additional vision encoders or multiple computer vision models in order to narrow the performance gap with powerful closed-source LLVMs. These advancements are attributed to multifaceted information required for diverse capabilities, including fundamental image understanding, real-world knowledge about common-sense and non-object concepts (e.g., charts, diagrams, symbols, signs, and math problems), and step-by-step procedures for solving complex questions. Drawing from the multifaceted information, we present a new efficient LLVM, Mamba-based traversal of rationales (Meteor), which leverages multifaceted rationale to enhance understanding and answering capabilities. To embed lengthy rationales containing abundant information, we employ the Mamba architecture, capable of processing sequential data with linear time complexity. We introduce a new concept of traversal of rationale that facilitates efficient embedding of rationale. Subsequently, the backbone multimodal language model (MLM) is trained to generate answers with the aid of rationale. Through these steps, Meteor achieves significant improvements in vision language performances across multiple evaluation benchmarks requiring diverse capabilities, without scaling up the model size or employing additional vision encoders and computer vision models.

paragraphs: Answering visual questions can require several kinds of information at once: recognizing image content, applying background knowledge, interpreting symbols or diagrams, and following a sequence of reasoning steps. Meteor uses rich rationales to bring these forms of information into a language-and-vision model's training.

The method employs Mamba to process lengthy rationales efficiently, drawing on its linear-time handling of sequential data. A proposed rationale traversal mechanism embeds this information, after which the backbone multimodal language model is trained to generate answers with help from the rationale. This makes the treatment of explanatory information a central part of the training approach.

The authors report significant improvements across multiple vision-language benchmarks covering diverse capabilities. These gains are achieved without increasing model size or adding vision encoders or other computer vision models. The results suggest that improving how a model incorporates multifaceted rationales can strengthen its visual understanding and answering capabilities while retaining the stated architectural scale.
summary.tldr: Meteor uses Mamba to embed rich rationales efficiently, improving vision-language performance without enlarging the model or adding vision encoders.

title: Meteor: Mamba-based Traversal of Rationale for Large Language and Vision Models

abstract: Our paper addresses the complex task of transferring a hairstyle from a reference image to an input photo for virtual hair try-on. This task is challenging due to the need to adapt to various photo poses, the sensitivity of hairstyles, and the lack of objective metrics. The current state of the art hairstyle transfer methods use an optimization process for different parts of the approach, making them inexcusably slow. At the same time, faster encoder-based models are of very low quality because they either operate in StyleGAN's W+ space or use other low-dimensional image generators. Additionally, both approaches have a problem with hairstyle transfer when the source pose is very different from the target pose, because they either don't consider the pose at all or deal with it inefficiently. In our paper, we present the HairFast model, which uniquely solves these problems and achieves high resolution, near real-time performance, and superior reconstruction compared to optimization problem-based methods. Our solution includes a new architecture operating in the FS latent space of StyleGAN, an enhanced inpainting approach, and improved encoders for better alignment, color transfer, and a new encoder for post-processing. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated on realism metrics after random hairstyle transfer and reconstruction when the original hairstyle is transferred. In the most difficult scenario of transferring both shape and color of a hairstyle from different images, our method performs in less than a second on the Nvidia V100.

The task must handle differences in pose while preserving convincing hair shape and color. The paper identifies a practical tradeoff in existing methods: optimization-based approaches are slow, while faster encoder-based systems can deliver poor quality. For the difficult setting where hairstyle shape and color come from different images, the method completes the transfer in under one second on an Nvidia V100. summary.tldr: HairFast combines StyleGAN FS-space encoding, alignment, and inpainting for realistic hairstyle transfer in under a second on an Nvidia V100.

title: HairFastGAN: Realistic and Robust Hair Transfer with a Fast Encoder-Based Approach

abstract: When evaluating stimuli reconstruction results it is tempting to assume that higher fidelity text and image generation is due to an improved understanding of the brain or more powerful signal extraction from neural recordings. However, in practice, new reconstruction methods could improve performance for at least three other reasons: learning more about the distribution of stimuli, becoming better at reconstructing text or images in general, or exploiting weaknesses in current image and/or text evaluation metrics. Here we disentangle how much of the reconstruction is due to these other factors vs. productively using the neural recordings. We introduce BrainBits, a method that uses a bottleneck to quantify the amount of signal extracted from neural recordings that is actually necessary to reproduce a method's reconstruction fidelity. We find that it takes surprisingly little information from the brain to produce reconstructions with high fidelity. In these cases, it is clear that the priors of the methods' generative models are so powerful that the outputs they produce extrapolate far beyond the neural signal they decode. Given that reconstructing stimuli can be improved independently by either improving signal extraction from the brain or by building more powerful generative models, improving the latter may fool us into thinking we are improving the former. We propose that methods should report a method-specific random baseline, a reconstruction ceiling, and a curve of performance as a function of bottleneck size, with the ultimate goal of using more of the neural recordings.

paragraphs: A convincing image or text reconstructed from brain recordings can seem like evidence of better neural decoding. The paper points out that reconstruction can also improve because a generative model knows more about likely stimuli, produces better outputs generally, or benefits from weaknesses in evaluation metrics. Output quality alone cannot separate these contributions.

BrainBits introduces an information bottleneck to measure how much signal from neural recordings is needed to preserve a method's reconstruction fidelity. Restricting the information that passes through this bottleneck helps distinguish what the reconstruction requires from the recordings and what the generative model can supply through its prior knowledge.

The authors find cases where surprisingly little neural information is sufficient for high-fidelity reconstruction. In those cases, the generated output extends substantially beyond the decoded signal. They propose reporting a method-specific random baseline, a reconstruction ceiling, and performance across bottleneck sizes. Together, these measurements would help assess whether better-looking reconstructions reflect greater use of brain recordings or improvements elsewhere in the system.
summary.tldr: BrainBits uses an information bottleneck to show that high-fidelity reconstructions can depend on surprisingly little neural signal.

title: BrainBits: How Much of the Brain are Generative Reconstruction Methods Using?

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known for their exceptional performance in natural language processing, making them highly effective in many human life-related tasks. The attention mechanism in the Transformer architecture is a critical component of LLMs, as it allows the model to selectively focus on specific input parts. The softmax unit, which is a key part of the attention mechanism, normalizes the attention scores. Hence, the performance of LLMs in various NLP tasks depends significantly on the crucial role played by the attention mechanism with the softmax unit.In-context learning is one of the celebrated abilities of recent LLMs. Without further parameter updates, Transformers can learn to predict based on few in-context examples. However, the reason why Transformers becomes in-context learners is not well understood.Recently, in-context learning has been studied from a mathematical perspective with simplified linear self-attention without softmax unit. Based on a linear regression formulation $\min_x\| Ax - b \|_2$, existing works show linear Transformers' capability of learning linear functions in context. The capability of Transformers with softmax unit approaching full Transformers, however, remains unexplored.In this work, we study the in-context learning based on a softmax regression formulation $\min_{x} \| \langle \exp(Ax), {\bf 1}_n \rangle^{-1} \exp(Ax) - b \|_2$. We show the upper bounds of the data transformations induced by a single self-attention layer with softmax unit and by gradient-descent on a $\ell_2$ regression loss for softmax prediction function.Our theoretical results imply that when training self-attention-only Transformers for fundamental regression tasks, the models learned by gradient-descent and Transformers show great similarity.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a transformer adapt its predictions using examples in the input without updating its parameters. Mathematical studies have investigated this behavior through linear attention, but removing softmax leaves out an important part of standard attention. This paper studies a regression formulation that retains softmax normalization.

The formulation measures the difference between a softmax prediction and a target using an L2 loss. Within this setting, the authors derive upper bounds for data transformations associated with one softmax self-attention layer and with gradient descent on the regression objective. This provides a mathematical basis for comparing attention-based transformations with changes produced through optimization.

The theoretical results indicate strong similarity between the models associated with these processes when training attention-only transformers on fundamental regression tasks. The significance is a connection between learning through contextual examples and learning through weight changes in a setting closer to standard attention than linear models. The claim remains scoped to the studied softmax-regression framework and does not assert an exact equivalence for full language models.
summary.tldr: A softmax-regression analysis establishes similarities between transformations produced by self-attention and gradient-based learning in a restricted theoretical setting.

title: The Closeness of In-Context Learning and Weight Shifting for Softmax Regression

abstract: World models empower model-based agents to interactively explore, reason, and plan within imagined environments for real-world decision-making. However, the high demand for interactivity poses challenges in harnessing recent advancements in video generative models for developing world models at scale. This work introduces Interactive VideoGPT (iVideoGPT), a scalable autoregressive transformer framework that integrates multimodal signals—visual observations, actions, and rewards—into a sequence of tokens, facilitating an interactive experience of agents via next-token prediction. iVideoGPT features a novel compressive tokenization technique that efficiently discretizes high-dimensional visual observations. Leveraging its scalable architecture, we are able to pre-train iVideoGPT on millions of human and robotic manipulation trajectories, establishing a versatile foundation that is adaptable to serve as interactive world models for a wide range of downstream tasks. These include action-conditioned video prediction, visual planning, and model-based reinforcement learning, where iVideoGPT achieves competitive performance compared with state-of-the-art methods. Our work advances the development of interactive general world models, bridging the gap between generative video models and practical model-based reinforcement learning applications. Code and pre-trained models are available at https://thuml.github.io/iVideoGPT.

paragraphs: World models let agents explore imagined outcomes to support decisions in the real world. Building them from video generators requires interactivity: the model must connect visual changes with an agent's actions and rewards. iVideoGPT addresses this by putting visual observations, actions, and rewards into a shared sequence of tokens processed by an autoregressive transformer.

Predicting subsequent tokens provides the framework for interactive modeling. A compressive tokenization method converts high-dimensional visual observations into discrete representations efficiently, helping make the approach scalable. The authors pretrain the model on millions of human and robotic manipulation trajectories, creating a foundation that can then be adapted for different downstream uses.

The evaluated applications include predicting video conditioned on actions, visual planning, and model-based reinforcement learning. iVideoGPT achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods in these settings. The contribution is a common sequence-modeling framework that links video generation to agent interaction, supported by large-scale pretraining and results across multiple uses of learned world models.
summary.tldr: iVideoGPT models observations, actions, and rewards as tokens, enabling scalable pretraining for interactive prediction, planning, and reinforcement learning.

title: iVideoGPT: Interactive VideoGPTs are Scalable World Models

abstract: Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have emerged as the {\em de facto} standard in graph representation learning. However, when it comes to link prediction, they are not always superior to simple heuristics such as Common Neighbor (CN). This discrepancy stems from a fundamental limitation: while MPNNs excel in node-level representation, they stumble with encoding the joint structural features essential to link prediction, like CN. To bridge this gap, we posit that, by harnessing the orthogonality of input vectors, pure message-passing can indeed capture joint structural features. Specifically, we study the proficiency of MPNNs in approximating CN heuristics. Based on our findings, we introduce the Message Passing Link Predictor (MPLP), a novel link prediction model. MPLP taps into quasi-orthogonal vectors to estimate link-level structural features, all while preserving the node-level complexities. We conduct experiments on benchmark datasets from various domains, where our method consistently outperforms the baseline methods, establishing new state-of-the-arts.

paragraphs: Predicting whether two graph nodes should be connected requires information about their relationship, not just useful descriptions of each node separately. This helps explain why message-passing neural networks do not always outperform simple common-neighbor heuristics. The paper investigates whether pure message passing can nevertheless capture the joint structural information those heuristics use.

The authors identify orthogonality of input vectors as a way to make such information accessible. They study how message-passing networks can approximate common-neighbor heuristics and build the Message Passing Link Predictor, or MPLP, around those findings. MPLP uses quasi-orthogonal vectors to estimate structural features of node pairs while retaining the ability to represent node-level complexity.

Experiments on benchmark datasets from several domains report consistent improvements over the compared baselines and new state-of-the-art results. The conceptual contribution is that a limitation associated with node representations can be addressed through the inputs and design of message passing itself. The findings support a richer role for pure message passing in link prediction.
summary.tldr: MPLP uses quasi-orthogonal input vectors so pure message passing can estimate common-neighbor structure for link prediction.

title: Pure Message Passing Can Estimate Common Neighbor for Link Prediction

abstract: Enhancing node-level Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) generalization on graphs remains a crucial area. In this paper, we develop a Structural Causal Model (SCM) to theoretically dissect the performance of two prominent invariant learning methods--Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) and Variance-Risk Extrapolation (VREx)--in node-level OOD settings. Our analysis reveals a critical limitation: these methods may struggle to identify invariant features due to the complexities introduced by the message-passing mechanism, which can obscure causal features within a range of neighboring samples. To address this, we propose Cross-environment Intra-class Alignment (CIA), which explicitly eliminates spurious features by aligning representations within the same class, bypassing the need for explicit knowledge of underlying causal patterns. To adapt CIA to node-level OOD scenarios where environment labels are hard to obtain, we further propose CIA-LRA (Localized Reweighting Alignment) that leverages the distribution of neighboring labels to selectively align node representations, effectively distinguishing and preserving invariant features while removing spurious ones, all without relying on environment labels. We theoretically prove CIA-LRA's effectiveness by deriving an OOD generalization error bound based on PAC-Bayesian analysis. Experiments on graph OOD benchmarks validate the superiority of CIA and CIA-LRA, marking a significant advancement in node-level OOD generalization.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why methods intended to learn stable features can struggle with node prediction when graph data changes between training and use. Using a structural causal model, the authors analyze Invariant Risk Minimization and Variance-Risk Extrapolation. They find that message passing can obscure causal features by mixing information across neighboring samples.

Their proposed Cross-environment Intra-class Alignment method addresses this by aligning representations of examples belonging to the same class across environments. The aim is to remove misleading features without requiring explicit knowledge of the underlying causal patterns. This directly targets representation differences that can undermine generalization beyond the training distribution.

Because environment labels can be difficult to obtain for graph nodes, the authors also introduce CIA-LRA. It uses neighboring label distributions to selectively align node representations without environment labels, preserving invariant information while removing spurious features. A PAC-Bayesian generalization bound supplies theoretical support, and graph benchmarks demonstrate advantages for both methods. Together, the analysis and methods connect a graph-specific failure mechanism to a targeted form of representation alignment.
summary.tldr: The paper traces invariant-learning failures to graph message passing and proposes class-based alignment methods for better out-of-distribution node prediction.

title: Dissecting the Failure of Invariant Learning on Graphs

abstract: We study the generalization of two-layer ReLU neural networks in a univariate nonparametric regression problem with noisy labels. This is a problem where kernels (\emph{e.g.} NTK) are provably sub-optimal and benign overfitting does not happen, thus disqualifying existing theory for interpolating (0-loss, global optimal) solutions. We present a new theory of generalization for local minima that gradient descent with a constant learning rate can \emph{stably} converge to. We show that gradient descent with a fixed learning rate $\eta$ can only find local minima that represent smooth functions with a certain weighted \emph{first order total variation} bounded by $1/\eta - 1/2 + \widetilde{O}(\sigma + \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}})$ where $\sigma$ is the label noise level, $\mathrm{MSE}$ is short for mean squared error against the ground truth, and $\widetilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides a logarithmic factor. Under mild assumptions, we also prove a nearly-optimal MSE bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-4/5})$ within the strict interior of the support of the $n$ data points. Our theoretical results are validated by extensive simulation that demonstrates large learning rate training induces sparse linear spline fits. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to obtain generalization bound via minima stability in the non-interpolation case and the first to show ReLU NNs without regularization can achieve near-optimal rates in nonparametric regression.

paragraphs: This paper studies two-layer ReLU networks for one-dimensional nonparametric regression with noisy labels. In this setting, kernels are provably suboptimal and fitting every training label does not yield benign overfitting. The authors therefore analyze local minima to which constant-learning-rate gradient descent can converge stably, rather than focusing on zero-training-loss solutions.

They show that such stable minima represent functions whose weighted first-order total variation is bounded. The bound depends on the inverse learning rate, label noise, and error against the true function. This links optimization stability to control over function variation: the learning rate constrains the kinds of fitted functions that can occur at stable minima.

Under mild assumptions, the paper also proves a nearly optimal mean squared error rate of n to the power of minus four-fifths, up to logarithmic factors, strictly inside the data support. Simulations show large learning rates producing sparse linear spline fits. Together, these results connect stable training to generalization without explicit regularization in this specific regression setting.
summary.tldr: For noisy one-dimensional regression, stability under fixed-step gradient descent constrains ReLU fits and yields near-optimal generalization under stated assumptions.

title: Stable Minima Cannot Overfit in Univariate ReLU Networks: Generalization by Large Step Sizes

abstract: The performance of modern reinforcement learning algorithms critically relieson tuning ever increasing numbers of hyperparameters. Often, small changes ina hyperparameter can lead to drastic changes in performance, and different environments require very different hyperparameter settings to achieve state-of-the-artperformance reported in the literature. We currently lack a scalable and widelyaccepted approach to characterizing these complex interactions. This work proposes a new empirical methodology for studying, comparing, and quantifying thesensitivity of an algorithm’s performance to hyperparameter tuning for a given setof environments. We then demonstrate the utility of this methodology by assessingthe hyperparameter sensitivity of several commonly used normalization variants ofPPO. The results suggest that several algorithmic performance improvements may,in fact, be a result of an increased reliance on hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning algorithm can perform very differently depending on its hyperparameters: settings chosen around the learning procedure. Small adjustments can produce large changes in results, and settings that work well in one environment may work poorly in another. This makes a strong reported score difficult to interpret without also understanding how much tuning it required.

The paper proposes an empirical methodology for studying that dependence across a chosen collection of environments. Its purpose is to make sensitivity something researchers can quantify and compare between algorithms. The approach therefore adds another dimension to evaluation: how performance responds to hyperparameter choices, alongside the performance achieved after tuning.

The authors demonstrate the methodology on several commonly used normalization variants of PPO. Their results suggest that some apparent algorithmic improvements may reflect greater reliance on tuning. This is a qualified empirical finding, rather than a claim that improvements generally disappear. It matters because an algorithm's best achievable result and its sensitivity to configuration describe different aspects of its usefulness.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a way to measure reinforcement learning algorithms' sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning and examines normalization variants of PPO.

title: A Method for Evaluating Hyperparameter Sensitivity in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Custom diffusion models (CDMs) have attracted widespread attention due to their astonishing generative ability for personalized concepts. However, most existing CDMs unreasonably assume that personalized concepts are fixed and cannot change over time. Moreover, they heavily suffer from catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect on old personalized concepts when continually learning a series of new concepts. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Concept-Incremental text-to-image Diffusion Model (CIDM), which can resolve catastrophic forgetting and concept neglect to learn new customization tasks in a concept-incremental manner. Specifically, to surmount the catastrophic forgetting of old concepts, we develop a concept consolidation loss and an elastic weight aggregation module. They can explore task-specific and task-shared knowledge during training, and aggregate all low-rank weights of old concepts based on their contributions during inference. Moreover, in order to address concept neglect, we devise a context-controllable synthesis strategy that leverages expressive region features and noise estimation to control the contexts of generated images according to user conditions. Experiments validate that our CIDM surpasses existing custom diffusion models. The source codes are available at https://github.com/JiahuaDong/CIFC.

paragraphs: Personalized image generators often assume that the concepts a user wants to generate remain fixed. This paper instead considers a sequence of customization tasks in which new concepts arrive over time. Learning those additions can make a model forget earlier concepts or neglect them when composing images, creating two related obstacles to continued customization.

The proposed Concept-Incremental text-to-image Diffusion Model addresses forgetting with a concept consolidation loss and elastic weight aggregation. These components distinguish knowledge specific to a task from knowledge shared across tasks. During inference, the method combines low-rank weights associated with earlier concepts according to their contributions, keeping previously learned customization knowledge involved in generation.

To address concept neglect, the model also uses a synthesis strategy that controls image context according to user conditions. It draws on region features and noise estimation to guide that control. Experiments report improvements over existing custom diffusion models. The contribution combines preservation of old concepts with control over how concepts appear, supporting customization that can evolve across successive learning tasks.
summary.tldr: CIDM combines concept-preserving learning and context-controlled synthesis to support successive image customization tasks.

title: How to Continually Adapt Text-to-Image Diffusion Models for Flexible Customization?

abstract: We study Bayesian persuasion under approximate best response, where the receiver may choose any action that is not too much suboptimal, given their posterior belief upon receiving the signal. We focus on the computational aspects of the problem, aiming to design algorithms that efficiently compute (almost) optimal strategies for the sender. Despite the absence of the revelation principle --- which has been one of the most powerful tools in Bayesian persuasion --- we design polynomial-time exact algorithms for the problem when either the state space or the action space is small, as well as a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) for the general problem. On the negative side, we show there is no polynomial-time exact algorithm for the general problem unless $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$. Our results build on several new algorithmic ideas, which might be useful in other principal-agent problems where robustness is desired.

Despite the absence of the revelation principle --- which has been one of the most powerful tools in Bayesian persuasion --- we design polynomial-time exact algorithms for the problem when either the state space or the action space is small, as well as a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) for the general problem. paragraphs: Bayesian persuasion studies how a sender chooses information to influence a receiver’s decision. Here, the receiver is allowed to select any action that is sufficiently close to optimal under the belief formed after seeing a signal. The sender’s computational problem must therefore accommodate approximate responses instead of relying on an exactly optimal receiver choice.

The authors develop algorithms for finding optimal or nearly optimal sender strategies despite the absence of the revelation principle, a simplification commonly used in persuasion problems. They obtain polynomial-time exact algorithms when either the state space or the action space is small. For the general setting, they provide a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme.

A complementary hardness result rules out a polynomial-time exact algorithm for the general problem unless P equals NP. Together, these results separate settings where exact computation is tractable from a broader setting where approximation offers an alternative. The paper also develops algorithmic ideas that may transfer to other principal-agent problems requiring robustness, although that wider applicability is presented as a possibility.
summary.tldr: The paper gives exact and approximate persuasion algorithms for near-optimal receiver responses, alongside a general computational hardness result.

title: Computational Aspects of Bayesian Persuasion under Approximate Best Response

abstract: In this paper, we investigate source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) for visible-infrared person re-identification (VI-ReID), aiming to adapt a pre-trained source model to an unlabeled target domain without access to source data. To address this challenging setting, we propose a novel learning paradigm, termed Source-Free Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification (SVIP), which fully exploits the prior knowledge embedded in the source model to guide target domain adaptation. The proposed framework comprises three key components specifically designed for the source-free scenario: 1) a Source-Guided Contrastive Learning (SGCL) module, which leverages the discriminative feature space of the frozen source model as a reference to perform contrastive learning on the unlabeled target data, thereby preserving discrimination without requiring source samples; 2) a Residual Transfer Learning (RTL) module, which learns residual mappings to adapt the target model’s representations while maintaining the knowledge from the source model; and 3) a Structural Consistency-Guided Cross-modal Alignment (SCCA) module, which enforces reciprocal structural constraints between visible and infrared modalities to identify reliable cross-modal pairs and achieve robust modality alignment without source supervision. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SVIP substantially enhances target domain performance and outperforms existing unsupervised VI-ReID methods under source-free settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to adapt a person re-identification model to a new environment containing visible and infrared images. The new data have no labels, and the original training data are unavailable. SVIP addresses this source-free setting by using knowledge retained in the pretrained model to guide adaptation across both the environment change and the imaging modalities.

Three components divide that work. Source-Guided Contrastive Learning keeps the original model frozen and uses its feature space as a reference for learning discriminative target representations. Residual Transfer Learning learns adjustments to those representations while preserving source knowledge. Structural Consistency-Guided Cross-modal Alignment uses reciprocal structural constraints to identify reliable visible–infrared pairs and align the modalities.

Together, these components provide guidance without requiring source examples or target annotations. The model supplies a reference for discrimination, while structural relationships help establish cross-modal correspondences. Benchmark experiments report substantial gains in target-domain performance and improvements over existing unsupervised visible–infrared re-identification methods under source-free conditions. The findings specifically support adaptation when only the pretrained source model remains accessible.
summary.tldr: SVIP adapts visible–infrared person re-identification models using unlabeled target data and knowledge retained in the source model.

title: Learning Source-Free Domain Adaptation for Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification

abstract: To migrate the remarkable successes of Large Language Models (LLMs), the community has made numerous efforts to generalize them to the table reasoning tasks for the widely deployed tabular data. Despite that, in this work, by showing a probing experiment on our proposed StructQA benchmark, we postulate that even the most advanced LLMs (such as GPTs) may still fall short of coping with tabular data. More specifically, the current scheme often simply relies on serializing the tabular data, together with the meta information, then inputting them through the LLMs. We argue that the loss of structural information is the root of this shortcoming. In this work, we further propose TAMO, which bears an ideology to treat the tables as an independent modality integrated with the text tokens. The resulting model in TAMO is a multimodal framework consisting of a hypergraph neural network as the global table encoder seamlessly integrated with the mainstream LLM. Empirical results on various benchmarking datasets, including HiTab, WikiTQ, WikiSQL, FeTaQA, and StructQA, have demonstrated significant improvements on generalization with an average relative gain of **42.65%**.

paragraphs: Language models commonly receive tables as serialized text together with descriptive information. This paper argues that the conversion can lose structural information needed for table reasoning. A probing experiment on the authors' StructQA benchmark leads them to suggest that even advanced language models may struggle with tabular data under this input scheme.

TAMO addresses the problem by treating tables as a separate modality integrated with text tokens. It uses a hypergraph neural network as a global table encoder and connects that encoder to a mainstream language model. The architecture gives table structure a dedicated representation rather than relying entirely on the language model's interpretation of serialized input.

Experiments on HiTab, WikiTQ, WikiSQL, FeTaQA, and StructQA report significant generalization improvements, with an average relative gain of 42.65%. These results support the usefulness of explicitly encoding table structure. The paper's explanation of the original shortcoming remains an argued interpretation, while the benchmark findings provide empirical evidence for the proposed multimodal approach.
summary.tldr: TAMO treats tables as a distinct modality, using a hypergraph encoder to preserve structure and improve table-reasoning generalization.

title: Table as a Modality for Large Language Models

abstract: Optimization plays a central role in Operations Research (OR) and numerous industrial applications, yet automating the end-to-end process of translating natural language descriptions into executable optimization programs remains a formidable challenge. While recent efforts have applied Large Language Models (LLMs) to this task, existing approaches are hindered by high inference costs, limited robustness across domains, and weak verification mechanisms. In this work, we propose MURKA, a reinforcement learning and knowledge distillation-based framework that enhances LLM-driven optimization modeling via collaborative agent alignment. MURKA orchestrates three specialized agents---Extractor, Solver, and Checker---to achieve accurate problem understanding, robust formulation, and verifiable execution. The Extractor is trained using group relative policy optimization with a composite reward function that incorporates semantic correctness and execution fidelity. The Solver benefits from knowledge distillation from a powerful teacher model, yielding structurally valid and executable formulations in AMPL. The Checker iteratively verifies solution correctness via solver feedback. We validate MURKA's generalizability through extensive experiments across diverse OR benchmarks, demonstrating its robustness and scalability. Experimental results on eight diverse OR benchmarks, including NLP4LP, ComplexOR, and NL4Opt, demonstrate that MURKA, built on the LLaMa3-8B backbone, achieves a 5.9\% absolute improvement in solution accuracy and a 5.1\% increase in execution success rate compared to leading baselines. These results establish MURKA as an effective and scalable paradigm for LLM-driven optimization, with strong potential for deployment in real-world OR applications.
