paragraphs: Turning a natural-language optimization problem into a working program requires accurate interpretation, a valid mathematical formulation, and verification of the result. MURKA organizes this process around three specialized agents: an Extractor, a Solver, and a Checker. The framework combines reinforcement learning and knowledge distillation to align their contributions.

The Extractor uses group relative policy optimization with rewards covering semantic correctness and execution fidelity. The Solver learns from a stronger teacher model through distillation, producing structurally valid, executable formulations in AMPL. The Checker then uses feedback from the optimization solver to iteratively verify solution correctness. This division assigns understanding, formulation, and checking their own explicit roles.

Built on LLaMa3-8B, MURKA is evaluated on eight operations-research benchmarks, including NLP4LP, ComplexOR, and NL4Opt. The reported results show a 5.9 percentage-point absolute improvement in solution accuracy and a 5.1% increase in execution success rate over leading baselines. These findings support the framework’s robustness across the tested problem domains and its potential for practical optimization applications.
summary.tldr: MURKA coordinates trained extraction, formulation, and checking agents to improve the accuracy and executability of optimization programs.

title: MURKA: Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning with Knowledge Alignment for Optimization Tasks

abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has opened new opportunities for AI-driven chemical problem solving. However, existing chemical LLMs are typically tailored to specific task formats or narrow domains, limiting their capacity to integrate knowledge and generalize across tasks. Model merging offers a promising route for efficiently combining specialized LLMs into a unified model without access to original training data, which is urgently needed in the chemical domain where in-house data and privacy preservation are critical. However, effective model merging in the chemical domain poses unique challenges: (1) significant disparities among chemical LLMs due to task-specific specialization, and (2) a highly imbalanced distribution of chemical LLMs in targeted downstream tasks, where some are over-benchmarked while others remain underexplored. These challenges intensify model inconsistencies such as parameter interference and accumulated fine-tuning noise, which collectively hinder effective model merging. To this end, we propose Curriculum Model Merging (CMM), a curriculum-based framework that progressively merges expert chemical LLMs in a moderate and continual manner. CMM aims to harmonize their inconsistencies while meantime preserve their domain-specific expertise. Comprehensive experiments on two benchmark datasets show that CMM effectively consolidates task-specific expertise and outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 29.03\% in terms of overall average performance. Moreover, CMM facilitates chemical knowledge generalization across prediction and generative tasks without sacrificing robustness, exhibiting promising merging performance under both expert-abundant and expert-sparse scenarios.

paragraphs: Chemical language models often specialize in particular tasks or output formats, leaving useful knowledge spread across separate experts. Merging offers a way to combine that expertise without accessing original training data, a valuable property when chemical datasets are private. However, specialization can make model parameters interfere, and available experts are distributed unevenly across tasks.

Curriculum Model Merging addresses these inconsistencies through a progressive merging process. It combines experts gradually, aiming to reconcile their differences while preserving domain-specific capabilities. The approach is motivated by both parameter interference and accumulated fine-tuning noise, which can obstruct a useful combination of specialized models.

Across two benchmark datasets, the authors report a 29.03% improvement in overall average performance over state-of-the-art methods. They also report generalization across prediction and generation tasks without sacrificing robustness, with promising results when experts are plentiful and when they are scarce. These findings support gradual merging as a way to consolidate chemical expertise across tasks under the evaluated conditions.
summary.tldr: Curriculum Model Merging progressively combines chemical language-model experts, improving cross-task performance without requiring their original training data.

title: Curriculum Model Merging: Harmonizing Chemical LLMs for Enhanced Cross-Task Generalization

abstract: Transformers have been widely adopted in natural language processing, computer vision, and other domains due to their exceptional performance across a variety of tasks. However, the computational cost of Transformers is prohibitively high, particularly when handling long input sequences, significantly increasing both training and inference time. Although various token pruning methods have been proposed to reduce the computational burden of Transformers, most approaches overlook critical differences in sequences in terms of length and complexity, leading to suboptimal compression efficiency. In this paper, we propose AD-TP, an Attribution-Driven Adaptive Token Pruning method designed to retain only the most informative tokens. We analyze the performance of using accumulated attention values to measure token importance and find that attention values do not accurately reflect the actual contribution of each token to text understanding. Additionally, we observe significant variations in the length and complexity of different sequences within the dataset. Based on these insights, we adopt Integrated Gradients to evaluate token importance and introduce a lightweight adaptive token retainer module that dynamically generates pruning configurations for each input sequence. In addition, we incorporate both teacher supervision and self-supervised learning objectives to enhance the training efficiency, accuracy, and robustness of the model. Experiments conducted on GLUE, SQuAD, and 20News demonstrate that AD-TP outperforms state-of-the-art token pruning and model compression methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency. On GLUE, AD-TP reduces FLOPs by an average of 7.8× while improving performance by 0.6%.

paragraphs: Token pruning reduces Transformer computation by removing parts of an input sequence. This paper argues that effective pruning needs to account for differences in sequence length and complexity. Its analysis also finds that accumulated attention values do not accurately represent how much individual tokens contribute to understanding text.

AD-TP uses Integrated Gradients to assess token importance and adds a lightweight module that chooses a pruning configuration for each input. This allows the amount and pattern of retained information to vary with the sequence. Teacher supervision and self-supervised objectives further support the model’s training efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

Experiments on GLUE, SQuAD, and 20News show better accuracy and computational efficiency than the token pruning and model compression methods used for comparison. On GLUE, the authors report an average 7.8-fold reduction in FLOPs alongside a 0.6% performance improvement. The findings support combining contribution-based token assessment with input-specific pruning: compression can preserve useful information more effectively when it responds to the particular sequence being processed.
summary.tldr: AD-TP combines token attribution with input-specific pruning to reduce Transformer computation while improving accuracy on the evaluated text benchmarks.

title: Attribution-Driven Adaptive Token Pruning for Transformers

abstract: Functional data play a pivotal role across science and engineering, yet their infinite-dimensional nature makes representation learning challenging. Conventional statistical models depend on pre-chosen basis expansions or kernels, limiting the flexibility of data-driven discovery, while many deep-learning pipelines treat functions as fixed-grid vectors, ignoring inherent continuity. In this paper, we introduce Functional Attention with a Mixture-of-Experts (FAME), an end-to-end, fully data-driven framework for function-on-function regression. FAME forms continuous attention by coupling a bidirectional neural controlled differential equation with MoE-driven vector fields to capture intra-functional continuity, and further fuses change to inter-functional dependencies via multi-head cross attention. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world functional regression benchmarks show that FAME achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and strong robustness to arbitrarily sampled discrete observations of functions.

paragraphs: Function-on-function regression predicts one function from other functions, making continuity part of the learning problem. Conventional approaches often choose basis functions or kernels in advance, while many neural methods reduce functions to vectors sampled on a fixed grid. FAME aims to learn representations directly from data while retaining the continuous character of the inputs.

Its continuous attention mechanism combines a bidirectional neural controlled differential equation with vector fields supplied through a mixture of experts. This component captures relationships within an individual function. Multi-head cross attention then connects information across functions, allowing the model to represent both internal continuity and dependencies between different functional inputs.

The entire framework is trained end to end. On synthetic and real-world functional regression benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy and strong robustness when functions are observed through arbitrarily sampled discrete measurements. That robustness matters because the observed samples need not form the same fixed grid. The findings support using continuous representations together with adaptive expert routing for this regression setting.
summary.tldr: FAME combines continuous attention and expert routing to predict functions accurately from flexibly sampled functional observations.

title: FAME: Adaptive Functional Attention with Expert Routing for Function-on-Function Regression

abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved significant milestones, but sample efficiency remains a bottleneck for real-world applications. Recently, CrossQ has demonstrated state-of-the-art sample efficiency with a low update-to-data (UTD) ratio of 1. In this work, we explore CrossQ's scaling behavior with higher UTD ratios. We identify challenges in the training dynamics, which are emphasized by higher UTD ratios. To address these, we integrate weight normalization into the CrossQ framework, a solution that stabilizes training, has been shown to prevent potential loss of plasticity, and keeps the effective learning rate constant. Our proposed approach reliably scales with increasing UTD ratios, achieving competitive performance across 25 challenging continuous control tasks on the DeepMind Control Suite and Myosuite benchmarks, notably the complex dog and humanoid environments. This work eliminates the need for drastic interventions, such as network resets, and offers a simple yet robust pathway for improving sample efficiency and scalability in model-free reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learner can try to extract more value from collected experience by performing more training updates per unit of new data. This update-to-data ratio is central to the paper's investigation of CrossQ. Although CrossQ already achieves strong sample efficiency at a ratio of one, increasing the ratio exposes difficulties in its training dynamics.

The proposed change adds weight normalization to the CrossQ framework. The authors describe this as stabilizing training and keeping the effective learning rate constant, with support for preventing potential loss of plasticity. Plasticity concerns the network's ability to continue adapting, which matters when repeated updates must remain useful throughout learning.

With this modification, the method reliably scales to higher update-to-data ratios and achieves competitive results across 25 continuous-control tasks from DeepMind Control Suite and Myosuite, including challenging dog and humanoid environments. The approach avoids drastic interventions such as resetting the network. The findings support normalization as a relatively simple way to improve sample efficiency when increasing training effort per collected sample.
summary.tldr: Adding weight normalization helps CrossQ remain stable as training updates per collected sample increase, improving reinforcement learning scalability.

title: Scaling Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning with Batch and Weight Normalization

abstract: Multimodal deep learning systems are deployed in dynamic scenarios due to the robustness afforded by multiple sensing modalities. Nevertheless, they struggle with varying compute resource availability (due to multi-tenancy, device heterogeneity, etc.) and fluctuating quality of inputs (from sensor feed corruption, environmental noise, etc.). Statically provisioned multimodal systems cannot adapt when compute resources change over time, while existing dynamic networks struggle with strict compute budgets. Additionally, both systems often neglect the impact of variations in modality quality. Consequently, modalities suffering substantial corruption may needlessly consume resources better allocated towards other modalities. We propose ADMN, a layer-wise Adaptive Depth Multimodal Network capable of tackling both challenges - it adjusts the total number of active layers across all modalities to meet compute resource constraints, and continually reallocates layers across input modalities according to their modality quality. Our evaluations showcase ADMN can match the accuracy of state-of-the-art networks while reducing up to 75% of their floating-point operations.

paragraphs: A system that combines several sensing modalities faces two changing conditions: how much computation it can use and how trustworthy each input is. A fixed network cannot readily adjust to a smaller compute budget. It can also waste computation on a badly corrupted input when another modality offers more useful information.

ADMN addresses both issues by changing the number of active layers. It adjusts the total depth used across modalities to satisfy resource constraints, then redistributes those layers according to input quality. This makes allocation sensitive to both the available resources and the information those resources will process. The adaptation happens at the level of layers rather than treating every modality as a fixed computational commitment.

The evaluations show that ADMN can match the accuracy of state-of-the-art networks while using up to 75% fewer floating-point operations. That is a reported maximum reduction, rather than a saving promised in every setting. The result supports jointly adapting computational depth and modality allocation when resource availability and sensor quality fluctuate.
summary.tldr: ADMN adapts network depth to compute budgets and input quality, matching leading accuracy with up to 75% fewer floating-point operations.

title: ADMN: A Layer-Wise Adaptive Multimodal Network for Dynamic Input Noise and Compute Resources

abstract: Graph Neural Networks learn on graph-structured data by iteratively aggregating local neighborhood information. While this local message passing paradigm imparts a powerful inductive bias and exploits graph sparsity, it also yields three key challenges: (i) oversquashing of long-range information, (ii) oversmoothing of node representations, and (iii) limited expressive power. In this work we inject randomized global embeddings of node features, which we term Sketched Random Features, into standard GNNs, enabling them to efficiently capture long-range dependencies. The embeddings are unique, distance-sensitive, and topology-agnostic---properties which we analytically and empirically show alleviate the aforementioned limitations when injected into GNNs. Experimental results on real-world graph learning tasks confirm that this strategy consistently improves performance over baseline GNNs, offering both a standalone solution and a complementary enhancement to existing techniques such as graph positional encodings.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks commonly update each node using information from nearby nodes. This local structure is useful, but distant information can become compressed as it travels, node representations can become overly similar, and some distinctions remain hard to express. The paper adds global feature information to standard graph networks to address these linked difficulties.

The proposed Sketched Random Features are randomized global embeddings of node features. They are designed to be unique and sensitive to distance without depending on graph topology. Injecting these embeddings gives the network access to information beyond what its ordinary local aggregation supplies. The authors use both analysis and experiments to show how these properties alleviate oversquashing, oversmoothing, and limits on expressive power.

Across real-world graph-learning tasks, the added features consistently improve performance over baseline graph networks. The method can be used on its own or alongside existing enhancements such as graph positional encodings. Its contribution is therefore a feature augmentation that helps standard architectures capture long-range dependencies while remaining compatible with other approaches to improving graph representations.
summary.tldr: Randomized global feature sketches help graph neural networks capture distant information and improve performance alongside existing representation techniques.

title: Sketch-Augmented Features Improve Learning Long-Range Dependencies in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Foundation models (FMs) have shown great promise in single-cell genomics, yet current approaches, such as scGPT, Geneformer, and scFoundation, rely on centralized training and language modeling objectives that overlook the tabular nature of single-cell data and raise significant privacy concerns. We present TABULA, a foundation model designed for single-cell transcriptomics, which integrates a novel tabular modeling objective and federated learning framework to enable privacy-preserving pretraining across decentralized datasets. TABULA directly models the cell-by-gene expression matrix through column-wise gene reconstruction and row-wise cell contrastive learning, capturing both gene-level relationships and cell-level heterogeneity without imposing artificial gene sequence order. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of TABULA: despite using only half the pretraining data, TABULA achieves state-of-the-art performance across key tasks, including gene imputation, perturbation prediction, cell type annotation, and multi-omics integration. It is important to note that as public single-cell datasets continue to grow, TABULA provides a scalable and privacy-aware foundation that not only validates the feasibility of federated tabular modeling but also establishes a generalizable framework for training future models under similar privacy-preserving settings.

paragraphs: Single-cell transcriptomics data naturally form a table of cells and gene-expression measurements. TABULA is a foundation model built around that structure. The paper argues that language-modeling objectives overlook this tabular organization, while centralized training raises privacy concerns. It combines a tabular learning objective with federated pretraining across decentralized datasets.

TABULA learns in two complementary directions. Column-wise gene reconstruction captures relationships at the gene level, and row-wise contrastive learning captures differences among cells. This directly models the cell-by-gene matrix without imposing an artificial order on genes. The federated framework allows the pretraining process to operate across distributed datasets in a privacy-aware setting.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on gene imputation, perturbation prediction, cell-type annotation, and multi-omics integration despite using only half the pretraining data. These results support both the chosen data representation and the feasibility of federated tabular modeling. The paper presents the combination as a scalable foundation for single-cell models and a framework for future training under similar privacy-preserving conditions.
summary.tldr: TABULA combines table-aware learning with federated pretraining and reports leading single-cell analysis results while using half the pretraining data.

title: Tabula: A Tabular Self-Supervised Foundation Model for Single-Cell Transcriptomics

abstract: Training deep learning models for point cloud prediction tasks such as shape completion and generation depends critically on loss functions that measure discrepancies between predicted and ground-truth point sets. Commonly used functions such as Chamfer Distance (CD), HyperCD, InfoCD and Density-aware CD rely on nearest-neighbor assignments, which often induce many-to-one correspondences, leading to point congestion in dense regions and poor coverage in sparse regions. These losses also involve non-differentiable operations due to index selection, which may affect gradient-based optimization. Earth Mover Distance (EMD) enforces one-to-one correspondences and captures structural similarity more effectively, but its cubic computational complexity limits its practical use. We propose the Adaptive Probabilistic Matching Loss (APML), a fully differentiable approximation of one-to-one matching that leverages Sinkhorn iterations on a temperature-scaled similarity matrix derived from pairwise distances. We analytically compute the temperature to guarantee a minimum assignment probability, eliminating manual tuning. APML achieves near-quadratic runtime, comparable to Chamfer-based losses, and avoids non-differentiable operations. When integrated into state-of-the-art architectures (PoinTr, PCN, FoldingNet) on ShapeNet benchmarks and on a spatio‑temporal Transformer (CSI2PC) that generates 3‑D human point clouds from WiFi‑CSI measurements, APM loss yields faster convergence, superior spatial distribution, especially in low-density regions, and improved or on-par quantitative performance without additional hyperparameter search. The code is available at: https://github.com/apm-loss/apml.

paragraphs: Models that reconstruct 3D point clouds need a training loss that compares predicted points with target points. Common nearest-neighbor losses can assign many predictions to the same target, crowding dense areas while leaving sparse areas poorly covered. Exact one-to-one matching better captures structure, but Earth Mover Distance has cubic computational cost that limits its practical use.

Adaptive Probabilistic Matching Loss approximates one-to-one correspondence with soft assignment probabilities. It applies Sinkhorn iterations to a similarity matrix built from pairwise distances and scaled by a temperature. The temperature is calculated analytically to guarantee a minimum assignment probability, removing manual temperature tuning. The resulting loss is fully differentiable and has near-quadratic runtime.

The authors integrate the loss into several point-cloud architectures and a model that reconstructs human point clouds from WiFi measurements. Across these evaluations, they report faster convergence and better spatial distribution, particularly in low-density regions, with quantitative performance that improves or matches existing results. The approach makes more structured matching practical without additional hyperparameter search.
summary.tldr: APML uses differentiable probabilistic matching to improve point-cloud coverage while avoiding the cubic cost of exact matching.

title: APML: Adaptive Probabilistic Matching Loss for Robust 3D Point Cloud Reconstruction

abstract: Vision-based intrusion detection has multiple applications in practical scenarios, e.g., autonomous driving, intelligent monitoring, and security. Previous works mainly focus on improving the intrusion detection performance, without a comprehensive and in-depth understanding of the intrusion scene. To fill this gap, we explore a novel task called Multimodal Large Language Models based Intrusion Scene Understanding (MLLM-ISU) and report a comprehensive benchmark for the task. Specifically, we first design an effective and automatic visual question-answer generation strategy, constructing a new MLLM-ISU dataset, with 3000 VQA evaluation Pairs, 8925 training Pairs, and six relevant subtasks. Then, we perform a comprehensive assessment on various state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source MLLMs, e.g., DeepSeek-VL2, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-VL, etc, and find that current MLLMs have weak abilities for this task. Further, in order to improve the intrusion understanding capabilities of current MLLMs, we propose a Post-Training Framework with three sequential training stages, i.e., Intrusion-aware Visual Instruction Pre-training, Intrusion Chain of Thought tuning, and Intrusion-centric VQA tuning, and sufficient experiments and comparisons are conducted to verify the effectiveness of the proposed three-stages training framework. Available datasets and codes: https://github.com/1012537710/MLLM-ISU.

paragraphs: Visual intrusion detection has applications in monitoring, security, and autonomous driving. This paper broadens the task toward understanding an intrusion scene in depth. It introduces MLLM-ISU, a task and benchmark for assessing how multimodal language models answer questions about such scenes across six relevant subtasks.

The authors develop an automatic strategy for generating visual questions and answers. The resulting dataset contains 3,000 evaluation pairs and 8,925 training pairs. They evaluate proprietary and open-source models, including DeepSeek-VL2, GPT-4o, and Qwen2.5-VL, and find that current models have weak capabilities on the task. The benchmark thus provides a concrete way to measure this gap in scene understanding.

To improve performance, the paper proposes three successive training stages: visual instruction pre-training focused on intrusions, tuning on intrusion-related chains of thought, and tuning on intrusion-centered visual questions and answers. Experiments and comparisons support the effectiveness of this sequence. The work combines an evaluation resource with a targeted training approach, making intrusion understanding both a measurable capability and a specific post-training objective.
summary.tldr: MLLM-ISU benchmarks visual intrusion understanding, finds weaknesses in current multimodal models, and improves them through three targeted training stages.

title: MLLM-ISU: The First-Ever Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Models based Intrusion Scene Understanding

abstract: Interpretable reinforcement learning policies are essential for high-stakes decision-making, yet optimizing decision tree policies in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) remains challenging. We propose SPOT, a novel method for computing decision tree policies, which formulates the optimization problem as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP). To enhance efficiency, we employ a reduced-space branch-and-bound approach that decouples the MDP dynamics from tree-structure constraints, enabling efficient parallel search. This significantly improves runtime and scalability compared to previous methods. Our approach ensures that each iteration yields the optimal decision tree. Experimental results on standard benchmarks demonstrate that SPOT achieves substantial speedup and scales to larger MDPs with a significantly higher number of states. The resulting decision tree policies are interpretable and compact, maintaining transparency without compromising performance. These results demonstrate that our approach simultaneously achieves interpretability and scalability, delivering high-quality policies an order of magnitude faster than existing approaches.

paragraphs: Decision trees can express reinforcement-learning policies through compact, interpretable decisions, but finding good trees for a Markov decision process is computationally difficult. SPOT tackles this optimization problem directly. It represents the search for a decision-tree policy as a mixed-integer linear program, making tree structure part of an explicit optimization formulation.

To make the search more efficient, SPOT uses a reduced-space branch-and-bound method. It separates the environment's transition dynamics from the constraints describing the decision tree, enabling parallel search. The paper states that each iteration yields the optimal decision tree, connecting its computational approach with an optimality property for the tree search.

On standard benchmarks, SPOT runs substantially faster than previous methods and handles Markov decision processes with many more states. The resulting policies remain compact and interpretable while preserving performance. The reported order-of-magnitude speed advantage supports the paper's main practical claim: improved optimization can make transparent tree policies feasible at scales that were harder for earlier approaches.
summary.tldr: SPOT accelerates decision-tree policy optimization through a mixed-integer formulation and parallel search that separates environment dynamics from tree constraints.

title: SPOT: Scalable Policy Optimization with Trees for Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Knowledge graph-based retrieval-augmented generation seeks to mitigate hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) caused by insufficient or outdated knowledge. However, existing methods often fail to fully exploit the prior knowledge embedded in knowledge graphs (KGs), particularly their structural information and explicit or implicit constraints. The former can enhance the faithfulness of LLMs' reasoning, while the latter can improve the reliability of response generations. Motivated by these, we propose a trustworthy reasoning framework, termed Deliberation over Priors (\texttt{DP}), which sufficiently utilizes the priors contained in KGs. Specifically, \texttt{DP} adopts a progressive knowledge distillation strategy that integrates structural priors into LLMs through a combination of supervised fine-tuning and Kahneman-Tversky Optimization, thereby improving the faithfulness of relation path generation. Furthermore, our framework employs a reasoning-introspection strategy, which guides LLMs to perform refined reasoning verification based on extracted constraint priors, ensuring the reliability of response generation. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that \texttt{DP} achieves new state-of-the-art performance, especially a Hit@1 improvement of 13% on the ComplexWebQuestions dataset, and generates highly trustworthy responses. We also conduct various analyses to verify its flexibility and practicality. Code is available at [https://github.com/reml-group/Deliberation-on-Priors](https://github.com/reml-group/Deliberation-on-Priors).

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs can supply facts that a language model lacks or remembers incorrectly. This paper argues that using them effectively also requires their structure and constraints. Connections between entities can guide a reasoning path, while explicit or implicit restrictions can help check whether the resulting answer is consistent with the available knowledge.

The proposed DP framework handles these two roles separately. Progressive knowledge distillation combines supervised fine-tuning with Kahneman-Tversky Optimization to teach the model structural information from the graph. This improves generation of relation paths, the linked relationships used during reasoning. A reasoning-introspection stage then draws on extracted constraints to verify and refine that reasoning before producing responses.

Experiments on three benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, including a 13% improvement in Hit@1 on ComplexWebQuestions, alongside highly trustworthy responses. The findings support using knowledge graphs as both reasoning guidance and a source of checks on generated answers. The framework's contribution is therefore broader than retrieving additional facts: it teaches and verifies how the model connects those facts.
summary.tldr: DP teaches language models knowledge-graph structure and checks their reasoning against graph constraints to improve answer reliability.

title: Deliberation on Priors: Trustworthy Reasoning of Large Language Models on Knowledge Graphs

abstract: Language models (LMs) and their extension, vision-language models (VLMs), have achieved remarkable performance across various tasks. However, they still struggle with complex reasoning tasks that require multimodal or multilingual real world knowledge. To support such capabilities, an external memory system that can efficiently provide relevant multimodal information is essential. Existing approaches generally concatenate image and text tokens into a long sequence as memory, which, however, may drastically increase context length and even degrade performance. In contrast, we propose using continuous memory-a compact set of dense embeddings-to more effectively and efficiently represent multimodal and multilingual knowledge. Our key insight is that a VLM can serve as its own continuous memory encoder. We empirically show that this design improves performance on complex multimodal reasoning tasks. Building on this, we introduce a data-efficient and parameter-efficient method to fine-tune the VLM into a memory encoder, requiring only 1.2\% of the model’s parameters and a small corpus of 15.6K self-synthesized samples. Our approach CoMEM utilizes VLM's original capabilities to encode arbitrary multimodal and multilingual knowledge into just 8 continuous embeddings. Since the inference-time VLM remains frozen, our memory module is plug-and-play and can be flexibly integrated as needed. Extensive experiments across eight multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Code and data is publicly released here https://github.com/WenyiWU0111/CoMEM.

The adapted encoder represents supplied knowledge in eight continuous embeddings. The vision-language model that uses this memory at inference remains frozen, allowing the memory component to be integrated when needed without updating that inference model.

The authors report improved performance on complex multimodal reasoning and evaluate the approach across eight benchmarks. The findings support compact learned representations as a useful alternative to long sequences of external knowledge tokens. The contribution combines a representation choice with an efficient adaptation procedure: the model's existing capabilities provide the foundation for turning varied knowledge into a small, reusable memory input.
summary.tldr: CoMEM adapts a vision-language model to encode external knowledge into eight embeddings, improving reported multimodal reasoning with a frozen inference model.

title: Towards General Continuous Memory for Vision-Language Models

abstract: Several recently introduced deep learning optimizers utilizing matrix-level preconditioning have shown promising speedups relative to the current dominant optimizer AdamW, particularly in relatively small-scale experiments. However, efforts to validate and replicate their successes have reported mixed results. To better understand the effectiveness of these optimizers at scale, in this work we investigate how to scale preconditioned optimizers via hyperparameter transfer, building on prior works such as $\mu$P. We study how the optimal learning rate and weight decay should scale with model width and depth for a wide range of optimizers, including Shampoo, SOAP, and Muon, accounting for the impact of commonly used techniques such as blocking and grafting. We find that scaling the learning rate according to $\mu$P improves transfer, but can still suffer from significant finite-width deviations that cause drifting optimal learning rates, which we show can be mitigated by blocking and explicit spectral normalization. For compute-optimal scaling, we find scaling independent weight decay as $1/\mathrm{width}$ is nearly optimal across optimizers. Applying these scaling rules, we show Muon, SOAP and Shampoo consistently achieve near $1.4\times$ speedup over AdamW for training Llama-architecture language models of sizes ranging from $190$M to $1.4$B, whereas the speedup vanishes rapidly with scale under incorrect scaling. Based on these results and further ablations, we argue that studying optimal hyperparameter transfer is essential for reliably comparing optimizers at scale given a realistic tuning budget.

paragraphs: Matrix-preconditioned optimizers have shown training speedups, but attempts to reproduce those gains at larger scales have produced mixed results. This paper examines whether hyperparameter transfer helps explain that inconsistency. It studies how learning rate and weight decay should change with model width and depth for optimizers including Shampoo, SOAP, and Muon.

Scaling learning rates according to μP improves transfer, but finite-width effects can still shift the best learning rate. The authors show that blocking and explicit spectral normalization can mitigate these deviations. For compute-optimal scaling, they find that scaling independent weight decay inversely with width is nearly optimal across the optimizers studied.

With these rules, Muon, SOAP, and Shampoo deliver roughly 1.4-fold speedups over AdamW when training Llama-architecture models from 190 million to 1.4 billion parameters. Incorrect scaling causes the speedups to disappear rapidly as size increases. The findings show why comparisons under realistic tuning budgets depend on how well each optimizer's hyperparameters transfer across scales.
summary.tldr: Appropriate hyperparameter scaling preserves roughly 1.4-fold training speedups for matrix-preconditioned optimizers across the studied language-model sizes.

title: Hyperparameter Transfer Enables Consistent Gains of Matrix-Preconditioned Optimizers Across Scales

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have exhibited impressive capabilities across diverse image understanding tasks, but still struggle in settings that require reasoning over extended sequences of camera frames from a video. This limits their utility in embodied settings, which require reasoning over long frame sequences from a continuous stream of visual input at each moment of a task attempt. To address this limitation, we propose ROVER (Reasoning Over VidEo Recursively), a framework that enables the model to recursively decompose long-horizon video trajectories into segments corresponding to shorter subtasks within the trajectory. In doing so, ROVER facilitates more focused and accurate reasoning over temporally localized frame sequences without losing global context. We evaluate ROVER, implemented using an in-context learning approach, on diverse OpenX Embodiment videos and on a new dataset derived from RoboCasa that consists of 543 videos showing both expert and perturbed non-expert trajectories across 27 manipulation tasks. ROVER outperforms strong baselines across three video reasoning tasks: task progress estimation, frame-level natural language reasoning, and video question answering. We observe that, by reducing the number of frames the model reasons over at each timestep, ROVER mitigates model hallucinations, especially during unexpected or non-optimal moments of a trajectory. In addition, by enabling the implementation of a subtask-specific sliding context window, ROVER's time complexity scales linearly with video length, an asymptotic improvement over baselines.

paragraphs: ROVER helps vision-language models reason about long videos of embodied tasks. Understanding individual images does not automatically translate into tracking an extended task attempt. The framework recursively divides a trajectory into shorter segments associated with subtasks, allowing reasoning to focus on local frame sequences while retaining the larger task context.

The implementation uses in-context learning and is evaluated on OpenX Embodiment videos and a new RoboCasa-derived dataset. summary.tldr: ROVER recursively splits task videos into subtasks, improving reasoning and reducing hallucinations with linear scaling in video length.

title: ROVER: Recursive Reasoning Over Videos with Vision-Language Models for Embodied Tasks

abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have driven rapid progress in time series forecasting, yet many state-of-the-art models continue to struggle with robust performance in real-world applications, even when they achieve strong results on standard benchmark datasets. This persistent gap can be attributed to the black-box nature of deep learning architectures and the inherent limitations of current evaluation frameworks, which frequently lack the capacity to provide clear, quantitative insights into the specific strengths and weaknesses of different models, thereby complicating the selection of appropriate models for particular forecasting scenarios.To address these issues, we propose a synthetic data-driven evaluation paradigm, SynTSBench, that systematically assesses fundamental modeling capabilities of time series forecasting models through programmable feature configuration. Our framework isolates confounding factors and establishes an interpretable evaluation system with three core analytical dimensions: (1) temporal feature decomposition and capability mapping, which enables systematic evaluation of model capacities to learn specific pattern types; (2) robustness analysis under data irregularities, which quantifies noise tolerance thresholds and anomaly recovery capabilities; and (3) theoretical optimum benchmarking, which establishes performance boundaries for each pattern type—enabling direct comparison between model predictions and mathematical optima.Our experiments show that current deep learning models do not universally approach optimal baselines across all types of temporal features.

paragraphs: SynTSBench asks what time-series forecasting models actually learn, beyond their overall scores on standard datasets. Strong benchmark results can coexist with unreliable real-world behavior. The paper argues that existing evaluation frameworks often do not clearly separate a model's strengths and weaknesses, making it difficult to choose a suitable model for a particular forecasting situation.

The framework generates synthetic data with programmable features so that individual capabilities can be examined with fewer confounding factors. One evaluation dimension maps models to the temporal patterns they can learn. Another measures robustness to irregular data, including tolerance to noise and recovery from anomalies. A third compares predictions with mathematically optimal performance boundaries for each pattern type.

Experiments show that current deep learning models do not consistently approach optimal baselines across every temporal feature type. This finding gives a more specific interpretation of forecasting performance: success on a benchmark does not establish uniformly strong pattern-learning capabilities. SynTSBench offers an interpretable way to investigate those differences by relating observed errors to controlled temporal structures, disturbances, and theoretical reference points.
summary.tldr: SynTSBench uses controlled synthetic time series and mathematical optima to reveal which patterns forecasting models learn and where they struggle.

title: SynTSBench: Rethinking Temporal Pattern Learning in Deep Learning Models for Time Series

abstract: Recently, there has been a growing focus on determining the minimum width requirements for achieving the universal approximation property in deep, narrow Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). Among these challenges, one particularly challenging task is approximating a continuous function under the uniform norm, as indicated by the significant disparity between its lower and upper bounds. To address this problem, we propose a framework that simplifies finding the minimum width for deep, narrow MLPs into determining a purely geometrical function denoted as $w(d_x, d_y)$. This function relies solely on the input and output dimensions, represented as $d_x$ and $d_y$, respectively. To achieve this, we first demonstrate that deep, narrow MLPs, when provided with a small additional width, can approximate any $C^2$-diffeomorphism. Subsequently, using this result, we prove that $w(d_x, d_y)$ equates to the optimal minimum width required for deep, narrow MLPs to achieve universality. By employing the aforementioned framework and the Whitney embedding theorem, we provide an upper bound for the minimum width, given by $\operatorname{max}(2d_x+1, d_y) + \alpha(\sigma)$, where $0 \leq \alpha(\sigma) \leq 2$ represents a constant depending explicitly on the activation function. Furthermore, we provide novel optimal values for the minimum width in several settings, including $w(2,2)=w(2,3) = 4$.

paragraphs: How narrow can a deep neural network be while still approximating continuous functions? This paper studies that question under the uniform norm, where approximation must control the largest error across the domain. The authors target a substantial gap between known lower and upper bounds on the width needed for universal approximation.

Their framework translates the network question into a geometric function, w(dx, dy), depending only on input and output dimensions. A key step shows that deep, narrow multilayer perceptrons with a small amount of additional width can approximate any twice-continuously-differentiable diffeomorphism. This connects the expressive power of networks to smooth, invertible geometric transformations.

Using that connection, the authors identify the geometric function with the optimal minimum width and apply the Whitney embedding theorem to derive an upper bound: max(2dx + 1, dy) + alpha(sigma). The activation-dependent term lies between zero and two. They also establish new exact values in several settings, including w(2,2) = w(2,3) = 4. The contribution provides both a geometric route to width analysis and concrete sharper results.
summary.tldr: A geometric framework yields new upper bounds and exact minimum widths for universal approximation by deep, narrow neural networks.

title: Minimum Width for Deep, Narrow MLP: A Diffeomorphism Approach

abstract: In the machine learning system, the hybrid model parallelism combining tensor parallelism (TP) and pipeline parallelism (PP) has become the dominant solution for distributed training of Large Language Models~(LLMs) and Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). However, TP introduces significant collective communication overheads, while PP suffers from synchronization inefficiencies such as pipeline bubbles. Existing works primarily address these challenges from isolated perspectives, focusing either on overlapping TP communication or on flexible PP scheduling to mitigate pipeline bubbles. In this paper, we propose a new synergistic tensor and pipeline parallelism schedule that simultaneously reduces both types of bubbles. Our proposed schedule decouples the forward and backward passes in PP into fine-grained computation units, which are then braided to form a composite computation sequence. This compositional structure enables near-complete elimination of TP-related bubbles. Building upon this structure, we further design the PP schedule to minimize PP bubbles. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves training throughput by up to 12\% for LLMs and 16\% for MLLMs compared to existing scheduling methods. Our source code is avaiable at https://github.com/MICLAB-BUPT/STP.

paragraphs: Distributed training often combines tensor parallelism with pipeline parallelism. Tensor parallelism incurs collective communication overhead, while pipeline parallelism leaves devices waiting during synchronization gaps known as bubbles. This paper argues that treating these scheduling problems separately misses opportunities to reduce idle time across both forms of parallelism.

The proposed schedule splits pipeline forward and backward passes into fine-grained computation units. It then interleaves these units into a composite sequence designed to nearly eliminate tensor-parallelism-related bubbles. Building on that sequence, the authors further arrange the pipeline schedule to minimize its own bubbles, making the two scheduling decisions work together.

Experiments report training-throughput gains of up to twelve percent for large language models and sixteen percent for multimodal large language models relative to existing schedules. These are maximum reported improvements, rather than uniform gains for every setting. The contribution shows how reorganizing computation can improve the efficiency of combined parallel training by addressing communication-related and pipeline-related waiting within a shared schedule.
summary.tldr: A coordinated tensor-and-pipeline schedule reduces both kinds of idle time, improving training throughput by up to twelve percent for LLMs and sixteen percent for multimodal LLMs.

title: Synergistic Tensor and Pipeline Parallelism

abstract: Deep neural networks achieve state-of-the-art results for accelerated MRI reconstruction. Most research on deep learning based imaging focuses on improving neural network architectures trained and evaluated on fixed and homogeneous training and evaluation data. In this work, we investigate data curation strategies for improving MRI reconstruction. We assemble a large dataset of raw k-space data from 18 public sources consisting of 1.1M images and construct a diverse evaluation set comprising 48 test sets, capturing variations in anatomy, contrast, number of coils, and other key factors. We propose and study different data filtering strategies to enhance performance of current state-of-the-art neural networks for accelerated MRI reconstruction. Our experiments show that filtering the training data leads to consistent, albeit modest, performance gains. These performance gains are robust across different training set sizes and accelerations, and we find that filtering is particularly beneficial when the proportion of in-distribution data in the unfiltered training set is low.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether better training-data selection can improve neural reconstruction for accelerated MRI. Much work in this area concentrates on network architecture while using fixed, relatively homogeneous datasets. The authors shift attention to data curation and evaluate reconstruction across a wider range of imaging conditions.

They assemble raw k-space data from 18 public sources, totaling 1.1 million images. Their evaluation contains 48 test sets covering differences in anatomy, contrast, coil count, and other factors. This setup allows the study to examine filtering strategies across varied conditions rather than drawing conclusions from a single homogeneous test set.

Filtering yields consistent but modest performance improvements for current state-of-the-art reconstruction networks. The gains persist across different training-set sizes and acceleration levels, and filtering is particularly helpful when the original training collection contains a small proportion of in-distribution data. The finding gives data composition a concrete role in reconstruction quality: selecting more suitable examples can improve results even when the underlying network is already strong.
summary.tldr: Filtering a diverse MRI training collection produces consistent, modest reconstruction gains, especially when initially relevant data are scarce.

title: Improving Deep Learning for Accelerated MRI With Data Filtering

abstract: Recent interpretability work on large language models (LLMs) has been increasingly dominated by a feature-discovery approach with the help of proxy modules. Then, the quality of features learned by, e.g., sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), is evaluated. This paradigm naturally raises a critical question: do such learned features have better properties than those already represented within the original model parameters, and unfortunately, only a few studies have made such comparisons systematically so far. In this work, we revisit the interpretability of feature vectors stored in feed-forward (FF) layers, given the perspective of FF as key-value memories, with modern interpretability benchmarks. Our extensive evaluation revealed that SAE and FFs exhibits a similar range of interpretability, although SAEs displayed an observable but minimal improvement in some aspects. Furthermore, in certain aspects, surprisingly, even vanilla FFs yielded better interpretability than the SAEs, and features discovered in SAEs and FFs diverged. These bring questions about the advantage of SAEs from both perspectives of feature quality and faithfulness, compared to directly interpreting FF feature vectors, and FF key-value parameters serve as a strong baseline in modern interpretability research.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders are widely used to discover interpretable features in language models. This paper asks whether those learned features are better than features already present in the model’s own parameters. That comparison matters because assessing a feature-discovery method alone does not establish how much it improves on directly examining the original network.

The authors revisit feed-forward layers as key-value memories and evaluate their stored feature vectors using modern interpretability benchmarks. They find that feed-forward features and sparse-autoencoder features occupy a similar range of interpretability. Sparse autoencoders show observable but small advantages in some aspects, while ordinary feed-forward features perform better in certain others.

The two approaches also uncover different features, raising questions about both feature quality and faithfulness to the original model. The findings do not establish that sparse autoencoders lack value; they challenge the size and consistency of their advantage in the evaluated comparisons. Direct interpretation of feed-forward key-value parameters emerges as a strong baseline for evaluating modern interpretability methods.
summary.tldr: Directly examined feed-forward features are nearly as interpretable as sparse-autoencoder features in the reported evaluations, providing a strong comparison baseline.

title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: Learning with non-modular losses is an important problem when sets of predictions are made simultaneously. The main tools for constructing convex surrogate loss functions for set prediction are margin rescaling and slack rescaling. In this work, we show that these strategies lead to tight convex surrogates iff the underlying loss function is increasing in the number of incorrect predictions. However, gradient or cutting-plane computation for these functions is NP-hard for non-supermodular loss functions. We propose instead a novel convex surrogate loss function for submodular losses, the Lovasz hinge, which leads to O(p log p) complexity with O(p) oracle accesses to the loss function to compute a gradient or cutting-plane. As a result, we have developed the first tractable convex surrogates in the literature for submodular losses. We demonstrate the utility of this novel convex surrogate through a real world image labeling task.

The main tools for constructing convex surrogate loss functions for set prediction are margin rescaling and slack rescaling. In this work, we show that these strategies lead to tight convex surrogates iff the underlying loss function is increasing in the number of incorrect predictions. However, gradient or cutting-plane computation for these functions is NP-hard for non-supermodular loss functions. We propose instead a novel convex surrogate loss function for submodular losses, the Lovasz hinge, which leads to O(p log p) complexity with O(p) oracle accesses to the loss function to compute a gradient or cutting-plane. As a result, we have developed the first tractable convex surrogates in the literature for submodular losses. We demonstrate the utility of this novel convex surrogate through a real world image labeling task.

paragraphs: When a system makes several predictions together, the cost of their combined errors may not decompose into separate costs for each prediction. This paper studies convex surrogate losses for such set-prediction problems. These surrogates provide optimization objectives for learning when the original loss depends on the collection of mistakes.

The authors show that margin and slack rescaling yield tight convex surrogates exactly when the underlying loss increases with the number of incorrect predictions. However, computing gradients or cutting planes for these constructions is NP-hard for non-supermodular losses. Thus, a favorable mathematical relationship to the original loss does not necessarily make training computationally tractable.

For submodular losses, the paper introduces the Lovasz hinge. Computing a gradient or cutting plane takes O(p log p) work and O(p) accesses to the loss function. The authors present it as the first tractable convex-surrogate construction for this class and demonstrate its utility on a real-world image-labeling task, connecting the optimization result to structured prediction.
summary.tldr: The Lovasz hinge provides a tractable convex surrogate for submodular prediction losses, avoiding a computational obstacle in standard rescaling approaches.

title: Learning Submodular Losses with the Lovasz Hinge

abstract: Granger causal analysis has been an important tool for causal analysis for time series in various fields, including neuroscience and economics, and recently it has been extended to include instantaneous effects between the time series to explain the contemporaneous dependence in the residuals. In this paper, we assume that the time series at the true causal frequency follow the vector autoregressive model. We show that when the data resolution becomes lower due to subsampling, neither the original Granger causal analysis nor the extended one is able to discover the underlying causal relations. We then aim to answer the following question: can we estimate the temporal causal relations at the right causal frequency from the subsampled data? Traditionally this suffers from the identifiability problems: under the Gaussianity assumption of the data, the solutions are generally not unique. We prove that, however, if the noise terms are non-Gaussian, the underlying model for the high frequency data is identifiable from subsampled data under mild conditions. We then propose an Expectation-Maximization (EM) approach and a variational inference approach to recover temporal causal relations from such subsampled data. Experimental results on both simulated and real data are reported to illustrate the performance of the proposed approaches.

This paper assumes that the process at its true causal frequency follows a vector autoregressive model. It shows that subsampling can prevent both ordinary Granger analysis and an extension incorporating instantaneous effects from recovering the underlying causal relationships.

Recovering the faster process requires distinguishing among models that could generate the same slower observations. Under Gaussian assumptions, the solutions are generally not unique. The authors prove that non-Gaussian noise makes the underlying high-frequency model identifiable from subsampled observations under mild conditions. The noise distribution therefore plays a substantive role in whether causal recovery is possible.

To estimate the relationships, the paper develops both an expectation-maximization approach and a variational inference approach. Experiments on simulated and real data illustrate their performance. The contribution combines an explanation of why conventional analysis fails at reduced resolution with a conditional identification result and methods for recovering temporal relationships in that setting.
summary.tldr: Under a vector autoregressive model and suitable conditions, non-Gaussian noise enables recovery of temporal causal relationships from subsampled data.

title: Discovering Temporal Causal Relations from Subsampled Data

abstract: We learn the structure of a Markov Network between two groups of random variables from joint observations. Since modelling and learning the full MN structure may be hard, learning the links between two groups directly may be a preferable option. We introduce a novel concept called the \emphpartitioned ratio whose factorization directly associates with the Markovian properties of random variables across two groups. A simple one-shot convex optimization procedure is proposed for learning the \emphsparse factorizations of the partitioned ratio and it is theoretically guaranteed to recover the correct inter-group structure under mild conditions. The performance of the proposed method is experimentally compared with the state of the art MN structure learning methods using ROC curves. Real applications on analyzing bipartisanship in US congress and pairwise DNA/time-series alignments are also reported.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn relationships between two groups of random variables from joint observations. Learning an entire Markov network may be difficult when the main interest is only in connections across the groups. The authors therefore formulate a method that targets this inter-group structure directly.

Their key construction is the partitioned ratio, whose factorization corresponds to Markovian relationships across the partition. They propose a single convex optimization procedure for learning sparse factorizations of this ratio. This connects an optimization problem to the desired network links, and the authors prove recovery of the correct inter-group structure under conditions they describe as mild.

The method is experimentally compared with state-of-the-art Markov-network structure-learning approaches using ROC curves. Applications include analyzing bipartisanship in the US Congress and pairwise DNA and time-series alignments. These examples illustrate the scope of learning cross-group relationships directly. The theoretical guarantee remains conditional on the stated recovery conditions, while the experiments examine how the targeted formulation behaves in practice.
summary.tldr: A partitioned-ratio formulation learns links between two variable groups through convex optimization, with conditional guarantees of correct structure recovery.

title: Structure Learning of Partitioned Markov Networks

abstract: Sum-Product Networks (SPNs) are probabilistic inference machines that admit exact inference in linear time in the size of the network. Existing parameter learning approaches for SPNs are largely based on the maximum likelihood principle and are subject to overfitting compared to more Bayesian approaches. Exact Bayesian posterior inference for SPNs is computationally intractable. Even approximation techniques such as standard variational inference and posterior sampling for SPNs are computationally infeasible even for networks of moderate size due to the large number of local latent variables per instance. In this work, we propose a novel deterministic collapsed variational inference algorithm for SPNs that is computationally efficient, easy to implement and at the same time allows us to incorporate prior information into the optimization formulation. Extensive experiments show a significant improvement in accuracy compared with a maximum likelihood based approach.

paragraphs: Sum-product networks support exact probabilistic inference in time proportional to network size, but learning their parameters presents a different computational problem. The paper explains that maximum-likelihood training can overfit compared with Bayesian approaches. Yet exact Bayesian posterior inference is intractable, so obtaining the benefits of Bayesian learning is not straightforward.

Standard approximation methods also face difficulties because each data instance introduces many local latent variables. According to the abstract, this makes ordinary variational inference and posterior sampling computationally infeasible even for moderately sized networks. The proposed solution is a deterministic collapsed variational inference algorithm designed specifically for sum-product networks.

The method offers an efficient optimization formulation that can incorporate prior information and is described as easy to implement. Experiments show a significant accuracy improvement over a maximum-likelihood approach. The result matters because it connects a practical training procedure with the ability to use prior information, while preserving the distinction between efficient inference in an existing network and the harder task of Bayesian parameter learning.
summary.tldr: Collapsed variational inference makes Bayesian-style parameter learning practical for sum-product networks and improves reported accuracy.

title: Collapsed Variational Inference for Sum-Product Networks

abstract: The graduated optimization approach, also known as the continuation method, is a popular heuristic to solving non-convex problems that has received renewed interest over the last decade.Despite being popular, very little is known in terms of its theoretical convergence analysis. In this paper we describe a new first-order algorithm based on graduated optimization and analyze its performance. We characterize a family of non-convex functions for which this algorithm provably converges to a global optimum. In particular, we prove that the algorithm converges to an ε-approximate solution within O(1 / ε^2) gradient-based steps. We extend our algorithm and analysis to the setting of stochastic non-convex optimization with noisy gradient feedback, attaining the same convergence rate. Additionally, we discuss the setting of “zero-order optimization", and devise a variant of our algorithm which converges at rate of O(d^2/ ε^4).

paragraphs: Graduated optimization, also called continuation, is a popular approach to nonconvex optimization whose convergence behavior has received limited theoretical explanation. This paper develops a new first-order algorithm based on that approach and identifies a family of nonconvex functions for which global convergence can be proved. The guarantee is explicitly tied to this characterized family.

For those problems, the authors show that the method reaches an ε-approximate solution within O(1/ε²) gradient-based steps. This gives a quantitative relationship between the requested accuracy and the number of optimization steps. They also extend the algorithm and analysis to stochastic optimization with noisy gradient feedback, obtaining the same stated convergence rate.

The paper additionally considers zero-order optimization, where the method must work without gradient feedback, and provides a variant with rate O(d²/ε⁴). The contribution is therefore a set of guarantees across different information settings. It establishes circumstances in which graduated optimization can reach a global optimum, while keeping that result distinct from a claim about arbitrary nonconvex objectives.
summary.tldr: A graduated optimization algorithm has global convergence guarantees for a specified nonconvex function family, including under noisy gradient feedback.

title: On Graduated Optimization for Stochastic Non-Convex Problems

abstract: The power grid is a complex and vital system that necessitates careful reliability management. Managing the grid is a difficult problem with multiple time scales of decision making and stochastic behavior due to renewable energy generations, variable demand and unplanned outages. Solving this problem in the face of uncertainty requires a new methodology with tractable algorithms. In this work, we introduce a new model for hierarchical decision making in complex systems. We apply reinforcement learning (RL) methods to learn a proxy, i.e., a level of abstraction, for real-time power grid reliability. We devise an algorithm that alternates between slow time-scale policy improvement, and fast time-scale value function approximation. We compare our results to prevailing heuristics, and show the strength of our method.

paragraphs: Electricity-grid management combines decisions made on different time scales with uncertainty from renewable generation, changing demand, and unexpected outages. Reliability must be managed across these interacting sources of variation. The paper introduces a hierarchical decision-making model intended to make this complex problem computationally tractable.

The approach uses reinforcement learning to construct a proxy for real-time grid reliability. This proxy provides a level of abstraction through which the decision process can represent reliability. The algorithm alternates between improving a policy at the slower time scale and approximating a value function at the faster time scale.

That alternating structure connects longer-horizon decision improvement with a learned assessment of faster system behavior. It directly addresses the mismatch between the time scales involved in grid management. Comparisons with prevailing heuristics demonstrate the strength of the approach in the reported results. The contribution is a model and learning procedure for coordinating these decisions under uncertainty, supported by comparative evidence rather than a claim of universal superiority.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical reinforcement learning method alternates slow policy improvement with fast value approximation to manage electricity-grid reliability under uncertainty.

title: Hierarchical Decision Making In Electricity Grid Management

abstract: Hierarchical clustering is a popular unsupervised data analysis method. For many real-world applications, we would like to exploit prior information about the data that imposes constraints on the clustering hierarchy, and is not captured by the set of features available to the algorithm. This gives rise to the problem of hierarchical clustering with structural constraints. Structural constraints pose major challenges for bottom-up approaches like average/single linkage and even though they can be naturally incorporated into top-down divisive algorithms, no formal guarantees exist on the quality of their output. In this paper, we provide provable approximation guarantees for two simple top-down algorithms, using a recently introduced optimization viewpoint of hierarchical clustering with pairwise similarity information (Dasgupta, 2016). We show how to find good solutions even in the presence of conflicting prior information, by formulating a constraint-based regularization of the objective. Furthemore, we explore a variation of this objective for dissimilarity information (Cohen-Addad et al., 2018) and improve upon current techniques. Finally, we demonstrate our approach on a real dataset for the taxonomy application.

Structural constraints express such knowledge. Incorporating them is challenging for bottom-up clustering, while simply adding them to top-down methods does not by itself establish the quality of the resulting hierarchy.

The paper provides approximation guarantees for two simple top-down algorithms. It uses an optimization formulation based on pairwise similarities, making clustering quality an objective that can be analyzed mathematically. The guarantees give a formal basis for evaluating these constrained hierarchical solutions.

Prior information can also conflict. The authors address this by regularizing the objective with constraints, allowing the optimization to seek good solutions even when the supplied guidance is inconsistent. They additionally study an objective using dissimilarity information and improve on existing techniques. A taxonomy application on a real dataset demonstrates the approach, connecting the theoretical treatment of constraints to a practical task involving hierarchical organization.
summary.tldr: Two top-down clustering algorithms gain approximation guarantees while accommodating structural guidance, including conflicting prior information.

title: Hierarchical Clustering with Structural Constraints

abstract: In this paper, we revisit the recurrent back-propagation (RBP) algorithm, discuss the conditions under which it applies as well as how to satisfy them in deep neural networks. We show that RBP can be unstable and propose two variants based on conjugate gradient on the normal equations (CG-RBP) and Neumann series (Neumann-RBP). We further investigate the relationship between Neumann-RBP and back propagation through time (BPTT) and its truncated version (TBPTT). Our Neumann-RBP has the same time complexity as TBPTT but only requires constant memory, whereas TBPTT’s memory cost scales linearly with the number of truncation steps. We examine all RBP variants along with BPTT and TBPTT in three different application domains: associative memory with continuous Hopfield networks, document classification in citation networks using graph neural networks and hyperparameter optimization for fully connected networks. All experiments demonstrate that RBPs, especially the Neumann-RBP variant, are efficient and effective for optimizing convergent recurrent neural networks.

The authors show that the original approach can be unstable. They propose two alternatives: CG-RBP, based on conjugate gradients applied to normal equations, and Neumann-RBP, based on a Neumann series.

A key contribution is the relationship between Neumann-RBP and back-propagation through time, including its truncated version. Neumann-RBP has the same time complexity as truncated back-propagation through time but needs constant memory. By comparison, the truncated method’s memory use grows linearly with the number of truncation steps, making the distinction meaningful when more steps are considered.

The experiments cover associative memory with continuous Hopfield networks, document classification with graph neural networks on citation networks, and hyperparameter optimization for fully connected networks. Across these applications, the recurrent back-propagation variants are efficient and effective, especially Neumann-RBP. The stated scope is optimization of convergent recurrent neural networks, which is central to interpreting these results.
summary.tldr: Improved recurrent back-propagation variants train convergent recurrent networks effectively, with Neumann-RBP offering constant-memory computation.

title: Reviving and Improving Recurrent Back-Propagation

abstract: In this paper, we propose a Minimax Concave Penalized Multi-Armed Bandit (MCP-Bandit) algorithm for a decision-maker facing high-dimensional data with latent sparse structure in an online learning and decision-making process. We demonstrate that the MCP-Bandit algorithm asymptotically achieves the optimal cumulative regret in sample size T, O(log T), and further attains a tighter bound in both covariates dimension d and the number of significant covariates s, O(s^2 (s + log d). In addition, we develop a linear approximation method, the 2-step Weighted Lasso procedure, to identify the MCP estimator for the MCP-Bandit algorithm under non-i.i.d. samples. Using this procedure, the MCP estimator matches the oracle estimator with high probability. Finally, we present two experiments to benchmark our proposed the MCP-Bandit algorithm to other bandit algorithms. Both experiments demonstrate that the MCP-Bandit algorithm performs favorably over other benchmark algorithms, especially when there is a high level of data sparsity or when the sample size is not too small.

paragraphs: The paper studies online decisions informed by many measured variables when only a small subset is relevant. Its MCP-Bandit algorithm uses a minimax concave penalty to exploit this latent sparse structure. The aim is to make effective sequential choices while learning which parts of the high-dimensional information matter.

The authors show that cumulative regret asymptotically grows as O(log T), achieving the stated optimal dependence on the number of decisions. They also derive tighter dependence on the overall covariate dimension and the number of significant covariates. These results connect decision quality to sparsity, rather than treating every available variable as equally consequential.

To compute the required estimator from non-independent, non-identically distributed samples, the paper develops a two-step weighted Lasso approximation. This procedure matches the oracle estimator with high probability. Two experiments show favorable performance relative to other bandit algorithms, particularly when the data are highly sparse or the sample size is not too small. Those qualifications identify where the reported empirical advantages are especially pronounced.
summary.tldr: MCP-Bandit exploits sparse structure in high-dimensional decision data, with asymptotically optimal logarithmic regret and favorable experimental results.

title: Minimax Concave Penalized Multi-Armed Bandit Model with High-Dimensional Covariates

abstract: Despite being robust to small amounts of label noise, convolutional neural networks trained with stochastic gradient methods have been shown to easily fit random labels. When there are a mixture of correct and mislabelled targets, networks tend to fit the former before the latter. This suggests using a suitable two-component mixture model as an unsupervised generative model of sample loss values during training to allow online estimation of the probability that a sample is mislabelled. Specifically, we propose a beta mixture to estimate this probability and correct the loss by relying on the network prediction (the so-called bootstrapping loss). We further adapt mixup augmentation to drive our approach a step further. Experiments on CIFAR-10/100 and TinyImageNet demonstrate a robustness to label noise that substantially outperforms recent state-of-the-art. Source code is available at https://git.io/fjsvE and Appendix at https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.11238.
