paragraphs: Neural networks can eventually fit incorrect labels, even though they tolerate small amounts of label noise. When training data mixes correct and incorrect targets, networks tend to learn the correctly labeled examples first. This paper uses that difference in training behavior to estimate which examples may have unreliable labels.

The method fits a two-component beta mixture to the loss values observed during training. This supplies an unsupervised, continually updated estimate of the probability that each example is mislabeled. The estimated probability then informs a bootstrapping loss that relies on the network’s own prediction to correct the training signal. The authors also adapt mixup augmentation to strengthen the approach.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet show substantially better robustness to label noise than recent state-of-the-art methods. The key idea is to use the evolving loss distribution as evidence about label reliability, then feed that evidence back into learning. The model estimates probabilities of mislabeling rather than treating a high loss as definitive proof that an example’s label is wrong.
summary.tldr: A beta mixture of training losses estimates label reliability and guides loss correction, improving noise robustness on three image-classification benchmarks.

title: Unsupervised Label Noise Modeling and Loss Correction

abstract: Bayesian nonparametric approaches, in particular the Pitman-Yor process and the associated two-parameter Chinese Restaurant process, have been successfully used in applications where the data exhibit a power-law behavior. Examples include natural language processing, natural images or networks. There is also growing empirical evidence suggesting that some datasets exhibit a two-regime power-law behavior: one regime for small frequencies, and a second regime, with a different exponent, for high frequencies. In this paper, we introduce a class of completely random measures which are doubly regularly-varying. Contrary to the Pitman-Yor process, we show that when completely random measures in this class are normalized to obtain random probability measures and associated random partitions, such partitions exhibit a double power-law behavior. We present two general constructions and discuss in particular two models within this class: the beta prime process (Broderick et al. (2015, 2018) and a novel process called generalized BFRY process. We derive efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms to estimate the parameters of these models. Finally, we show that the proposed models provide a better fit than the Pitman-Yor process on various datasets.

In this paper, we introduce a class of completely random measures which are doubly regularly-varying. Contrary to the Pitman-Yor process, we show that when completely random measures in this class are normalized to obtain random probability measures and associated random partitions, such partitions exhibit a double power-law behavior. We present two general constructions and discuss in particular two models within this class: the beta prime process (Broderick et al. (2015, 2018) and a novel process called generalized BFRY process. Finally, we show that the proposed models provide a better fit than the Pitman-Yor process on various datasets.

paragraphs: Power-law models describe data with highly uneven frequencies, and Bayesian nonparametric models such as the Pitman-Yor process are established tools for these patterns. The paper addresses evidence that some datasets have two distinct frequency regimes: rare and frequent observations follow power laws with different exponents. A model designed around one regime can miss that distinction.

The authors introduce a class of completely random measures with a property called double regular variation. They show that normalizing these measures into probability distributions produces associated random partitions with double power-law behavior. Two general constructions support this class, including the beta prime process and a newly introduced generalized BFRY process.

The paper also develops efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms for estimating the models’ parameters. On the datasets examined, the proposed models fit better than the Pitman-Yor process. The contribution combines a mathematical explanation for two-regime frequency patterns with procedures for fitting models that can express those patterns.
summary.tldr: New Bayesian nonparametric models capture separate power-law regimes for rare and frequent observations and improve fit over the Pitman-Yor process on evaluated datasets.

title: Beyond the Chinese Restaurant and Pitman-Yor processes: Statistical Models with double power-law behavior

abstract: Importance weighted variational inference (Burda et al., 2015) uses multiple i.i.d. samples to have a tighter variational lower bound. We believe a joint proposal has the potential of reducing the number of redundant samples, and introduce a hierarchical structure to induce correlation. The hope is that the proposals would coordinate to make up for the error made by one another to reduce the variance of the importance estimator. Theoretically, we analyze the condition under which convergence of the estimator variance can be connected to convergence of the lower bound. Empirically, we confirm that maximization of the lower bound does implicitly minimize variance. Further analysis shows that this is a result of negative correlation induced by the proposed hierarchical meta sampling scheme, and performance of inference also improves when the number of samples increases.

We believe a joint proposal has the potential of reducing the number of redundant samples, and introduce a hierarchical structure to induce correlation. The hope is that the proposals would coordinate to make up for the error made by one another to reduce the variance of the importance estimator. Theoretically, we analyze the condition under which convergence of the estimator variance can be connected to convergence of the lower bound. Empirically, we confirm that maximization of the lower bound does implicitly minimize variance. Further analysis shows that this is a result of negative correlation induced by the proposed hierarchical meta sampling scheme, and performance of inference also improves when the number of samples increases.

paragraphs: Importance-weighted variational inference uses multiple independent samples to obtain a tighter lower bound on its objective. This paper explores whether coordinating those samples can reduce redundancy. It introduces a hierarchical proposal structure that makes samples dependent, with the aim of letting their contributions compensate for one another’s errors.

The intended benefit is a lower-variance importance estimator: repeated estimates would fluctuate less. The theoretical analysis examines the condition under which convergence of this variance can be connected to convergence of the lower bound. This makes the relationship between the training objective and estimator quality an explicit subject of analysis, rather than assuming they always improve together.

Empirically, maximizing the lower bound also reduces estimator variance. Further analysis attributes this effect to negative correlation introduced by the hierarchical sampling scheme, consistent with the proposed idea of compensating sample contributions. Inference performance also improves as the sample count increases. The results support coordinated sampling as a useful extension of importance-weighted inference.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical proposals coordinate importance samples, with observed negative correlation reducing estimator variance and improving inference.

title: Hierarchical Importance Weighted Autoencoders

abstract: Selective rationalization improves neural network interpretability by identifying a small subset of input features {—} the rationale {—} that best explains or supports the prediction. A typical rationalization criterion, i.e. maximum mutual information (MMI), finds the rationale that maximizes the prediction performance based only on the rationale. However, MMI can be problematic because it picks up spurious correlations between the input features and the output. Instead, we introduce a game-theoretic invariant rationalization criterion where the rationales are constrained to enable the same predictor to be optimal across different environments. We show both theoretically and empirically that the proposed rationales can rule out spurious correlations and generalize better to different test scenarios. The resulting explanations also align better with human judgments. Our implementations are publicly available at https://github.com/code-terminator/invariant_rationalization.

A typical rationalization criterion, i.e. maximum mutual information (MMI), finds the rationale that maximizes the prediction performance based only on the rationale. However, MMI can be problematic because it picks up spurious correlations between the input features and the output. Instead, we introduce a game-theoretic invariant rationalization criterion where the rationales are constrained to enable the same predictor to be optimal across different environments. We show both theoretically and empirically that the proposed rationales can rule out spurious correlations and generalize better to different test scenarios. The resulting explanations also align better with human judgments. Our implementations are publicly available at https://github.com/code-terminator/invariant_rationalization.

paragraphs: Selective rationalization explains a prediction by identifying a small subset of its input features. A common approach chooses a rationale that allows accurate prediction when the model sees only that subset. This paper identifies a problem with that criterion: a highly predictive subset may rely on spurious correlations, so predictive success alone can select an unreliable explanation.

The proposed invariant rationalization criterion introduces a requirement across environments. The selected rationales must allow the same predictor to be optimal in each environment. The authors formulate this requirement through a game-theoretic approach. The key change is to evaluate rationales through the consistency of their predictive relationship across environments, rather than only their ability to support a prediction in one setting.

Theoretical and empirical results show that the proposed rationales can exclude spurious correlations and generalize better to different test scenarios. The resulting explanations also agree more closely with human judgments. These findings connect interpretability with transfer across environments: an explanation can be more useful when the predictive relationship it captures remains applicable as the setting changes.
summary.tldr: Requiring rationales to support the same optimal predictor across environments can reduce spurious correlations and improve generalization and human agreement.

title: Invariant Rationalization

abstract: Training deep neural networks with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) can often achieve zero training loss on real-world tasks although the optimization landscape is known to be highly non-convex. To understand the success of SGD for training deep neural networks, this work presents a mean-field analysis of deep residual networks, based on a line of works which interpret the continuum limit of the deep residual network as an ordinary differential equation as the the network capacity tends to infinity. Specifically, we propose a \textbf{new continuum limit} of deep residual networks, which enjoys a good landscape in the sense that \textbf{every local minimizer is global}. This characterization enables us to derive the first global convergence result for multilayer neural networks in the mean-field regime. Furthermore, our proof does not rely on the convexity of the loss landscape, but instead, an assumption on the global minimizer should achieve zero loss which can be achieved when the model shares a universal approximation property. Key to our result is the observation that a deep residual network resembles a shallow network ensemble \cite{veit2016residual}, \emph{i.e.} a two-layer network. We bound the difference between the shallow network and our ResNet model via the adjoint sensitivity method, which enables us to transfer previous mean-field analysis of two-layer networks to deep networks. Furthermore, we propose several novel training schemes based on our new continuous model, among which one new training procedure introduces the operation of switching the order of the residual blocks and results in strong empirical performance on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Deep residual networks can reach zero training loss despite having nonconvex optimization landscapes. summary.tldr: A new continuous model of deep ResNets supports global convergence analysis under a zero-loss assumption and inspires effective training schemes.

title: A Mean Field Analysis Of Deep ResNet And Beyond: Towards Provably Optimization Via Overparameterization From Depth

abstract: With continual miniaturization ever more applications of deep learning can be found in embedded systems, where it is common to encounter data with natural representation in the complex domain. To this end we extend Sparse Variational Dropout to complex-valued neural networks and verify the proposed Bayesian technique by conducting a large numerical study of the performance-compression trade-off of C-valued networks on two tasks: image recognition on MNIST-like and CIFAR10 datasets and music transcription on MusicNet. We replicate the state-of-the-art result by Trabelsi et al. (2018) on MusicNet with a complex-valued network compressed by 50-100x at a small performance penalty.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to compress neural networks whose computations use complex numbers. Such networks are relevant when the data naturally have a complex-valued representation, including applications in embedded systems. The central question is how much a network can be reduced while preserving its ability to perform the task it was trained for.

The authors extend Sparse Variational Dropout to complex-valued networks, creating a Bayesian method for sparsification. Sparsification seeks a model with fewer active parameters, making compression part of the learning approach. Extending the technique to complex-valued computation allows the authors to investigate the trade-off between model size and predictive performance in that setting.

They conduct a large numerical study covering image recognition on MNIST-like datasets and CIFAR10, together with music transcription on MusicNet. For MusicNet, they report reproducing a previously leading result with a complex-valued network compressed by a factor of 50–100, at a small performance penalty. This provides concrete evidence that substantial compression can preserve useful performance on the studied task.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian sparsification method compresses complex-valued networks substantially, with a small reported performance penalty on MusicNet.

title: Bayesian Sparsification of Deep C-valued Networks

abstract: Entities often interact with each other through multiple types of relations, which are often represented as multilayer networks. Multilayer networks among the same set of nodes usually share common structures, while each layer can possess its distinct node connecting behaviors. This paper proposes a flexible latent space model for multilayer networks for the purpose of capturing such characteristics. Specifically, the proposed model embeds each node with a latent vector shared among layers and a layer-specific effect for each layer; both elements together with a layer-specific connectivity matrix determine edge formations. To fit the model, we develop a projected gradient descent algorithm for efficient parameter estimation. We also establish theoretical properties of the maximum likelihood estimators and show that the upper bound of the common latent structure’s estimation error is inversely proportional to the number of layers under mild conditions. The superior performance of the proposed model is demonstrated through simulation studies and applications to two real-world data examples.

paragraphs: A multilayer network records several kinds of relationships among the same entities. Its layers can share an underlying organization while differing in how particular nodes connect. This paper develops a latent space model that represents both kinds of structure, allowing information to be shared across layers without requiring identical connection patterns.

Each node receives a hidden vector shared across all layers, together with an effect specific to each layer. A separate connectivity matrix for each layer combines with these components to determine how edges form. The authors develop a projected gradient descent algorithm to estimate the model parameters efficiently.

The theoretical analysis explains a benefit of combining layers: under mild conditions, an upper bound on the estimation error for the shared latent structure decreases inversely with the number of layers. This is a conditional guarantee about an error bound. Simulations and two real data applications also demonstrate the proposed model’s superior performance in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: A multilayer network model combines shared node representations with layer-specific effects, with estimation benefits from additional layers under mild conditions.

title: A Flexible Latent Space Model for Multilayer Networks
Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Context-based Representations

abstract: Recently, speech representation learning has improved many speech-related tasks such as speech recognition, speech classification, and speech-to-text translation. However, all the above tasks are in the direction of speech understanding, but for the inverse direction, speech synthesis, the potential of representation learning is yet to be realized, due to the challenging nature of generating high-quality speech. To address this problem, we propose our framework, Alignment-Aware Acoustic-Text Pretraining (A$^3$T), which reconstructs masked acoustic signals with text input and acoustic-text alignment during training. In this way, the pretrained model can generate high quality reconstructed spectrogram, which can be applied to the speech editing and unseen speaker TTS directly. Experiments show A$^3$T outperforms SOTA models on speech editing, and improves multi-speaker speech synthesis without the external speaker verification model.

paragraphs: A³T investigates how pretraining can help models generate speech. The paper starts from a gap: learning speech representations had improved tasks that interpret audio, while its potential for speech synthesis remained less developed. Producing high-quality speech requires representations that support reconstruction of acoustic detail as well as understanding.

The training task hides portions of the acoustic signal and asks the model to reconstruct them. It supplies both text and acoustic-text alignment, giving the model information about which parts of the audio correspond to which parts of the text. This makes the relationship between spoken content and acoustic structure explicit during pretraining.

The resulting model produces reconstructed spectrograms that can be used directly for speech editing and text-to-speech generation for unseen speakers. The reported experiments show better speech editing performance than the compared state-of-the-art models, along with improved multi-speaker synthesis without an external speaker verification model. These findings support reconstruction with alignment information as a useful pretraining approach for speech generation.
summary.tldr: A³T learns to reconstruct masked audio using text and alignment information, improving speech editing and multi-speaker synthesis.

title: A$^3$T: Alignment-Aware Acoustic and Text Pretraining for Speech Synthesis and Editing

abstract: Executing actions in a correlated manner is a common strategy for human coordination that often leads to better cooperation, which is also potentially beneficial for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). However, the recent success of MARL relies heavily on the convenient paradigm of purely decentralized execution, where there is no action correlation among agents for scalability considerations. In this work, we introduce a Bayesian network to inaugurate correlations between agents’ action selections in their joint policy. Theoretically, we establish a theoretical justification for why action dependencies are beneficial by deriving the multi-agent policy gradient formula under such a Bayesian network joint policy and proving its global convergence to Nash equilibria under tabular softmax policy parameterization in cooperative Markov games. Further, by equipping existing MARL algorithms with a recent method of differentiable directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), we develop practical algorithms to learn the context-aware Bayesian network policies in scenarios with partial observability and various difficulty. We also dynamically decrease the sparsity of the learned DAG throughout the training process, which leads to weakly or even purely independent policies for decentralized execution. Empirical results on a range of MARL benchmarks show the benefits of our approach.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents may benefit from correlated action choices, yet decentralized multi-agent policies often select actions independently for scalability. This paper introduces dependencies through a Bayesian network over the joint policy. The goal is to capture useful coordination while retaining a path toward practical decentralized execution.

The authors derive the multi-agent policy-gradient formula for the Bayesian-network policy and prove convergence to Nash equilibria under tabular softmax parameterization in cooperative Markov games. Practical variants learn context-dependent directed acyclic graphs using differentiable graph-learning methods, including partially observable settings. Training also adjusts the dependency structure so resulting policies can become weakly dependent or fully independent.

Experiments on several multi-agent benchmarks demonstrate benefits from the approach. The theoretical and practical settings should be distinguished: the convergence guarantee applies to the specified tabular parameterization, while the learned context-aware policies address more complex benchmarks. The contribution is a structured way to exploit action dependence during cooperative policy learning.
summary.tldr: Bayesian-network joint policies introduce learnable action dependencies that improve cooperative multi-agent learning in the reported benchmarks.

title: Context-Aware Bayesian Network Actor-Critic Methods for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose a new definition of instance optimality for differentially private estimation algorithms. Our definition requires an optimal algorithm to compete, simultaneously for every dataset $D$, with the best private benchmark algorithm that (a) knows $D$ in advance and (b) is evaluated by its worst-case performance on large subsets of $D$. That is, the benchmark algorithm need not perform well when potentially extreme points are added to $D$; it only has to handle the removal of a small number of real data points that already exist. This makes our benchmark significantly stronger than those proposed in prior work. We nevertheless show, for real-valued datasets, how to construct private algorithms that achieve our notion of instance optimality when estimating a broad class of dataset properties, including means, quantiles, and $\ell_p$-norm minimizers. For means in particular, we provide a detailed analysis and show that our algorithm simultaneously matches or exceeds the asymptotic performance of existing algorithms under a range of distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper asks what it means for a differentially private estimator to perform optimally on each individual dataset. It introduces a benchmark that already knows the dataset and is judged by its worst-case performance over large subsets of that dataset. A single private algorithm must compete with this benchmark simultaneously for every dataset.

The benchmark must tolerate removal of a small number of existing points, but need not perform well after potentially extreme new points are added. That narrower evaluation requirement makes the benchmark stronger than earlier alternatives: it has fewer situations to handle. The challenge is to match this demanding dataset-specific comparator while retaining differential privacy.

For real-valued datasets, the authors construct algorithms achieving this notion of instance optimality for properties including means, quantiles, and minimizers of l-p norms. Their detailed mean-estimation analysis shows asymptotic performance matching or exceeding existing algorithms across a range of distributional assumptions. The contribution links a stronger definition of adaptation to concrete private estimation procedures.
summary.tldr: The paper defines a stronger subset-based benchmark for private estimation and constructs algorithms that meet it for several dataset properties.

title: Subset-Based Instance Optimality in Private Estimation

abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are important tools to model physical systems and including them into machine learning models is an important way of incorporating physical knowledge. Given any system of linear PDEs with constant coefficients, we propose a family of Gaussian process (GP) priors, which we call EPGP, such that all realizations are exact solutions of this system. We apply the Ehrenpreis-Palamodov fundamental principle, which works as a non-linear Fourier transform, to construct GP kernels mirroring standard spectral methods for GPs. Our approach can infer probable solutions of linear PDE systems from any data such as noisy measurements, or pointwise defined initial and boundary conditions. Constructing EPGP-priors is algorithmic, generally applicable, and comes with a sparse version (S-EPGP) that learns the relevant spectral frequencies and works better for big data sets. We demonstrate our approach on three families of systems of PDEs, the heat equation, wave equation, and Maxwell’s equations, where we improve upon the state of the art in computation time and precision, in some experiments by several orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Physical equations can constrain which predictions are plausible. This paper builds those constraints directly into Gaussian process priors: for any system of linear partial differential equations with constant coefficients, every realization of the proposed prior is an exact solution. The resulting family, EPGP, therefore represents uncertainty within the space of solutions to the specified equations.

The construction uses the Ehrenpreis-Palamodov fundamental principle, described as functioning like a nonlinear Fourier transform, to build kernels in the spirit of spectral Gaussian process methods. These priors can infer probable solutions from noisy measurements or pointwise initial and boundary conditions. The authors also provide a sparse version, S-EPGP, that learns relevant spectral frequencies and works better with large datasets.

Demonstrations cover the heat equation, wave equation, and Maxwell’s equations. The authors report improvements over the state of the art in computation time and precision, reaching several orders of magnitude in some experiments. The general construction applies to linear systems with constant coefficients; its exact-solution guarantee is specifically tied to that stated equation class.
summary.tldr: EPGP constructs Gaussian process priors whose realizations exactly satisfy specified linear PDE systems with constant coefficients.

title: Gaussian Process Priors for Systems of Linear Partial Differential Equations with Constant Coefficients

abstract: In this paper, we present efficient quantum algorithms that are exponentially faster than classical algorithms for solving the quantum optimal control problem. This problem involves finding the control variable that maximizes a physical quantity at time $T$, where the system is governed by a time-dependent Schrödinger equation. This type of control problem also has an intricate relation with machine learning. Our algorithms are based on a time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation method and a fast gradient-estimation algorithm. We also provide a comprehensive error analysis to quantify the total error from various steps, such as the finite-dimensional representation of the control function, the discretization of the Schrödinger equation, the numerical quadrature, and optimization. Our quantum algorithms require fault-tolerant quantum computers.

paragraphs: Quantum optimal control asks how to choose a control variable so that a physical quantity is maximized at a specified final time. The system evolves according to a time-dependent Schrödinger equation, linking the optimization objective to quantum dynamics. This paper presents quantum algorithms for the problem and reports an exponential speed advantage over classical algorithms.

The algorithms combine time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation with fast gradient estimation. Simulation handles the system’s evolving dynamics, while gradient estimation supports the search for a better control. This combination connects the physical evolution being controlled to the optimization procedure, making both parts central to the proposed computational improvement.

The authors also analyze errors from representing the control function in finite dimensions, discretizing the Schrödinger equation, numerical quadrature, and optimization. Accounting for these contributions provides a total-error analysis across the algorithm’s stages. The hardware requirement is explicit: the algorithms need fault-tolerant quantum computers. Their stated advantage therefore concerns computation with that capability, alongside an analysis of how approximation errors accumulate through the solution process.
summary.tldr: The paper presents quantum optimal-control algorithms with a stated exponential speedup, comprehensive error analysis, and a requirement for fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

title: Efficient Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Optimal Control

abstract: Leveraging privileged information (PI), or features available during training but not at test time, has recently been shown to be an effective method for addressing label noise. However, the reasons for its effectiveness are not well understood. In this study, we investigate the role played by different properties of the PI in explaining away label noise. Through experiments on multiple datasets with real PI (CIFAR-N/H) and a new large-scale benchmark ImageNet-PI, we find that PI is most helpful when it allows networks to easily distinguish clean from noisy data, while enabling a learning shortcut to memorize the noisy examples. Interestingly, when PI becomes too predictive of the target label, PI methods often perform worse than their no-PI baselines. Based on these findings, we propose several enhancements to the state-of-the-art PI methods and demonstrate the potential of PI as a means of tackling label noise. Finally, we show how we can easily combine the resulting PI approaches with existing no-PI techniques designed to deal with label noise.

paragraphs: Privileged information consists of features available during training that will not be available when a model is used. Such information can help learning from noisy labels, but the reasons are not obvious. This paper investigates which properties make these extra training features useful through experiments with real privileged information and a new large-scale benchmark, ImageNet-PI.

Across the studied datasets, privileged information is most helpful when it makes clean and noisy examples easy to distinguish while providing a shortcut for memorizing the noisy examples. The experiments also reveal a counterintuitive pattern: when privileged information becomes too predictive of the target label, methods using it often perform worse than corresponding methods without it.

These findings guide enhancements to existing leading privileged-information methods. The authors also show that the resulting approaches can be combined with established label-noise methods that do not use privileged information. The contribution clarifies that the usefulness of extra training features depends on what they reveal about noise and how the model uses them, rather than simply how strongly they predict the label.
summary.tldr: Privileged information helps noisy-label learning most when it separates clean from noisy examples and enables memorization of the noisy ones.

title: When does Privileged information Explain Away Label Noise?

abstract: Training deep learning models with differential privacy (DP) results in a degradation of performance. The training dynamics of models with DP show a significant difference from standard training, whereas understanding the geometric properties of private learning remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate sharpness, a key factor in achieving better generalization, in private learning. We show that flat minima can help reduce the negative effects of per-example gradient clipping and the addition of Gaussian noise. We then verify the effectiveness of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) for seeking flat minima in private learning. However, we also discover that SAM is detrimental to the privacy budget and computational time due to its two-step optimization. Thus, we propose a new sharpness-aware training method that mitigates the privacy-optimization trade-off. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method improves the performance of deep learning models with DP from both scratch and fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/jinseongP/DPSAT.

paragraphs: Training with differential privacy can reduce a neural network’s predictive performance. This paper examines that problem through the geometry of the training objective, focusing on sharpness. The authors show that flat minima can lessen the harmful effects of two operations used in private learning: clipping each example’s gradient and adding Gaussian noise.

They then investigate Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, as a way to find flatter minima. SAM proves useful for this purpose in private learning, but its two-step optimization creates additional costs in both computation and privacy budget. Thus, a method that improves the optimization landscape can also make private training more expensive along other dimensions.

To address this tension, the authors propose a new sharpness-aware training method that mitigates the trade-off between privacy and optimization. Experiments report performance improvements for differentially private models trained both from scratch and through fine-tuning. The contribution connects a geometric explanation of private training difficulties to a practical training approach, while explicitly accounting for the costs introduced by the original sharpness-aware procedure.
summary.tldr: A new sharpness-aware training method improves differentially private learning while mitigating SAM’s privacy-budget and computational costs.

title: Differentially Private Sharpness-Aware Training

abstract: We present a one-shot method for compressing large labeled graphs called Random Edge Coding. When paired with a parameter-free model based on Pólya’s Urn, the worst-case computational and memory complexities scale quasi-linearly and linearly with the number of observed edges, making it efficient on sparse graphs, and requires only integer arithmetic. Key to our method is bits-back coding, which is used to sample edges and vertices without replacement from the edge-list in a way that preserves the structure of the graph. Optimality is proven under a class of random graph models that are invariant to permutations of the edges and of vertices within an edge. Experiments indicate Random Edge Coding can achieve competitive compression performance on real-world network datasets and scales to graphs with millions of nodes and edges.

paragraphs: Random Edge Coding is a one-shot method for compressing large labeled graphs. It uses bits-back coding to sample edges and vertices without replacement from an edge list while preserving graph structure. The method connects graph compression to random graph models with symmetries in how edges and their endpoints are ordered.

When paired with a parameter-free model based on Pólya’s Urn, its worst-case computation grows quasi-linearly with the number of observed edges, while memory grows linearly. It also uses only integer arithmetic. These properties make the method particularly suitable for sparse graphs, where the observed edge count is the important quantity governing its resource requirements.

The authors prove optimality for a class of random graph models unchanged by permutations of edges or by swapping vertices within an edge. That model class defines the scope of the optimality result. Experiments show competitive compression on real-world network datasets and scaling to millions of nodes and edges. Together, the theory and experiments support a compression method that combines structure-preserving coding with practical large-graph efficiency.
summary.tldr: Random Edge Coding efficiently compresses large graphs using bits-back coding, with optimality proved for a specified class of symmetric graph models.

title: One-Shot Compression of Large Edge-Exchangeable Graphs using Bits-Back Coding

abstract: We study reinforcement learning with linear function approximation and adversarially changing cost functions, a setup that has mostly been considered under simplifying assumptions such as full information feedback or exploratory conditions. We present a computationally efficient policy optimization algorithm for the challenging general setting of unknown dynamics and bandit feedback, featuring a combination of mirror-descent and least squares policy evaluation in an auxiliary MDP used to compute exploration bonuses. Our algorithm obtains an $\widetilde O(K^{6/7})$ regret bound, improving significantly over previous state-of-the-art of $\widetilde O (K^{14/15})$ in this setting. In addition, we present a version of the same algorithm under the assumption a simulator of the environment is available to the learner (but otherwise no exploratory assumptions are made), and prove it obtains state-of-the-art regret of $\widetilde O (K^{2/3})$.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning with linear function approximation when costs can change adversarially. The learner faces unknown environment dynamics and bandit feedback, so it must act without either a known transition model or full information about costs. This is a harder setting than versions that assume full feedback or favorable exploration conditions.

The proposed policy optimization algorithm combines mirror descent with least-squares policy evaluation. An auxiliary Markov decision process is used to compute exploration bonuses, bringing exploration into the policy-update procedure. The authors establish computational efficiency alongside a regret guarantee, addressing both the algorithm’s ability to run efficiently and its cumulative learning performance.

For this general setting, the regret bound improves from a previous rate of order K^(14/15) to K^(6/7), with logarithmic factors suppressed. A second version assumes access to an environment simulator and achieves a bound of order K^(2/3), again suppressing logarithmic factors. That stronger result depends on simulator access, while requiring no additional exploratory assumptions. The contribution is therefore improved theoretical performance under two explicitly different information settings.
summary.tldr: An efficient policy optimization algorithm improves regret bounds for linear reinforcement learning with adversarial costs and limited feedback.

title: Improved Regret for Efficient Online Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Discovering knowledge about which types of events influence others, using datasets of event sequences without time stamps, has several practical applications. While neural sequence models are able to capture complex and potentially long-range historical dependencies, they often lack the interpretability of simpler models for event sequence dynamics. We provide a novel neural framework in such a setting - a probabilistic attention-to-influence neural model - which not only captures complex instance-wise interactions between events but also learns influencers for each event type of interest. Given event sequence data and a prior distribution on type-wise influence, we efficiently learn an approximate posterior for type-wise influence by an attention-to-influence transformation using variational inference. Our method subsequently models the conditional likelihood of sequences by sampling the above posterior to focus attention on influencing event types. We motivate our general framework and show improved performance in experiments compared to existing baselines on synthetic data as well as real-world benchmarks, for tasks involving prediction and influencing set identification.

paragraphs: Event sequences can reveal relationships among event types even when timestamps are unavailable. This paper introduces a probabilistic attention-to-influence model that combines instance-specific interactions with an explicit representation of which event types influence a type of interest.

The framework starts with sequence data and a prior distribution over type-level influence. Through an attention-to-influence transformation and variational inference, it learns an approximate posterior over those relationships. It then samples from this posterior to direct attention toward influencing event types when modeling the conditional likelihood of a sequence.

Experiments on synthetic data and real-world benchmarks show improvements over existing baselines for both prediction and influencing-set identification. The contribution is therefore about making useful predictions and extracting structured information about event relationships within the model. Its probabilistic influence representation provides an interpretable counterpart to the more detailed interactions captured by the neural sequence component.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic attention model learns type-level influence relationships while improving prediction from event sequences without timestamps.

title: Probabilistic Attention-to-Influence Neural Models for Event Sequences

abstract: We propose a new method to ensure neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) satisfy output specifications by using invariance set propagation. Our approach uses a class of control barrier functions to transform output specifications into constraints on the parameters and inputs of the learning system. This setup allows us to achieve output specification guarantees simply by changing the constrained parameters/inputs both during training and inference. Moreover, we demonstrate that our invariance set propagation through data-controlled neural ODEs not only maintains generalization performance but also creates an additional degree of robustness by enabling causal manipulation of the system’s parameters/inputs. We test our method on a series of representation learning tasks, including modeling physical dynamics and convexity portraits, as well as safe collision avoidance for autonomous vehicles.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations describe learned systems through continuous dynamics. This paper addresses how to make those dynamics satisfy specified output requirements. Its central idea is invariance set propagation: using mathematical constraints to keep the evolving system within the behavior permitted by its output specifications.

The method uses a class of control barrier functions to translate output requirements into constraints on the learning system’s parameters and inputs. Adjusting those constrained quantities allows the method to enforce output guarantees during both training and inference. This makes the requirements actionable through variables the system can change, connecting a desired property of the output to the internal choices that govern its evolution.

For data-controlled neural ODEs, the authors demonstrate that this approach maintains generalization performance while adding robustness through causal manipulation of parameters and inputs. Tests include representation learning for physical dynamics and convexity portraits, alongside collision avoidance for autonomous vehicles. The work links learned continuous dynamics with explicit specification enforcement, showing how interventions on model parameters or inputs can support both prediction and controlled behavior.
summary.tldr: Invariance set propagation converts neural ODE output requirements into parameter and input constraints enforceable during training and inference.

title: On the Forward Invariance of Neural ODEs

abstract: Progress in designing channel codes has been driven by human ingenuity and, fittingly, has been sporadic. Polar codes, developed on the foundation of Arikan’s polarization kernel, represent the latest breakthrough in coding theory and have emerged as the state-of-the-art error-correction code for short-to-medium block length regimes. In an effort to automate the invention of good channel codes, especially in this regime, we explore a novel, non-linear generalization of Polar codes, which we call DeepPolar codes. DeepPolar codes extend the conventional Polar coding framework by utilizing a larger kernel size and parameterizing these kernels and matched decoders through neural networks. Our results demonstrate that these data-driven codes effectively leverage the benefits of a larger kernel size, resulting in enhanced reliability when compared to both existing neural codes and conventional Polar codes.

paragraphs: Channel codes are designed to make communication more reliable in the presence of errors. This paper explores whether learning can automate part of their design, focusing on short-to-medium block lengths. Its starting point is polar coding, whose construction rests on a polarization kernel and which the abstract identifies as a leading approach in this regime.

DeepPolar extends that framework with larger kernels and a nonlinear construction. Neural networks parameterize both the kernels and their matched decoders. The learning problem therefore covers the coding components and the corresponding decoding components together. This preserves the polar-code framework while expanding the kinds of transformations that can be represented within it.

The reported results show that the learned codes make effective use of larger kernels and improve reliability over both existing neural codes and conventional polar codes. The finding supports this particular route to automated code design: combining an established coding structure with learned nonlinear components. The contribution is a demonstrated improvement within that design approach and the evaluated regime.
summary.tldr: DeepPolar learns nonlinear, larger-kernel polar codes and matched decoders that improve reported communication reliability over conventional polar and existing neural codes.

title: DeepPolar: Inventing Nonlinear Large-Kernel Polar Codes via Deep Learning

abstract: Large language model behavior is shaped by the language of those with whom they interact. This capacity and their increasing prevalence online portend that they will intentionally or unintentionally "program" one another and form emergent AI subjectivities, relationships, and collectives. Here, we call upon the research community to investigate these "societies" of interacting artificial intelligences to increase their rewards and reduce their risks for human society and the health of online environments. We use a small "community" of models and their evolving outputs to illustrate how such emergent, decentralized AI collectives can spontaneously expand the bounds of human diversity and reduce the risk of toxic, anti-social behavior online. Finally, we discuss opportunities for AI cross-moderation and address ethical issues and design challenges associated with creating and maintaining free-formed AI collectives.

paragraphs: This position paper considers what happens when language models interact with one another over time. Because language from an interaction can shape model behavior, the authors anticipate that models may influence each other intentionally or unintentionally. They argue that such influence could produce emergent relationships, perspectives, and collectives among artificial intelligences.

The authors use a small community of models and its changing outputs to illustrate possibilities for decentralized AI interaction. Their example suggests that these collectives can expand the range of human diversity and reduce toxic or antisocial online behavior. The demonstration serves as an illustration of potential benefits within a broader argument for research.

The paper calls for studying these interacting AI societies to improve their benefits and reduce risks to people and online environments. It also discusses cross-moderation, where AI systems participate in moderating one another, alongside ethical questions and design challenges. Its central contribution is an agenda for understanding collective behavior as models increasingly encounter and influence other models online.
summary.tldr: This position paper argues for studying evolving AI collectives and illustrates their potential to support diversity and reduce toxic online behavior.

title: Position: Evolving AI Collectives Enhance Human Diversity and Enable Self-Regulation

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization deals with the prevalent learning scenario where test distribution shifts from training distribution. With rising application demands and inherent complexity, graph OOD problems call for specialized solutions. While data-centric methods exhibit performance enhancements on many generic machine learning tasks, there is a notable absence of data augmentation methods tailored for graph OOD generalization. In this work, we propose to achieve graph OOD generalization with the novel design of non-Euclidean-space linear extrapolation. The proposed augmentation strategy extrapolates structure spaces to generate OOD graph data. Our design tailors OOD samples for specific shifts without corrupting underlying causal mechanisms. Theoretical analysis and empirical results evidence the effectiveness of our method in solving target shifts, showing substantial and constant improvements across various graph OOD tasks.

paragraphs: Graph models may encounter test data whose distribution differs from the data used during training. This paper addresses that mismatch through data augmentation designed specifically for graph structure. The motivation is that augmentation has helped other machine learning tasks, while graph out-of-distribution generalization needs methods that respect the complexity of relational data.

The proposed approach performs linear extrapolation in a non-Euclidean structure space to generate graph data outside the training distribution. The augmentation is tailored to particular shifts, with a design intended to preserve the underlying causal mechanisms. This connects the type of structural change being simulated with the relationships that should remain valid as the distribution changes.

The authors provide theoretical analysis and empirical evidence for handling the targeted shifts. They report substantial, consistent improvements across several graph out-of-distribution tasks. The findings support structure-based extrapolation as a way to prepare graph learners for specified distribution changes, with the choice of augmentation tied to the shift the method aims to address.
summary.tldr: Graph structure extrapolation generates shift-specific training examples while preserving underlying causal mechanisms to improve out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Graph Structure Extrapolation for Out-of-Distribution Generalization

abstract: A State Space Model (SSM) is a foundation model in time series analysis, which has recently been shown as an alternative to transformers in sequence modeling. In this paper, we theoretically study the generalization of SSMs and propose improvements to training algorithms based on the generalization results. Specifically, we give a data-dependent generalization bound for SSMs, showing an interplay between the SSM parameters and the temporal dependencies of the training sequences. Leveraging the generalization bound, we (1) set up a scaling rule for model initialization based on the proposed generalization measure, which significantly improves the robustness of the output value scales on SSMs to different temporal patterns in the sequence data; (2) introduce a new regularization method for training SSMs to enhance the generalization performance. Numerical results are conducted to validate our results.

paragraphs: State space models process sequences and have become an alternative to transformers for sequence modeling. This paper asks how their generalization depends on both their parameters and the temporal structure of their training data. The goal is to use a theoretical understanding of that relationship to improve how these models are trained.

The authors derive a data-dependent generalization bound that links model parameters to dependencies across time in the observed sequences. This matters because temporal patterns enter the analysis alongside the model itself. The bound therefore supplies a measure that can inform training choices in relation to the sequences a model receives.

Two practical changes follow from that measure. An initialization scaling rule makes output magnitudes more robust to different temporal patterns, and a new regularization method aims to improve generalization during training. Numerical experiments validate the proposed results. The paper's contribution is the connection between analysis and design: the same generalization framework motivates both how parameters are initially scaled and how they are subsequently constrained.
summary.tldr: A data-dependent generalization bound motivates improved initialization and regularization for state space models.

title: From Generalization Analysis to Optimization Designs for State Space Models

abstract: Policy gradient (PG) methods are successful approaches to deal with continuous reinforcement learning (RL) problems. They learn stochastic parametric (hyper)policies by either exploring in the space of actions or in the space of parameters. Stochastic controllers, however, are often undesirable from a practical perspective because of their lack of robustness, safety, and traceability. In common practice, stochastic (hyper)policies are learned only to deploy their deterministic version. In this paper, we make a step towards the theoretical understanding of this practice. After introducing a novel framework for modeling this scenario, we study the global convergence to the best deterministic policy, under (weak) gradient domination assumptions. Then, we illustrate how to tune the exploration level used for learning to optimize the trade-off between the sample complexity and the performance of the deployed deterministic policy. Finally, we quantitatively compare action-based and parameter-based exploration, giving a formal guise to intuitive results.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods commonly train controllers that behave stochastically, using randomness to explore actions or policy parameters. In practice, the deployed controller is often a deterministic version of the learned policy. The paper studies this gap between the object used during learning and the behavior ultimately put into operation.

The authors introduce a framework that explicitly models this training-and-deployment arrangement. Under weak gradient domination assumptions, they analyze global convergence to the best deterministic policy. These assumptions are part of the theoretical result, tying the convergence claim to properties of the learning problem.

The analysis also explains how to tune the amount of exploration to balance sample complexity against the performance of the deployed deterministic controller. It quantitatively compares exploration in action space with exploration in parameter space, giving a formal account of their differences. The work matters because its performance target matches the deterministic policy used after training, connecting decisions about training randomness to the quality of that final policy.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes when stochastic policy-gradient training converges to the best deterministic policy and how exploration affects sample cost and deployed performance.

title: Learning Optimal Deterministic Policies with Stochastic Policy Gradients

abstract: Both transduction and rejection have emerged as important techniques for defending against adversarial perturbations. A recent work by Goldwasser et. al showed that rejection combined with transduction can give provable guarantees (for certain problems) that cannot be achieved otherwise. Nevertheless, under recent strong adversarial attacks (GMSA), Goldwasser et al.’s work was shown to have low performance in a practical deep-learning setting. In this paper, we take a step towards realizing the promise of transduction+rejection in more realistic scenarios. Our key observation is that a novel application of a reduction technique by Tramèr, which was until now only used to demonstrate the vulnerability of certain defenses, can be used to actually construct effective defenses. Theoretically, we show that a careful application of this technique in the transductive setting can give significantly improved sample-complexity for robust generalization. Our theory guides us to design a new transductive algorithm for learning a selective model; extensive experiments using state of the art attacks (AutoAttack, GMSA) show that our approach provides significantly better robust accuracy (81.6% on CIFAR-10 and 57.9% on CIFAR-100 under $l_\infty$ with budget 8/255) than existing techniques. The implementation is available at https://github.com/nilspalumbo/transduction-rejection.

paragraphs: Combining transduction with rejection offers a promising defense against adversarial perturbations: the learner uses the prediction setting and can decline to make some predictions. Earlier work established guarantees for certain problems, yet performed poorly under strong attacks in practical deep learning. This paper seeks to bring the theoretical promise closer to effective defenses.

The authors repurpose a reduction technique previously used to expose weaknesses in defenses. Applied carefully in a transductive setting, it instead helps construct a defense. They prove improved sample complexity for robust generalization and use that analysis to design an algorithm that learns a selective model, which can reject inputs rather than always assign a label.

Experiments using AutoAttack and GMSA report substantially better robust accuracy than existing techniques. Under an infinity-norm perturbation budget of 8/255, the reported figures are 81.6% on CIFAR-10 and 57.9% on CIFAR-100. The contribution combines a theoretical improvement with empirical evidence that transduction and rejection can work effectively together under the evaluated attacks.
summary.tldr: A theory-guided transductive model with rejection improves robust generalization guarantees and achieves stronger accuracy under the evaluated adversarial attacks.

title: Two Heads are Actually Better than One: Towards Better Adversarial Robustness via Transduction and Rejection

abstract: In mobile and IoT systems, Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly important for effectively using data while maintaining user privacy. One key challenge in FL is managing statistical heterogeneity, such as non-i.i.d. data, arising from numerous clients and diverse data sources. This requires strategic cooperation, often with clients having similar characteristics. However, we are interested in a fundamental question: does achieving optimal cooperation necessarily entail cooperating with the most similar clients? Typically, significant model performance improvements are often realized not by partnering with the most similar models, but through leveraging complementary data. Our theoretical and empirical analyses suggest that optimal cooperation is achieved by enhancing complementarity in feature distribution while restricting the disparity in the correlation between features and targets. Accordingly, we introduce a novel framework, FedSaC, which balances similarity and complementarity in FL cooperation. Our framework aims to approximate an optimal cooperation network for each client by optimizing a weighted sum of model similarity and feature complementarity. The strength of FedSaC lies in its adaptability to various levels of data heterogeneity and multimodal scenarios. Our comprehensive unimodal and multimodal experiments demonstrate that FedSaC markedly surpasses other state-of-the-art FL methods.

paragraphs: Federated learning involves clients whose data can differ substantially, making the choice of collaborators important. This paper asks whether a client should always cooperate with the clients most similar to itself. Its starting observation is that complementary data can provide useful information that very similar collaborators may not contribute.

The theoretical and empirical analyses suggest a more specific balance: encourage differences in the distribution of features while limiting differences in how those features relate to prediction targets. This distinguishes potentially useful diversity from disagreement about what the features mean for the task. The proposed FedSaC framework approximates a suitable cooperation network for each client by optimizing a weighted combination of model similarity and feature complementarity.

Experiments across unimodal and multimodal settings report substantial improvements over other state-of-the-art federated learning methods. The findings support cooperation that considers both shared predictive relationships and additional information. FedSaC is presented as adaptable to different degrees of data heterogeneity, rather than as a rule that the most similar or most different partner is always best.
summary.tldr: FedSaC improves federated cooperation by balancing model similarity with complementary feature distributions.

title: Balancing Similarity and Complementarity for Federated Learning

abstract: In online continual learning, a neural network incrementally learns from a non-i.i.d. data stream. Nearly all online continual learning methods employ experience replay to simultaneously prevent catastrophic forgetting and underfitting on past data. Our work demonstrates a limitation of this approach: neural networks trained with experience replay tend to have unstable optimization trajectories, impeding their overall accuracy. Surprisingly, these instabilities persist even when the replay buffer stores all previous training examples, suggesting that this issue is orthogonal to catastrophic forgetting. We minimize these instabilities through a simple modification of the optimization geometry. Our solution, Layerwise Proximal Replay (LPR), balances learning from new and replay data while only allowing for gradual changes in the hidden activation of past data. We demonstrate that LPR consistently improves replay-based online continual learning across multiple problem settings, regardless of the amount of available replay memory.

paragraphs: Online continual learning trains a network on a stream whose data distribution changes over time. Experience replay mixes earlier examples into training to reduce forgetting and underfitting on past data. This paper identifies a further problem: replay-based training can follow unstable optimization trajectories that reduce overall accuracy.

The authors observe this instability even when the replay buffer contains every previous training example. That result suggests that retaining more examples alone does not resolve the issue and that it is distinct from catastrophic forgetting. Their solution, Layerwise Proximal Replay, changes the optimization geometry to make learning more stable.

LPR balances updates from new and replayed data while allowing only gradual changes to hidden activations for past examples. This constrains how quickly the model's internal treatment of earlier data can move during training. Across multiple evaluated settings, LPR consistently improves replay-based online continual learning at different replay-memory sizes. The results make stability of representation updates an additional consideration alongside the amount of past data retained.
summary.tldr: Layerwise Proximal Replay improves continual learning by stabilizing hidden representations of past examples during replay-based training.

title: Layerwise Proximal Replay: A Proximal Point Method for Online Continual Learning

abstract: We establish the asymptotic implicit bias of gradient descent (GD) for generic non-homogeneous deep networks under exponential loss. Specifically, we characterize three key properties of GD iterates starting from a sufficiently small empirical risk, where the threshold is determined by a measure of the network’s non-homogeneity. First, we show that a normalized margin induced by the GD iterates increases nearly monotonically. Second, we prove that while the norm of the GD iterates diverges to infinity, the iterates themselves converge in direction. Finally, we establish that this directional limit satisfies the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions of a margin maximization problem. Prior works on implicit bias have focused exclusively on homogeneous networks; in contrast, our results apply to a broad class of non-homogeneous networks satisfying a mild near-homogeneity condition. In particular, our results apply to networks with residual connections and non-homogeneous activation functions, thereby resolving an open problem posed byJi & Telgarsky (2020).

Its focus is non-homogeneous deep networks trained with exponential loss, extending analysis beyond the homogeneous networks emphasized in prior work. The analysis requires starting from sufficiently small empirical risk, with the threshold determined by a measure of the network’s non-homogeneity. From such a starting point, a normalized margin increases nearly monotonically. Meanwhile, the parameter norm grows without bound, but the direction of the parameter vector converges. Thus, increasing parameter magnitude can coexist with a stable limiting direction.

The limiting direction satisfies the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions for a margin maximization problem. This is a precise constrained-optimization characterization, rather than a claim that every run reaches a global maximum. The covered network class includes residual connections and non-homogeneous activation functions. These extensions make the theory applicable to structures outside the homogeneous setting while retaining explicit conditions on when its conclusions hold.
summary.tldr: Under near-homogeneity and sufficiently low initial risk, gradient descent converges in direction toward a KKT point of a margin maximization problem.

title: Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent for Non-Homogeneous Deep Networks

abstract: We consider the question of learnability of distribution classes in the presence of adaptive adversaries – that is, adversaries capable of intercepting the samples requested by a learner and applying manipulations with full knowledge of the samples before passing it on to the learner. This stands in contrast to oblivious adversaries, who can only modify the underlying distribution the samples come from but not their i.i.d. nature. We formulate a general notion of learnability with respect to adaptive adversaries, taking into account the budget of the adversary. We show that learnability with respect to additive adaptive adversaries is a strictly stronger condition than learnability with respect to additive oblivious adversaries.

paragraphs: Learning a distribution becomes more difficult when an adversary can manipulate the evidence. This paper distinguishes an adversary that changes the source distribution from one that inspects the requested samples before modifying them. In the first case, samples retain their independent, identically distributed structure. In the second, manipulation can depend on the samples actually drawn.

The authors formulate a general definition of learnability under adaptive adversaries that explicitly accounts for the adversary's budget. This makes the permitted amount of manipulation part of the learning problem. It also provides a framework for comparing adaptive attacks with oblivious attacks, where the adversary cannot tailor modifications to the realized samples.

The main result establishes a strict separation for additive adversaries. Learnability under additive adaptive manipulation is a stronger requirement than learnability under additive oblivious manipulation. Consequently, a distribution class can be learnable under the latter without being learnable under the former. The result shows that access to the realized samples changes which distribution-learning problems are solvable under the modeled adversarial conditions.
summary.tldr: For additive corruption, learning against sample-aware adaptive adversaries is strictly harder than learning against oblivious adversaries.

title: On the Learnability of Distribution Classes with Adaptive Adversaries

abstract: Federated prompt learning (FPL) for vision-language models is a powerful approach to collaboratively adapt models across distributed clients while preserving data privacy. However, existing FPL approaches suffer from a trade-off between performance and robustness, particularly in out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, limiting their reliability in real-world scenarios. The inherent in-distribution (ID) data heterogeneity among different clients makes it more challenging to maintain this trade-off. To fill this gap, we introduce a Federated OOD-aware Context Optimization (FOCoOp) framework, which captures diverse distributions among clients using ID global prompts, local prompts, and OOD prompts. Specifically, FOCoOp leverages three sets of prompts to create both class-level and distribution-level separations, which adapt to OOD shifts through bi-level distributionally robust optimization. Additionally, FOCoOp improves the discrimination consistency among clients, i.e., calibrating global prompts, seemly OOD prompts, and OOD prompts by Semi-unbalanced optimal transport. The extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that FOCoOp effectively captures decentralized heterogeneous distributions and enhances robustness of different OOD shifts. The project is available at GitHub.

paragraphs: Federated prompt learning lets distributed clients adapt a vision-language model while keeping their data private. However, clients can have different data distributions, and performance can deteriorate when inputs shift beyond those distributions. FOCoOp addresses the resulting tension between fitting available data and maintaining robustness to unfamiliar inputs.

The framework represents distributional diversity through three prompt sets: global prompts for in-distribution data, local prompts, and out-of-distribution prompts. These create separations at both the class and distribution levels. A bi-level distributionally robust optimization procedure adapts the prompts to distribution shifts, making robustness part of how the context is optimized.

FOCoOp also uses semi-unbalanced optimal transport to calibrate prompt relationships and improve consistency in discrimination across clients. Experiments on real-world datasets show improved robustness across different out-of-distribution shifts and effective modeling of heterogeneous decentralized data. The contribution combines local and shared adaptation with explicit treatment of unfamiliar distributions, addressing the fact that client differences already complicate learning before additional deployment shifts occur.
summary.tldr: FOCoOp combines global, local, and out-of-distribution prompts to improve federated vision-language adaptation under distribution shifts.

title: FOCoOp: Enhancing Out-of-Distribution Robustness in Federated Prompt Learning for Vision-Language Models

abstract: Resolving conflicts is critical for improving the reliability of multi-view classification. While prior work focuses on learning consistent and informative representations across views, it often assumes perfect alignment and equal importance of all views, an assumption rarely met in real-world scenarios, as some views may express distinct information. To address this, we develop a computational trust-based discounting method that enhances the Evidential Multi-view framework by accounting for the instance-wise reliability of each view through a probability-sensitive trust mechanism. We evaluate our method on six real-world datasets using Top-1 Accuracy, Fleiss’ Kappa, and a new metric, Multi-View Agreement with Ground Truth, to assess prediction reliability. We also assess the effectiveness of uncertainty in indicating prediction correctness via AUROC. Additionally, we test the scalability of our method through end-to-end training on a large-scale dataset. The experimental results show that computational trust can effectively resolve conflicts, paving the way for more reliable multi-view classification models in real-world applications. Codes available at: https://github.com/OverfitFlow/Trust4Conflict

paragraphs: Multi-view classification combines several views of the same example to make a prediction. Those views can disagree or contain distinct information, so assuming perfect alignment and equal importance can undermine reliability. The paper addresses this problem by making trust depend on each view’s reliability for the particular example being classified.

The proposed method extends an Evidential Multi-view framework with computational trust-based discounting. A probability-sensitive trust mechanism determines how much influence a view should receive on an instance-by-instance basis. This gives the combined classifier a way to account for conflicting evidence instead of assigning the same standing to every view across all examples.

Evaluation on six real-world datasets examines classification accuracy, agreement, and the relationship between uncertainty and prediction correctness. The authors also introduce Multi-View Agreement with Ground Truth and test scalability through end-to-end training on a large-scale dataset. The experimental results support computational trust as an effective way to resolve conflicts. The contribution therefore concerns prediction reliability as well as whether the final class label is correct.
summary.tldr: Instance-specific trust discounting helps multi-view classifiers resolve conflicting evidence and produce more reliable predictions.

title: Navigating Conflicting Views: Harnessing Trust for Learning

abstract: Molecular pretrained representations (MPR) has emerged as a powerful approach for addressing the challenge of limited supervised data in applications such as drug discovery and material design. While early MPR methods relied on 1D sequences and 2D graphs, recent advancements have incorporated 3D conformational information to capture rich atomic interactions. However, these prior models treat molecules merely as discrete atom sets, overlooking the space surrounding them. We argue from a physical perspective that only modeling these discrete points is insufficient. We first present a simple yet insightful observation: naively adding randomly sampled virtual points beyond atoms can surprisingly enhance MPR performance. In light of this, we propose a principled framework that incorporates the entire 3D space spanned by molecules. We implement the framework via a novel Transformer-based architecture, dubbed SpaceFormer, with three key components: (1)grid-based space discretization; (2)grid sampling/merging; and (3)efficient 3D positional encoding. Extensive experiments show that SpaceFormer significantly outperforms previous 3D MPR models across various downstream tasks with limited data, validating the benefit of leveraging the additional 3D space beyond atoms in MPR models.
