paragraphs: Molecular pretraining helps models learn useful representations before they face tasks with limited labeled data. Although newer approaches include three-dimensional conformations, they still commonly represent molecules as collections of atom positions. This paper argues that the surrounding space also matters physically and should become part of the learned representation.

The authors first report a simple observation: adding randomly sampled virtual points beyond the atoms can improve representation performance. They then develop SpaceFormer, a Transformer architecture that models the three-dimensional space spanned by a molecule more systematically. Its components discretize space into a grid, sample or merge grid elements, and encode three-dimensional positions efficiently.

Experiments show significant improvements over previous three-dimensional molecular pretraining models across downstream tasks with limited data. These findings support the value of representing spatial information beyond discrete atom locations. The connection between the initial virtual-point observation and SpaceFormer is central: an observed benefit from extra spatial samples motivates a structured architecture for incorporating that information into molecular representations.
summary.tldr: SpaceFormer improves molecular representations by explicitly modeling three-dimensional space beyond atom positions.

title: Beyond Atoms: Enhancing Molecular Pretrained Representations with 3D Space Modeling

abstract: Autoregressive attention-based time series forecasting (TSF) has drawn increasing interest, with mechanisms like linear attention often outperforming vanilla attention. However, deeper Transformer architectures frequently misalign with autoregressive objectives, obscuring the underlying VAR structure embedded within linear attention and hindering their ability to capture the data generative processes in TSF. In this work, we first show that a single linear attention layer can be interpreted as a dynamic vector autoregressive (VAR) structure. We then explain that existing multi-layer Transformers have structural mismatches with the autoregressive forecasting objective, which impair interpretability and generalization ability. To address this, we show that by rearranging the MLP, attention, and input-output flow, multi-layer linear attention can also be aligned as a VAR model. Then, we propose Structural Aligned Mixture of VAR (SAMoVAR), a linear Transformer variant that integrates interpretable dynamic VAR weights for multivariate TSF. By aligning the Transformer architecture with autoregressive objectives, SAMoVAR delivers improved performance, interpretability, and computational efficiency, comparing to SOTA TSF models.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether the structure of a forecasting Transformer matches its autoregressive task: predicting future values from earlier observations. The authors show that one linear-attention layer can be interpreted as a dynamic vector autoregressive model. That interpretation connects attention with a forecasting structure that describes relationships among multiple time series.

The difficulty arises when layers are stacked. The paper identifies structural mismatches in existing multilayer Transformers that obscure the underlying autoregressive form and impair interpretability and generalization. It shows that rearranging the multilayer perceptron, attention, and input-output flow allows multilayer linear attention to retain a vector autoregressive interpretation.

The resulting architecture, Structural Aligned Mixture of VAR, or SAMoVAR, incorporates interpretable dynamic VAR weights for multivariate forecasting. Compared with state-of-the-art forecasting models, the authors report improvements in prediction performance, interpretability, and computational efficiency. The contribution links architectural organization to the forecasting objective, showing how preserving an explicit autoregressive structure can support both understandable model behavior and stronger empirical results.
summary.tldr: SAMoVAR reorganizes linear Transformers to preserve a vector autoregressive structure, improving multivariate forecasting, interpretability, and efficiency.

title: Linear Transformers as VAR Models: Aligning Autoregressive Attention Mechanisms with Autoregressive Forecasting

abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) enhance the interpretability of neural networks by basing predictions on human-understandable concepts. However, current CBMs typically rely on concept sets extracted from large language models or extensive image corpora, limiting their effectiveness in data-sparse scenarios. We propose Data-efficient CBMs (DCBMs), which reduce the need for large sample sizes during concept generation while preserving interpretability. DCBMs define concepts as image regions detected by segmentation or detection foundation models, allowing each image to generate multiple concepts across different granularities. Exclusively containing dataset-specific concepts, DCBMs are well suited for fine-grained classification and out-of-distribution tasks. Attribution analysis using Grad-CAM demonstrates that DCBMs deliver visual concepts that can be localized in test images. By leveraging dataset-specific concepts instead of predefined or general ones, DCBMs enhance adaptability to new domains. The code is available at: https://github.com/KathPra/DCBM.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through human-understandable concepts, giving people an intermediate representation to inspect. Building those concepts often depends on language models or large image collections. This paper introduces DCBM to reduce the amount of data needed for concept generation while keeping predictions connected to interpretable visual evidence.

DCBM builds its concepts from image regions identified by segmentation or detection foundation models. A single image can supply several concepts at different levels of granularity. The concept collection therefore comes specifically from the dataset being studied, rather than from a predefined or general-purpose inventory. This approach increases the concept information available from each image.

The authors describe these dataset-specific concepts as suitable for fine-grained classification and out-of-distribution tasks, and as supporting adaptation to new domains. Their Grad-CAM attribution analysis shows that the visual concepts can be localized in test images. That result connects the intermediate concepts to observable regions, making the model’s concept-based reasoning more inspectable. The contribution centers on efficient concept construction together with this spatial connection to visual evidence.
summary.tldr: DCBM creates dataset-specific concepts from multiple regions per image, reducing concept-generation data needs while preserving visual interpretability.

title: DCBM: Data-Efficient Visual Concept Bottleneck Models

abstract: Reward-guided text generation (RGTG) has emerged as a viable alternative to offline reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). RGTG methods can align baseline language models to human preferences without further training as in standard RLHF methods. However, they rely on a reward model to score each candidate token generated by the language model at inference, incurring significant test-time overhead. Additionally, the reward model is usually only trained to score full sequences, which can lead to sub-optimal choices for partial sequences. In this work, we present a novel reward model architecture that is trained, using a Bradley-Terry loss, to prefer the optimal expansion of a sequence with just a single call to the reward model at each step of the generation process. That is, a score for all possible candidate tokens is generated simultaneously, leading to efficient inference. We theoretically analyze various RGTG reward models and demonstrate that prior techniques prefer sub-optimal sequences compared to our method during inference. Empirically, our reward model leads to significantly faster inference than other RGTG methods. It requires fewer calls to the reward model and performs competitively compared to previous RGTG and offline RLHF methods.

paragraphs: Reward-guided generation steers a language model toward preferred responses during inference without further training the base model. Existing methods can be expensive because they score candidate next tokens separately. They also commonly use reward models trained on complete responses, even though generation requires choosing how to extend an unfinished sequence.

The paper introduces a reward-model architecture trained with a Bradley–Terry loss to prefer the optimal sequence expansion. A single call produces scores for every candidate token at a generation step. This addresses both the cost of repeated scoring and the mismatch between evaluating completed text and selecting the next continuation.

The authors theoretically analyze reward-guided methods and show that earlier techniques prefer suboptimal sequences compared with their method during inference. Experiments report substantially faster inference through fewer reward-model calls, with performance competitive with previous reward-guided methods and offline reinforcement learning from human feedback. The result supports improving preference-guided decoding by redesigning what the reward model predicts at each step.
summary.tldr: A reward model scores all next-token candidates in one call, making preference-guided generation faster while retaining competitive performance.

title: Towards Cost-Effective Reward Guided Text Generation

abstract: Imbalanced learning occurs in classification settings where the distribution of class-labels is highly skewed in the training data, such as when predicting rare diseases or in fraud detection. This class imbalance presents a significant algorithmic challenge, which can be further exacerbated when privacy-preserving techniques such as differential privacy are applied to protect sensitive training data. Our work formalizes these challenges and provides a number of algorithmic solutions. We consider DP variants of pre-processing methods that privately augment the original dataset to reduce the class imbalance, alongside DP variants of in-processing techniques, which adjust the learning algorithm to account for the imbalance. For each method, we either adapt an existing imbalanced learning technique to the private setting or demonstrate its incompatibility with differential privacy. Finally, we empirically evaluate these privacy-preserving imbalanced learning methods under various data and distributional settings. We find that private synthetic data methods perform well as a data pre-processing step, while class-weighted ERMs are an alternative in higher-dimensional settings where private synthetic data suffers from the curse of dimensionality.

paragraphs: Classification becomes difficult when some labels are much rarer than others, as in rare-disease prediction or fraud detection. Differential privacy can intensify this challenge while protecting sensitive training data. This paper formalizes the interaction between privacy and class imbalance, then investigates how established approaches to imbalance can be made compatible with privacy requirements.

The authors examine two families of solutions. Pre-processing methods privately augment the dataset to reduce imbalance before learning begins. In-processing methods change the learning algorithm so that it accounts for the uneven class distribution. For the techniques considered, the paper either develops a private adaptation or demonstrates incompatibility with differential privacy.

Empirical evaluations across different data and distributional settings find that private synthetic data works well as a pre-processing approach. In higher dimensions, however, synthetic-data methods suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Class-weighted empirical risk minimization offers an alternative in those settings. The findings therefore support choosing the imbalance treatment with the data’s dimensionality in mind, rather than expecting one method to dominate throughout.
summary.tldr: The paper develops private methods for imbalanced classification and finds different strengths for synthetic-data augmentation and class-weighted learning.

title: Differential Privacy Under Class Imbalance: Methods and Empirical Insights

abstract: The progress in materials science and drug discovery is impeded by the availability of labeled data and the high costs of manual annotation, driving the need for efficient strategies to capture molecular representations and enable accurate predictions. Pretrained Graph Neural Networks have shown promise in capturing universal molecular representations, but adapting them to task-specific applications remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Multilevel Informed Prompt-Tuning (MIPT), a novel framework for effectively tailoring pretrained models to molecule-related tasks. MIPT utilizes a lightweight, multi-level prompt learning module to capture node-level and graph-level task-specific knowledge, ensuring adaptable and efficient tuning. Additionally, a noise penalty mechanism is introduced to address mismatches between pretrained representations and downstream tasks, reducing irrelevant or noisy information. Experimental results show that MIPT surpasses all baselines, aligning graph space and task space while achieving significant improvements in molecule-related tasks, demonstrating its scalability and versatility for molecular tasks.

paragraphs: Molecular prediction tasks often have limited labeled data because annotation is costly. Pretrained graph neural networks offer reusable molecular representations, but those representations still need to be adapted to a particular prediction task. The paper addresses this adaptation step with Multilevel Informed Prompt-Tuning, or MIPT.

MIPT introduces a lightweight prompt-learning module that captures task-specific information at both node and whole-graph levels. This lets adaptation account for local molecular information and the representation of the molecule as a whole. A separate noise penalty targets mismatches between pretrained representations and downstream requirements, reducing information that is irrelevant or noisy for the task.

The experiments report improvements over all evaluated baselines on molecule-related tasks. The authors interpret the results as evidence that MIPT better aligns graph representations with task requirements, while supporting scalable and versatile adaptation. Its central contribution is to combine multilevel task conditioning with explicit suppression of distracting representation content, addressing both what the pretrained model should emphasize and what it should discount.
summary.tldr: MIPT adapts pretrained molecular graph models using multilevel prompts and a penalty for task-irrelevant information.

title: MIPT: Multilevel Informed Prompt Tuning for Robust Molecular Property Prediction

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized various natural language processing tasks with their remarkable capabilities. However, challenges persist in effectively integrating new knowledge into LLMs without compromising their performance, particularly in the Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized various natural language processing tasks with their remarkable capabilities. However, a challenge persists in effectively processing new information, particularly in the area of long-term knowledge updates without compromising model performance. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel memory augmentation framework that conceptualizes memory as a peripheral component (akin to physical RAM), with the LLM serving as the information processor (analogous to a CPU). Drawing inspiration from RAM architecture, we design memory as a sequence of memory banks, each modeled using Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) to ensure smooth state transitions. Memory read and write operations are dynamically controlled by query signals derived from the LLMs’ internal states, closely mimicking the interaction between a CPU and RAM. Furthermore, a dedicated memory bank is used to generate a mask value that indicates the relevance of the retrieved data, inspired by the sign bit in binary coding schemes. The retrieved memory feature is then integrated as a prefix to enhance the model prediction. Extensive experiments on knowledge-based model editing validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our peripheral memory.

paragraphs: Updating a language model with new information while preserving its performance is a difficult knowledge-management problem. This paper proposes an attached memory system, using a CPU-and-RAM analogy: the language model processes information, while a peripheral component stores and supplies knowledge. The framework focuses on supporting longer-term knowledge updates.

Memory is organized as a sequence of banks, each modeled with a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network to support smooth state transitions. A dedicated bank produces a mask indicating the relevance of retrieved information, and the retrieved memory feature is integrated as a prefix to aid prediction. Experiments on knowledge-based model editing report that this design is effective and efficient. The contribution brings storage, adaptive access, and relevance assessment into one memory augmentation mechanism, with the reported evidence showing its utility for editing the knowledge available to a language model.
summary.tldr: Sequential memory banks let a language model dynamically read, write, and assess retrieved knowledge for effective model editing.

title: Peripheral Memory for LLMs: Integration of Sequential Memory Banks with Adaptive Querying

abstract: Machine unlearning seeks to remove the influence of specific training data from a model, a need driven by privacy regulations and robustness concerns. Existing approaches typically modify model parameters, but such updates can be unstable, computationally costly, and limited by local approximations. We introduce Representation Unlearning, a framework that performs unlearning directly in the model’s representation space. Instead of modifying model parameters, we learn a transformation over representations that imposes an information bottleneck: maximizing mutual information with retained data while suppressing information about data to be forgotten. We derive variational surrogates that make this objective tractable and show how they can be instantiated in two practical regimes: when both retain and forget data are available, and in a zero-shot setting where only forget data can be accessed. Experiments across several benchmarks demonstrate that Representation Unlearning achieves more reliable forgetting, better utility retention, and greater computational efficiency than parameter-centric baselines.

We derive variational surrogates that make this objective tractable and show how they can be instantiated in two practical regimes: when both retain and forget data are available, and in a zero-shot setting where only forget data can be accessed. paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training data while preserving useful behavior. This paper moves the intervention into the model's representation space. It learns a transformation of representations, addressing instability, computational expense, and local-approximation constraints associated with approaches that update the underlying model's parameters.

The transformation implements an information bottleneck: its objective encourages information about retained data while suppressing information about the data designated for forgetting. Because that information-based objective is difficult to optimize directly, the authors derive tractable variational surrogates. These provide practical ways to train the transformation while preserving the intended balance between retention and forgetting.

The framework covers two data-access regimes: one with both retain and forget data, and a zero-shot regime with access only to forget data. Across several benchmarks, the authors report more reliable forgetting, better preservation of utility, and greater computational efficiency than parameter-centric baselines. The findings support representation transformation as an alternative place to carry out selective forgetting while maintaining useful model behavior.
summary.tldr: Representation Unlearning learns an information-compressing transformation that suppresses forget-data information while preserving useful retained information.

title: Representation Unlearning: Forgetting through Information Compression

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong capabilities by scaling model capacity and training data, yet many real-world deployments rely on smaller models trained or adapted from low-resource data. This gap motivates the need for mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large, high-resource models to smaller, low-resource targets. While model merging provides an effective transfer mechanism, most existing approaches assume architecture-compatible models and therefore cannot directly transfer knowledge from large high-resource LLMs to heterogeneous low-resource targets. In this work, we propose a cross-architecture merging framework based on optimal transport (OT) that aligns activations to infer cross-neuron correspondences between heterogeneous models. The resulting transport plans are then used to guide direct weight-space fusion, enabling effective high-resource to low-resource transfer using only a small set of inputs. Extensive experiments across low-resource languages and specialized domains demonstrate consistent improvements over target models.

This paper uses optimal transport to infer correspondences between neurons from their activations. Rather than assuming that units already line up across models, it estimates how their responses relate. The resulting transport plans then guide direct fusion in weight space. Experiments across low-resource languages and specialized domains show consistent improvements over the target models. The findings support activation alignment as a practical bridge between heterogeneous architectures, enabling the source model’s information to influence the target’s weights. The contribution extends the applicability of merging to a setting where architectural differences otherwise prevent direct transfer through conventional compatibility-dependent methods.
summary.tldr: Optimal-transport alignment enables direct weight merging between differently structured language models to improve low-resource targets.

title: Transport and Merge: Cross-Architecture Merging for Large Language Models

abstract: We revisit the problem of sequentially testing the mean of bounded distributions in a level-$\alpha$ power-one framework. We study a $\mathrm{KL_{inf}}$-based sequential test that is known to attain the information-theoretic lower bound on the expected stopping time with exact constants as $\alpha \to 0$. Going beyond first-order asymptotics, we establish a central limit theorem (CLT) for the stopping time of this test. Our analysis proceeds in two steps. First, we prove a novel CLT for the $\mathrm{KL_{inf}}$ statistic itself, characterizing its fluctuations around its deterministic limit. We then leverage this result to show that the stopping time, centered appropriately and scaled by $\sqrt{\log(1/\alpha)}$, converges in distribution to a Gaussian limit with an explicit variance. This yields a second-order characterization of an asymptotically optimal sequential test for bounded distributions. Finally, we present numerical experiments that corroborate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: A sequential mean test examines incoming observations and decides when enough evidence has accumulated to stop. This paper asks a more detailed question about that stopping time: how does it fluctuate around its leading behavior? The authors first establish a central limit theorem for the KL-inf statistic underlying the test. This describes the statistic’s random deviations around its deterministic limit and supplies the foundation for analyzing the test’s timing.

They then prove that an appropriately centered stopping time, divided by the square root of log(1/alpha), converges in distribution to a Gaussian with an explicit variance. This second-order result describes variability that the leading expected-time guarantee leaves unresolved. Numerical experiments support the theory. The analysis remains within the stated setting of bounded distributions and a level-alpha, power-one sequential test.
summary.tldr: A central limit theorem describes stopping-time fluctuations beyond the leading efficiency guarantee for a sequential mean test on bounded distributions.

title: Beyond First-order Asymptotics in Sequential Mean Testing

abstract: Deep neural networks learn representations where individual features often lack interpretable meaning; a single neuron may activate for scattered, unrelated inputs. We introduce coherence, a geometric property inspired by neural coding in the brain, where neurons like grid cells and head direction cells respond to contiguous regions of state space. A non-negative matrix is coherent if each row (sample) attends to geometrically clustered columns (features) and vice versa, and in addition every sample is well described by some feature and every feature is needed by some sample. We prove that coherent matrices induce a bounded interleaving between the Vietoris-Rips filtrations of samples and features, guaranteeing that both spaces share compatible topological structure. This geometric constraint facilitates interpretability. For example, if data lies on a circle, coherent features must tile that circle into contiguous arcs. We introduce Coh, a differentiable objective function based on Fréchet variance that enforces coherence during training. Unlike sparsity, which bounds how many samples a feature activates on, coherence bounds which samples, requiring geometric connectivity rather than only rarity. This yields not just interpretable features but an interpretable feature space. We validate Coh in an auto-encoder using synthetic and rotated MNIST datasets and in a token embedding of BERT using language data.

paragraphs: A learned feature can activate for scattered, unrelated inputs, making its meaning difficult to interpret. This paper proposes coherence as a geometric requirement for representations. Samples should attend to clustered features, and features should respond to clustered samples, with every sample represented and every feature serving some sample.

The authors prove that coherent non-negative matrices connect the topological structure of sample space and feature space through a bounded interleaving of their Vietoris–Rips filtrations. In more intuitive terms, the two spaces have compatible shape across scales. For data arranged on a circle, coherent features must cover contiguous arcs instead of unrelated scattered points.

To encourage this structure during training, the paper introduces Coh, a differentiable objective based on Fréchet variance. Sparsity restricts how many samples activate a feature; coherence also constrains which samples belong together geometrically. Evaluations use autoencoders on synthetic and rotated MNIST data and a BERT token embedding on language data. The aim is interpretability of both individual features and their collective organization.
summary.tldr: A coherence objective encourages features to represent connected regions of data and gives sample and feature spaces compatible topological structure.

title: Learning Coherent Representations: A Topological Approach to Interpretability

abstract: Representing the past in a compressed, efficient, and informative manner is a central problem for systems trained on sequential data. The HiPPO framework, originally proposed by Gu & Dao et al., provides a principled approach to sequential compression by projecting signals onto orthogonal polynomial (OP) bases via structured linear ordinary differential equations. Subsequent works have embedded these dynamics in state space models (SSMs), where HiPPO structure serves as an initialization. Nonlinear successors of these SSM methods such as Mamba are state-of-the-art for many tasks with long-range dependencies, but the mechanisms by which they represent and prioritize history remain largely implicit. In this work, we revisit the HiPPO framework with the goal of making these mechanisms explicit. We show how polynomial representations of history can be extended to support capabilities of modern SSMs such as adaptive memory allocation and associative memory, while retaining direct interpretability in the OP basis. We introduce a unified framework comprising five such extensions, which we collectively refer to as a “HiPPO zoo.” Each extension exposes a specific modeling capability through an explicit, interpretable modification of the HiPPO framework. The resulting models adapt their memory online and train in streaming settings with efficient updates. We illustrate the behaviors and modeling advantages of these extensions through a range of synthetic sequence modeling tasks, demonstrating that capabilities typically associated with modern SSMs can be realized through explicit, interpretable polynomial memory structures.

title: HiPPO Zoo: Explicit Memory Mechanisms for Interpretable State Space Models

abstract: Safety alignment of large language models is fragile: even small fine-tuning perturbations elastically revert behaviors toward those of the pre-training, with degradation inversely proportional to the size of the alignment set. We ask how to achieve safety alignment with minimal augmentation. To this end, we model augmentation as a set of group actions on sequences and formalize robustness gains as a normalized, monotone submodular function over transformations. We then leverage submodular optimization to select minimal augmentations that provably improve robustness. Experiments confirm that our approach efficiently restores safety alignment while minimizing the overhead of augmentation.

paragraphs: Safety alignment can deteriorate after small fine-tuning changes, with behavior moving back toward what the model learned during pretraining. The paper describes this degradation as inversely related to alignment-set size. It asks how to strengthen alignment while adding as little augmentation as possible.

The authors represent augmentations as group actions on sequences and model their robustness benefit with a normalized, monotone submodular function. Monotonicity expresses that adding transformations does not reduce the modeled benefit. Submodularity captures diminishing returns: a transformation can contribute less when many useful transformations have already been selected. This structure makes economical selection a mathematical optimization problem.

Using submodular optimization, the method selects minimal augmentations with provable robustness improvements within the formalization. Experiments show that the approach efficiently restores safety alignment while limiting augmentation overhead. The contribution links the practical goal of using fewer augmented examples or transformations to an explicit model of their combined benefit. Its guarantees arise from that model, while the experiments support the usefulness of the resulting selection strategy.
summary.tldr: The paper models augmentation benefits as submodular and selects minimal transformations that provably improve robustness within that framework.

title: Submodular Optimization for Minimal Augmentation in Robust Language Model Alignment

abstract: To handle ambiguous and open-ended requests, Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly trained to interact with users to surface intents they have not yet expressed (e.g., ask clarification questions). However, users are often ambiguous because they have not yet formed their intents: they must observe and explore outcomes to discover what they want. Simply asking "what kind of tone do you want?" fails when users themselves do not know. We introduce DiscoverLLM, a novel and generalizable framework that trains LLMs to help users form and discover their intents. Central to our approach is a novel user simulator that models cognitive state with a hierarchy of intents that progressively concretize as the model surfaces relevant options—where the degree of concretization serves as a reward signal that models can be trained to optimize. Resulting models learn to collaborate with users by adaptively diverging (i.e., explore options) when intents are unclear, and converging (i.e., refine and implement) when intents concretize. Across proposed interactive benchmarks in creative writing, technical writing, and SVG drawing, DiscoverLLM achieves over 10% higher task performance while reducing conversation length by up to 40%. In a user study with 75 human participants, DiscoverLLM improved conversation satisfaction and efficiency compared to baselines.

paragraphs: An ambiguous request does not always hide a preference that the user can explain if asked. Sometimes people need to see possible outcomes before deciding what they want. DiscoverLLM trains language models to support that process, treating the formation of user intent as part of the task rather than assuming intent already exists.

The framework uses a simulated user whose cognitive state contains a hierarchy of intentions. Those intentions become more concrete as the assistant presents relevant options, and the degree of concretization supplies a training reward. This encourages the assistant to explore alternatives when preferences remain unclear, then shift toward refinement and execution as the user develops a clearer direction.

The findings suggest that productive interaction can involve helping users discover preferences through exploration, with clarification and implementation adapting to how formed those preferences are.
summary.tldr: DiscoverLLM trains assistants to help users form preferences by exploring options before refining and implementing a chosen direction.

title: DiscoverLLM: From Executing Intents to Discovering Them

abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) has shifted their role from passive information providers to active agents capable of executing complex workflows. However, the realization of a true "AI worker" is currently hindered by benchmarks that fail to capture the intricacy of professional environments, which demand long-horizon planning, complex tool usage, and adherence to strict access protocols. To bridge this gap, we introduce EnterpriseOps-Gym, a benchmark environment designed to evaluate agentic planning in realistic enterprise settings. EnterpriseOps-Gym provides: (i) 1,150 expert-curated tasks across eight interconnected domains (including HR, IT, Customer Service and productivity tools) that require managing persistent state and adhering to strict outcome-based verification logic; and (ii) a high-fidelity, containerized sandbox environment hosting 164 database tables and 512 functional tools. Our evaluation reveals critical limitations in state-of-the-art models: even the top-performing Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieves only 34.1% success, struggling significantly with planning consistency, error recovery, and policy constraints. Furthermore, we observe that agents frequently fail to refuse infeasible tasks, leading to unintended and potentially harmful side effects on the system. These findings indicate that current agents are not yet ready for enterprise deployment. By releasing EnterpriseOps-Gym, we provide a concrete testbed to advance the reliability of autonomous agents in professional workflows.

paragraphs: Professional workflows require an agent to coordinate many actions while respecting permissions and tracking changes that persist. It targets the gap between answering questions or completing isolated tool calls and reliably carrying out a longer workplace process.

title: EnterpriseOps-Gym: Environments and Evaluations for Stateful Agentic Planning and Tool Use in Enterprise Settings

abstract: Accurate and efficient Video Quality Assessment (VQA) has long been a key research challenge. Current mainstream VQA methods typically improve performance by pretraining on large-scale classification datasets, followed by fine-tuning on VQA datasets. However, this strategy presents two significant challenges: (1) merely transferring semantic knowledge learned from pretraining is insufficient for VQA, as video quality depends on multiple factors (e.g., semantics, distortion, motion); (2) pretraining on large-scale datasets demands enormous computational resources, often dozens to hundreds of times more than training on VQA datasets. Recently, Contrastive Vision-Language Models (CVLMs) have shown strong generalization across visual tasks and promising potential for quality assessment. In this work, we propose Q-CLIP, the first fully CVLMs-based framework for VQA. Q-CLIP enhances both visual and textual representations through a Shared Cross-Modal Adapter (SCMA), which contains only a minimal number of trainable parameters and is the only component that requires training. This design significantly reduces computational cost. In addition, we introduce a set of five learnable quality-level prompts to guide the CVLMs in perceiving subtle quality variations. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of different frame sampling strategies on VQA performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Q-CLIP exhibits excellent performance on several VQA datasets. Code: https://github.com/xiao-mi-d/Q-CLIP

The paper argues that transferring semantic knowledge from large classification datasets is insufficient, while the pretraining itself can be expensive. Q-CLIP builds video quality assessment around pretrained contrastive vision-language models and a small adaptation mechanism.

It contains few trainable parameters and is described as the only component requiring training, substantially reducing computational cost. The framework also introduces five learnable quality-level prompts to help distinguish subtle differences in quality. The authors additionally investigate how choosing different video frames affects assessment.

Experiments report strong performance on several video-quality datasets. The approach matters because it connects efficient adaptation with the need to represent quality through both visual and textual information. Its stated results support using a compact shared adapter to draw more useful quality judgments from existing vision-language representations, while the frame-sampling investigation addresses another consequential part of the assessment pipeline.
summary.tldr: Q-CLIP uses a small shared visual-textual adapter and quality-level prompts for efficient video quality assessment.

title: Q-CLIP: Unleashing the Power of Vision-Language Models for Video Quality Assessment through Unified Cross-Modal Adaptation

abstract: We study the problem of fairly allocating indivisible goods to agents in an online setting, where goods arrive sequentially and must be allocated irrevocably. Focusing on the popular fairness notions of envy-freeness, proportionality, and maximin share fairness (and their approximate variants), we investigate how access to future information changes what guarantees are achievable. Without any information, we prove strong impossibility results even for approximate fairness. With normalization information (agents’ total values), we provide an algorithm that achieves stronger fairness guarantees than previously known results, and show matching impossibilities for stronger notions. With frequency predictions (value multisets without order), we design a meta-algorithm that lifts a broad class of offline “share-based” guarantees to the online setting, matching the best-known offline bounds. Finally, we provide learning-augmented variants of both models: under noisy totals or noisy frequency predictions, our guarantees are robust and degrade gracefully with the error parameters.

paragraphs: Online fair division assigns indivisible goods as they arrive, with each allocation becoming permanent. This makes fairness difficult because a decision must be made before later goods are known. The paper studies how different kinds of future information change achievable guarantees for envy-freeness, proportionality, maximin share fairness, and approximate versions of these goals.

Without future information, the authors prove strong impossibility results even for approximate fairness. Knowing each agent's total value for the goods enables an algorithm with stronger guarantees than previously known, alongside matching impossibility results for stronger notions. A second information model supplies value multisets without their arrival order, giving frequency information while preserving uncertainty about the sequence.

For frequency predictions, a meta-algorithm transfers a broad class of offline share-based fairness guarantees to the online setting, matching the best-known offline bounds. Learning-augmented versions also accommodate errors in totals or frequency predictions, with guarantees that degrade gracefully as prediction errors grow. The results distinguish which information helps irreversible allocation and how imperfect predictions affect that benefit.
summary.tldr: Future value information enables stronger online fair-division guarantees, with prediction-aware variants that degrade gracefully under errors.

title: Online Fair Division with Additional Information

abstract: Cosine similarity estimation is a core primitive in coarse-to-fine retrieval pipelines, where early-stage candidate selection relies on approximate similarity estimates whose errors are amplified downstream. Widely used sign-based sketches arising from extreme quantization of random projections exhibit a structural variance peak near $\theta$ $\approx$ 90$^\circ$, the near-background region where candidate selection is most difficult. We propose QA-Cos, a query-aware decoder-side estimator that departs from the Hamming-agreement paradigm, treating sign bits as probabilistic observations rather than deterministic votes. Across simulations and BEIR benchmarks, QA-Cos reduces estimation error by up to $\sim$15–20% in the near-orthogonal region and translates these gains into improved candidate selection in two-stage ANN pipelines, improving Hit@K by up to $\sim$30 percentage points at fixed budgets and reducing candidates by up to $\sim$45–50% at fixed recall. In a native hnswlib scorer-replacement experiment, the same decoder improves the quality of the final HNSW frontier, and in a focused storage-aware setting a practical gated variant reduces end-to-end wall-clock latency at matched recall.

paragraphs: Retrieval systems often use cheap similarity estimates to select candidates before applying more expensive processing. Errors at this early stage affect which candidates remain available later. This paper studies binary cosine sketches, which compress random projections into sign bits. Their usual estimator has especially high variance when vectors are nearly perpendicular, a difficult region for separating candidates from background.

QA-Cos changes the decoder used to interpret those bits. Instead of treating matching signs as deterministic votes through Hamming agreement, it treats the bits as probabilistic observations and uses information from the query. The approach targets the estimation step that drives early candidate selection.

In simulations and BEIR evaluations, QA-Cos reduces estimation error by up to roughly 15–20% near perpendicularity. Reported retrieval gains reach about 30 percentage points in Hit@K at fixed budgets, or roughly 45–50% fewer candidates at fixed recall. A scorer replacement also improves the final HNSW frontier, while a gated variant reduces total latency in a focused storage-aware setting.
summary.tldr: A query-aware probabilistic decoder improves binary cosine estimates and translates those gains into more efficient candidate retrieval.

title: Beyond Hamming: Query-Aware Decoding of Binary Cosine Sketches

abstract: Verbal logic and visual mental simulation are two essential components of human intelligence. Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong verbal reasoning capabilities through textual Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. In contrast, current Video Generation Models (VGMs) struggle with visual reasoning tasks such as spatial planning. We attribute this limitation to two fundamental gaps: (i) VGMs are predominantly trained on general-purpose video corpora emphasizing perceptual fidelity over visual reasoning, leaving reasoning abilities underdeveloped; (ii) most VGMs generate videos in a single pass without mechanisms to explore alternative reasoning trajectories and to revise intermediate errors. Motivated by these limitations, we introduce ReaForest, a framework that fosters the reasoning capacity of VGMs in spatial planning through both training-time activation and inference-time scaling. ReaForest comprises three key components: (1) ReaGen-27k, a dataset covering diverse spatial planning tasks that require multi-step reasoning, which activates basic reasoning capabilities of VGMs for spatial planning; (2) Reflective Entropy-Aware Test-Time Scaling (ReaTTS), an inference framework that evolves multiple reasoning branches while enabling failure recovery; (3) Hierarchical constraint verification, which provides actionable feedback for ReaTTS based on decomposed constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReaForest substantially surpasses advanced textual reasoning models (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Pro) and video generation models (e.g., Sora-2). ReaForest exhibits emergent properties including self-correction, parallel thinking, and scalable reasoning, advancing VGMs toward human-like visual mental simulation.

paragraphs: Producing realistic video does not by itself establish an ability to solve spatial planning problems. This paper attributes video models' difficulty to training data that prioritize appearance and to generation procedures that provide little opportunity to explore alternatives or repair mistakes. ReaForest addresses both the training and inference sides of that problem.

The framework introduces ReaGen-27k, a dataset of spatial planning tasks requiring multiple reasoning steps. At inference time, Reflective Entropy-Aware Test-Time Scaling develops several reasoning branches and supports recovery from failures. A hierarchical verifier decomposes constraints and supplies actionable feedback, giving the branching process information about what needs correction.

The authors also observe self-correction, parallel thinking, and reasoning that benefits from increased inference effort. Together, these findings support treating video generation as an iterative planning process whose intermediate results can be checked and revised. The claimed progress concerns visual spatial reasoning, with human-like mental simulation presented as the direction of advancement.
summary.tldr: ReaForest improves video-based spatial planning through reasoning-focused training, branching inference, and constraint feedback that enables correction.

title: ReaForest: Fostering Generative Video Reasoning for Spatial Planning

abstract: We introduce Robust Filter Attention (RFA), a formulation of self-attention as a robust state estimator. Each token is treated as a noisy observation of a latent trajectory governed by a linear stochastic differential equation (SDE), and attention weights are determined by consistency under this model rather than static feature similarity. Under isotropic noise and decay assumptions, RFA matches the computational complexity of standard attention. On language modeling benchmarks, RFA achieves lower perplexity than RoPE within the training window while remaining stable under zero-shot extrapolation to longer contexts. The framework also provides a dynamical interpretation of standard positional mechanisms, connecting rotational embeddings and recency biases to transport and uncertainty propagation induced by stochastic dynamics.

paragraphs: Robust Filter Attention treats tokens as noisy observations of an underlying trajectory. That trajectory follows a linear stochastic differential equation, giving the model an explicit account of how hidden state evolves. Attention weights reflect whether observations are consistent with this dynamical account, making state estimation the organizing principle for combining token information.

This formulation also connects attention to uncertainty. Under isotropic noise and decay assumptions, its computational complexity matches standard attention. Those assumptions are part of the stated efficiency result. The framework further interprets familiar positional mechanisms dynamically, linking rotational embeddings and preferences for recent tokens to transport and the propagation of uncertainty.

On language-modeling benchmarks, RFA achieves lower perplexity than RoPE within the training window and remains stable when applied to longer contexts without additional training. These findings combine an empirical modeling result with a conceptual contribution: positional behavior and attention weighting can be understood through a shared model of evolving state and noisy observations.
summary.tldr: Robust Filter Attention uses dynamical consistency to weight tokens, improving reported language-model perplexity and remaining stable on longer contexts.

title: Robust Filter Attention: Self-Attention as Precision-Weighted State Estimation

abstract: Diffusion policies have achieved remarkable success in robotic manipulation, yet they often fail to satisfy strict physical constraints required for safe deployment. Existing approaches impose safety either prematurely during training or reactively via external guardrails at test time, limiting policy expressivity and overall scalability. We propose Physical safety Alignment for Constrained Trajectories (PACT), a self-evolving post-training framework that projects pretrained diffusion policies onto constraint-feasible regions without accessing demonstration data or task rewards. PACT distills constraint gradients into the diffusion model through a reverse-KL objective with dense supervision across timesteps. It incorporates a curriculum that progressively tightens constraints while maintaining theoretically bounded policy shift and monotone improvement, mitigating the safety-performance trade-off from catastrophic forgetting. On simulated and real-world embodied manipulation benchmarks, PACT significantly reduces safety violations by 31.0% on average while improving task success by 30.7%.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies can generate effective robot actions while still violating physical constraints. PACT addresses safety after a policy has been pretrained. It adapts the policy toward feasible trajectories without accessing demonstration data or task rewards, making physical constraints the basis for this additional training stage.

The framework distills constraint gradients into the diffusion model using a reverse-KL objective, with supervision distributed across diffusion timesteps. A curriculum gradually tightens constraints rather than imposing their full strength immediately. The authors connect this progression to theoretical bounds on policy change and monotone improvement. Controlling how far the policy shifts is intended to reduce catastrophic forgetting and the resulting tension between safety and task performance.

On simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks, PACT reduces safety violations by 31.0% on average while improving task success by 30.7%. These reported results show that the evaluated safety alignment also benefits task completion. The contribution is a post-training mechanism that incorporates constraint information into the policy itself while managing disruption to its existing behavior.
summary.tldr: PACT post-trains diffusion robot policies using physical constraints, reducing violations while improving task success in the reported evaluations.

title: PACT: Self-Evolving Physical Safety Alignment for Diffusion Policies in Embodied Manipulation

abstract: Despite recent progress in calibration-free monocular SLAM via 3D vision foundation models, scale drift remains severe on long sequences. Motion-agnostic partitioning breaks contextual coherence and causes zero-motion drift, while conventional geometric alignment is computationally expensive. To address these issues, we propose VGGT-Motion, a calibration-free SLAM system for efficient and robust global consistency over kilometer-scale trajectories. Specifically, we first propose a motion-aware submap construction mechanism that uses optical flow to guide adaptive partitioning, prune static redundancy, and encapsulate turns for stable local geometry. We then design an anchor-driven direct Sim(3) registration strategy. By exploiting context-balanced anchors, it achieves search-free, pixel-wise dense alignment and efficient loop closure without costly feature matching. Finally, a lightweight submap-level pose graph optimization enforces global consistency with linear complexity, enabling scalable long-range operation. Experiments show that VGGT-Motion markedly improves trajectory accuracy and efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot, long-range calibration-free monocular SLAM.

paragraphs: Calibration-free monocular SLAM estimates motion and maps scenes from a single camera without prior calibration, but long sequences can accumulate severe scale drift. VGGT-Motion addresses this by making local map construction sensitive to motion and by simplifying the alignment of those maps over kilometer-scale trajectories.

Optical flow guides adaptive partitioning into submaps, removes redundant static observations, and keeps turns together to stabilize local geometry. Context-balanced anchors then support direct Sim(3) registration, aligning submaps in rotation, translation, and scale. This provides dense pixel-wise alignment and efficient loop closure without a feature-matching search.

A lightweight pose-graph optimization operates at the submap level to enforce global consistency with linear complexity. The design connects motion-sensitive local organization to efficient long-range correction, addressing both geometric drift and computation. Experiments report marked improvements in trajectory accuracy and efficiency, reaching state-of-the-art performance in the evaluated zero-shot, long-range calibration-free monocular SLAM setting.
summary.tldr: VGGT-Motion reduces long-range monocular SLAM drift through motion-aware submaps, direct anchor alignment, and lightweight global optimization.

title: VGGT-Motion: Motion-Aware Calibration-Free Monocular SLAM for Long-Range Consistency

abstract: Tool calling extends large language models (LLMs) by enabling grounded interaction with external executable interfaces, thereby supporting environment-coupled problem solving. However, mainstream in-context learning (ICL) approaches typically incorporate detailed tool documentation and usage examples directly into the context. This results in substantial inference overhead and heightened risks of hallucination as the context length grows. Conversely, while tuning-based methods improve general tool-calling capabilities, they often fail to effectively internalize the specific details of previously seen tools, thereby retaining a dependency on in-context documentation. To address these limitations, we propose ParaTool, a framework that projects each tool into a dedicated, loadable set of parameters. By equipping a dynamic integration of these parameterized tools, the LLM can perform tool calling without relying on in-context documents or examples. Specifically, our approach consists of three stages: (1) parametric tool pre-training encapsulates the knowledge of different tools into independent parameter modules; (2) soft tool selection employs a gating network to dynamically weigh and aggregate relevant tool parameters; and (3) parametric tool fine-tuning jointly updates tool parameters to align the training and inference processes. Experiments on Stable ToolBench and BFCL demonstrate that ParaTool significantly outperforms strong ICL-based baselines, achieving superior performance while reducing computational complexity.

paragraphs: Language models commonly receive tool documentation and examples in their context before calling external interfaces. This adds inference overhead, and longer contexts can increase hallucination risks. ParaTool aims to internalize the details of tools in dedicated parameter modules so tool calling does not depend on supplying those documents and examples at inference.

The framework has three stages. Tool pretraining encodes each tool’s knowledge into an independent, loadable parameter module. A gating network then performs soft selection, weighing and combining relevant modules dynamically. Finally, joint fine-tuning updates the tool parameters to bring training and inference behavior into alignment.

Experiments on Stable ToolBench and BFCL show significant improvements over strong in-context-learning baselines while reducing computational complexity. The contribution goes beyond training general tool-use ability: it explicitly represents tool-specific knowledge in modules that the model can integrate as needed. The reported findings support parameterized tool representations as an alternative means of providing the detailed interface knowledge required for successful calls.
summary.tldr: ParaTool stores tool knowledge in dynamically combined parameter modules, improving tool calling while reducing reliance on lengthy in-context documentation.

title: ParaTool: Shifting Tool Representations from Context to Parameters

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at high-level reasoning yet fail on OCR tasks where fine-grained visual details are compromised or misaligned. We identify an overlooked optimization issue in multi-layer feature fusion. Skip pathways introduce direct back-propagation paths from high-level semantic objectives to early visual layers. This mechanism overwrites low-level signals and destabilizes training. To mitigate this gradient interference, we propose Detached Skip-Links, a minimal modification that reuses shallow features in the forward pass while stopping gradients through the skip branch during joint training. This asymmetric design reduces gradient interference, improving stability and convergence without adding learnable parameters. To diagnose whether fine-grained information is preserved and usable by an LLM, we introduce $R$-Probe, which measures pixel-level reconstructability of projected visual tokens using a shallow decoder initialized from the first quarter of the LLM layers. Across multiple ViT backbones and multimodal benchmarks, and at scales up to 7M training samples, our approach consistently improves OCR-centric benchmarks and delivers clear gains on general multimodal tasks.

paragraphs: Reading text in images requires preserving small visual details that high-level semantic reasoning may overlook. The paper identifies a training problem in models that combine features from several visual layers. Skip connections let early visual features reach later processing stages, but they also create direct routes for gradients from semantic objectives to alter those early layers.

Detached Skip-Links retain the useful forward flow of shallow features while stopping gradients through the skip branch during joint training. This separates feature reuse from one source of optimization interference. The modification adds no learnable parameters, and the authors report improved training stability and convergence as low-level visual signals face less disruption.

The paper also introduces R-Probe to test whether projected visual tokens preserve detailed information in a form usable by the language model. A shallow decoder initialized from the first quarter of its layers measures pixel-level reconstruction. Across multiple vision-transformer backbones, multimodal benchmarks, and training scales up to seven million samples, the approach consistently improves OCR-focused results and also benefits general multimodal tasks.
summary.tldr: Detached Skip-Links preserve useful visual features while blocking interfering gradients, improving OCR and broader multimodal performance.

title: Detached Skip-Links and $R$-Probe: Decoupling Feature Aggregation from Gradient Propagation for MLLM OCR

abstract: Most self-supervised learning (SSL) methods learn continuous visual representations by aligning different views of the same input, offering limited control over how information is structured across representation dimensions. In this work, we frame visual self-supervised learning as a discrete communication process between a teacher and a student network, where semantic information is transmitted through a fixed-capacity binary channel. Rather than aligning continuous features, the student predicts multi-label binary messages produced by the teacher. Discrete agreement is enforced through an element-wise binary cross-entropy objective, while a coding-rate regularization term encourages effective utilization of the constrained channel, promoting structured representations. We further show that periodically reinitializing the projection head strengthens this effect by encouraging embeddings that remain predictive across multiple discrete encodings. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over continuous agreement baselines on image classification, retrieval, and dense visual prediction tasks, as well as under domain shift through self-supervised adaptation. Beyond backbone representations, we analyze the learned binary codes and show that they form a compact and informative discrete language, capturing semantic factors reusable across classes.

paragraphs: Visual self-supervised learning often trains representations by aligning continuous features from different views of an image. This paper instead treats learning as communication between teacher and student networks through a binary channel with fixed capacity. The student learns to predict the teacher's multi-label binary messages, making the information exchanged explicitly discrete.

An element-wise binary cross-entropy objective encourages agreement on the message, while coding-rate regularization encourages effective use of the limited channel. Periodically reinitializing the projection head strengthens the effect by encouraging embeddings that remain useful across different discrete encodings. Together, these choices aim to give the learned representation more structure than continuous agreement alone provides.

Experiments report consistent gains over continuous-agreement baselines in image classification, retrieval, and dense visual prediction, as well as adaptation under domain shift. Analysis of the binary messages finds compact, informative codes that capture semantic factors reusable across classes. The findings therefore concern both stronger backbone representations and the structure of the discrete messages used to train them.
summary.tldr: Training a student to predict a teacher's capacity-limited binary messages produces structured visual representations with reported gains across several tasks.

title: Self-Supervised Learning as Discrete Communication

abstract: Machine learning model performance arises from competition and application. For deployment, we consider the prescriptive scaling laws: given a pre-training compute budget, what downstream accuracy is attainable with contemporary post-training practice, and how stable is that mapping as the field evolves? Using large-scale observational evaluations with 5k observational and 2k newly sampled data on model performance, we estimate capability boundaries—high conditional quantiles of benchmark scores as a function of log pre-training FLOPs, via smoothed quantile regression with a monotone, saturating sigmoid parameterization. We validate the temporal reliability by fitting on earlier model generations and evaluating on later releases. Across various tasks, the estimated boundaries are mostly stable, with the exception of math reasoning that exhibits a consistently advancing boundary over time. We then extend our approach to analyze task-dependent saturation and to probe contamination-related shifts on math reasoning tasks. Finally, we introduce an efficient algorithm that recovers near-full-data frontiers using roughly 20% of evaluation budget. Together, our work releases the Proteus-2k, the latest model performance evaluation dataset, and introduces a practical methodology for translating compute budgets into reliable performance expectations and for monitoring when capability boundaries move.

paragraphs: This paper asks what downstream accuracy is attainable for a given pretraining compute budget under contemporary post-training practice. It estimates capability boundaries from observational model evaluations, focusing on high conditional quantiles of benchmark performance. These boundaries describe the stronger observed outcomes associated with compute levels, rather than the performance every model should achieve.

summary.tldr: Observational capability curves are mostly stable across model generations, while math reasoning improves at comparable pretraining compute.

title: Prescriptive Scaling Reveals the Evolution of Language Model Capabilities

abstract: Real-world videos often extend over thousands of frames. Existing generative video super-resolution (VSR) approaches, however, face two persistent challenges when processing long sequences: (1) inefficiency due to the heavy cost of multi-step denoising for full-length sequences; and (2) poor consistency hindered by temporal decomposition that causes artifacts and discontinuities. To break these limits, we propose InfVSR, which reformulates VSR as an autoregressive-one-step-diffusion paradigm, and enables streaming inference with video diffusion priors. First, we adapt the pretrained DiT into a causal structure, maintaining both local and global coherence via rolling KV-cache and joint visual guidance. Second, we distill the diffusion process into a single step efficiently, with patch-wise pixel supervision and cross-chunk distribution matching. To fill the gap in long-form video evaluation, we build a new benchmark tailored for extended sequences and further introduce semantic-level metrics to comprehensively assess temporal consistency. Our method pushes the frontier of long-form VSR, achieves state-of-the-art quality with enhanced semantic consistency, and delivers up to 58x speed-up over existing methods such as MGLD-VSR. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/InfVSR .

paragraphs: Generative video super-resolution becomes difficult on long sequences because repeated denoising is expensive and splitting videos into pieces can introduce discontinuities. InfVSR addresses these problems together by combining autoregressive streaming with one-step diffusion. The aim is to improve video resolution while maintaining coherence across an extended sequence.

The method adapts a pretrained diffusion transformer into a causal architecture. A rolling attention cache and joint visual guidance support local and global consistency as processing proceeds. It then distills the diffusion process into a single step, using patch-level pixel supervision alongside distribution matching across chunks. The training design therefore addresses both reconstructed detail and agreement between successive portions of video.

The authors introduce a benchmark for long-form video and semantic-level measures of temporal consistency. They report state-of-the-art quality, improved semantic consistency, and speedups of up to 58 times over existing approaches such as MGLD-VSR. These are reported experimental outcomes, with the maximum speedup representing the upper end of the stated results. The contribution combines faster generation with evaluation focused on sustained consistency.
summary.tldr: InfVSR combines streaming generation and one-step diffusion to improve long-video super-resolution quality and consistency while reporting up to 58× acceleration.

title: InfVSR: Toward Consistency-Driven Streaming Generative Video Super-Resolution

abstract: Adversarial training breaks down in long-tailed settings, exhibiting severe robustness degradation on worst-performing (often tail) classes. We identify a key cause of this failure as a posterior mismatch: coarse-grained absolute labels collapse class posteriors into point estimates, leading to biased class-frequency estimation and an enlarged robust generalization gap, which ultimately amplifies worst-class vulnerability. To address this issue, we propose Posterior-driven Adversarial Training (PAT), which learns a posterior surrogate to provide fine-grained probabilistic supervision for adversarial training, and integrates weight perturbations to encourage a flatter loss landscape. Our theory shows that accurate posterior approximation simultaneously tightens class-frequency estimation error and robust generalization bounds, while a flat weight loss landscape stabilizes sensitivity to posterior approximation errors. Extensive experiments on long-tailed benchmarks confirm that PAT consistently improves robustness, with especially large gains on worst-class.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can perform poorly when some classes are much rarer than others, with especially weak robustness in the worst-performing classes. The authors identify a key cause in the supervision: absolute class labels collapse richer class probabilities into point estimates. They link this mismatch to biased class-frequency estimation and a larger robust generalization gap.

Posterior-driven Adversarial Training, or PAT, learns a surrogate for those class probabilities and uses it to provide finer-grained supervision. It also perturbs model weights to encourage a flatter loss landscape. These two components address complementary concerns: the quality of the probability estimates and the sensitivity of training to errors in those estimates.

The theory shows that accurate posterior approximation tightens class-frequency estimation error and robust generalization bounds. It also shows how a flat weight-loss landscape stabilizes sensitivity to approximation errors. Experiments on long-tailed benchmarks report consistent robustness improvements, especially for the worst class. The findings support treating probabilistic supervision and stability to its imperfections as related parts of improving adversarial robustness under class imbalance.
summary.tldr: PAT combines learned class-probability supervision with weight perturbations to improve adversarial robustness on imbalanced datasets.

title: Posterior Mismatch Matters: Adversarial Training for Long-Tailed Robustness

abstract: The CLIP model has established itself as a cornerstone of large-scale retrieval systems. However, its performance often degrades under distributional shifts such as multilingual, long-form, or multimodal queries. To avoid the prohibitive costs associated with retriever retraining or corpus re-embedding, we propose GRAPE (Grouped Ranking-Aware Policy Optimization Enhancement), a plug-and-play approach that leverages LLM-based query rewriting to bridge these gaps. Unlike existing methods that lack explicit supervision, GRAPE integrates ranking signals into the rewriting LLM via Grouped Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), ensuring rewritten queries are better aligned with the frozen retriever’s latent distribution. Crucially, we identify a score inflation phenomenon in naive similarity-based finetuning—where irrelevant candidates receive indiscriminately high scores—and mitigate it with a novel corpus-relative ranking-based reward. Extensive experiments across multilingual (Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, XM3600), long-form (Wikipedia), and multimodal (CIRR) benchmarks demonstrate that GRAPE consistently improves performance, achieving an average gain of 4.9% in Recall@10 without any modification to the underlying retriever.The code is available at https://github.com/mogulzhang/GRAPE.
originalAbstract: The CLIP model has established itself as a cornerstone of large-scale retrieval systems. However, its performance often degrades under distributional shifts such as multilingual, long-form, or multimodal queries. To avoid the prohibitive costs associated with retriever retraining or corpus re-embedding, we propose GRAPE (Grouped Ranking-Aware Policy Optimization Enhancement), a plug-and-play approach that leverages LLM-based query rewriting to bridge these gaps. Unlike existing methods that lack explicit supervision, GRAPE integrates ranking signals into the rewriting LLM via Grouped Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), ensuring rewritten queries are better aligned with the frozen retriever’s latent distribution. Crucially, we identify a score inflation phenomenon in naive similarity-based finetuning—where irrelevant candidates receive indiscriminately high scores—and mitigate it with a novel corpus-relative ranking-based reward. Extensive experiments across multilingual (Flickr30k-CN, CVLUE, XM3600), long-form (Wikipedia), and multimodal (CIRR) benchmarks demonstrate that GRAPE consistently improves performance, achieving an average gain of 4.9% in Recall@10 without any modification to the underlying retriever.The code is available at https://github.com/mogulzhang/GRAPE.

paragraphs: A retrieval model can struggle when queries differ from those it handles well, including multilingual, lengthy, or multimodal queries. Updating the retriever or recomputing representations for an entire corpus can be costly. GRAPE instead trains a language model to rewrite queries so that an existing, frozen CLIP retriever can use them more effectively.

The rewriting model learns through Grouped Relative Policy Optimization using retrieval rankings as supervision. The authors identify a problem with rewards based naively on similarity scores: training can raise scores for irrelevant candidates as well as useful ones. GRAPE addresses this score inflation with a corpus-relative ranking reward, directing learning toward the ordering of retrieved candidates rather than indiscriminate score increases.

Experiments cover multilingual, long-form, and multimodal retrieval benchmarks. GRAPE consistently improves performance and reports an average 4.9% gain in Recall@10 without modifying the underlying retriever. The findings support query rewriting as a way to adapt retrieval behavior while preserving the existing model and avoiding corpus re-embedding.
summary.tldr: GRAPE trains query rewriting with corpus-relative ranking rewards, improving retrieval without changing the frozen retriever.

title: GRAPE: Let GRPO Supervise Query Rewriting by Ranking for Retrieval

abstract: Incorporating code into training corpora has become a widely acknowledged practice in the development of modern foundation language models (LMs). Compared with a general Internet corpus, code offers high-quality, well-structured signals that substantially augment the coding proficiency of models. Beyond programming skills, prior research has suggested that code data may also contribute to non-coding capabilities. Nevertheless, through a series of rigorous controlled experiments, we demonstrate that the influence of code on other domains, particularly reasoning, remains limited. Our principal findings are as follows: (1) Code corpus yields substantial gains in programming-related abilities but only competed with knowledge-intensive tasks. (2) We identify a core subset that functions as cognitive scaffolding for mathematical reasoning, especially for complex problem-solving scenarios. (3) Formal reasoning provides more pronounced improvements in challenging mathematical reasoning tasks, while natural language–based reasoning proves more effective for simpler reasoning problems. Finally, by probing the internal mechanisms of LMs, we reveal how training data modulates routing patterns, thereby shaping emergent model behavior. As a central driver of model capability, our findings disentangle domain-specific data into finer-grained, cross-domain ability dimensions and underscore promising directions for future data optimization.
